## I Read the WORST Book of 2026 So You Don’t Have To

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IMk0mNE5cGI>
Caption file: IMk0mNE5cGI.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Story Analysis & Examples
Secondary Topics: Writing Craft, Character, Editing & Revision, Reader Experience & Engagement
Tertiary Topics: Twists & Reveals, Character Development, Overwriting, Thriller, Audience, Sentence Craft, Narrative Voice, Protagonist

I just finished the most disappointing
book I've read all year. Honestly, that
I've read in a long time. And I need to
talk to you about it. Here's what's
wild. It's written by one of the most
popular contemporary authors, Colleen
Hoover. Her books have sold millions of
copies and have massive film
adaptations. But her latest novel,
released earlier this year, Woman Down,
is currently sitting at a sad 3.48
on Goodreads. It's one of her lowest
reviewed novels, even though she has an
incredibly devoted fan base. So, what
the heck went wrong with this novel? As
an editor, I can tell you a lot. Now,
I'm not at all saying that her prior
books were known to be literary
masterpieces. She's a commercial author,
best known for romance and romantic
suspense. And there's absolutely nothing
wrong with commercial fiction. These are
the books that top bestseller charts,
the books that get made into massive
films, and the books that go down easy
like candy on a vacation. That's why
millions of people read them. But in
this particular novel, I was surprised
to notice many of the exact same
mistakes that I see in the manuscripts
that come to me for editing. And I
realized it actually provides some great

thrillers that I'm editing. Woman Down
has two major reveals, and neither of

ending now, so continue watching at your
own risk. Though, I doubt this video has

halfway through the book, so it's
operating as the midpoint twist. Petra

cabin, enjoying her escapades with Saint

## Does It Really Cost $25,000 to Get Published?

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r15y57eBoB8>
Caption file: r15y57eBoB8.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Publishing
Secondary Topics: Editing & Revision, Writer Development, Story Structure
Tertiary Topics: Literary Agents, Query Letters, Writing Conferences, Writing Degrees & MFA, QueryTracker, Developmental Editing, Slush Pile, Audience

An article went viral on Substack
claiming that it costs $25,000
to get a literary agent to read your
manuscript. The price of a used car,
just to have a literary agent look at
your work. Several writers forwarded it
to me asking if it was true, and the
comment section is flooded with people
saying they're giving up on traditional
publishing entirely. And when I read the
claims that this person was making, I
was furious because I spent years
reviewing manuscripts at a top literary
agency and at an imprint of Penguin
Random House, and I can tell you that
most of what this article says is
complete nonsense. So, let's look closer
at what this author is saying and why
they're completely misguided about the
industry because the evidence the author
cites is even more bizarre than the
$25,000 number. The author's core claim
in the article is this: Querying for
free doesn't work. In his words, "If you
try to query for free, you will be
rejected unread. And after you burn
through the small number of agents who
can place in your genre, your book will
be dead." He says that agents fill,
quote, "90% of their slots through
referrals" without giving any actual
hard data on that, of course. And that
to break in without a referral, you have
to pay for one of the following: an MFA,
a fancy writing conference, or editing
services from a professional who will
refer you directly to an agent. I've
heard versions of these claims for
years, and don't worry, we're going to
talk about each one. But first, where is
this wild statement that agents
automatically reject all free queries
coming from? One of my first jobs in the
publishing industry was literally
reviewing queries at a top literary
agency. I was going into the slush pile
every day, and I can promise you I read
every single query. Why would the agents
pay me to do that if they planned to
just reject all the queries without
looking at them? And if If were the
case, why would they even have an open
query inbox in the first place? It's not
like anyone is forcing them to receive
hundreds of emails per week. I was
curious about the evidence the author
had to back his false claim that agents
don't read their queries. And here's
where things get bizarre. He cites a

prove that literary agents don't read

were closed to queries, which, okay, but

bestseller. There was no pitch for a

was not seeking representation. I
wouldn't be caught dead using the query
process in earnest." So, it's crystal
clear why this experiment wouldn't have
gotten any responses. He sent zero
genuine queries. But, the weird part is

## I'm an Editor. Most Writers Get This Key Element Wrong.

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9wnUEIwx9tA>
Caption file: 9wnUEIwx9tA.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Editing & Revision
Secondary Topics: Writing Craft, Reader Experience & Engagement, Scene Craft, Character
Tertiary Topics: Conflict & Stakes, Openings, Character Development, Dialogue, Protagonist, Audience, First Pages, Revision

Your opening chapters aren't boring
because your writing is bad. Nine times
out of 10, the issue is how you're
bringing the reader into your novel's
world. Let me explain. I worked at a top
literary agency and at an imprint of
Penguin Random House before starting my
own editing business, so I've read
hundreds of manuscripts over the years
and I can tell you that exposition, the
way you deliver backstory and setup, is
one of the most misunderstood elements
of writing. Most writers either drown
their reader in exposition or starve
them of it. But finding the right
balance is key to making your opening

scrambled around Pia. She looked
beautiful, but that was never hard for
Pia. Margo caught a glimpse of her own
frizzy hair in the large mirror and
regretted not scrounging up $300 for her
own glam squad. Maybe then she would
have felt better about returning to
Harborside for the first time in 10
years. "Margo!" Finally, Pia turned

with disgust. "That's what you're
wearing? The invite said black tie."

guilt. But, she wouldn't have been able
to afford a new dress anyway, not on top
of the flight from Seattle. "Looks like
the one you wore to prom." Margo
stiffened but kept her face neutral.

little sister win. Prom was the worst
night of Margo's life, the reason she
ran away from this town and from Pia. We
have the same scene and characters here,

wanted to set the scene first to give us
the backdrop for working in the
exposition. We still get the key detail

now it's also indicating how she feels
about being back. I've stripped out all

witch-hunt fear is real and has so many
authors on edge. So, instead of just
blindly trusting the score, I think we
should turn to the text itself and see
if we can spot what others have been
pointing out. I know we can't look at it
totally fresh now because we're already
aware of the AI accusations and may be
looking for those patterns, but let's
break down this passage that has been
widely circulated. Wilfred's rum shop
leaned into the road like a rotten
tooth. Inside, boards blackened by smoke
and sweat, the air sweet with cane and
forgetting. Coins meant for rice or
kerosene slid across the counter and
came back white rum hot as apology. One
drink opened the chest, two turned fear
into courageous cheap cousin, three
studied the hand enough to write the
future in invisible ink. Okay, here's
what struck me as an editor. We have a
simile in the first line, like a rotten
tooth, [snorts]
but I wouldn't necessarily flag that as
AI-generated. The next two lines start
to raise my spidey senses, though. The
air sweet with cane and forgetting.
What does that mean? And how can coins
come back white rum hot as apology? I've
noticed AI likes to try to describe
intangible abstract emotions and
concepts in physical terms. Human
writers do too, of course, but usually
you can trace the logic of their
comparison. AI tends to just throw terms
together in a way that sounds insightful
and lyrical at first, but really means
nothing. We see that describing of the
intangible again in the line, "Two
turned fear into courage's cheap
cousin." I don't really understand that.
The phrase, "Write the future in
invisible ink." also feels empty. Why
must the ink be invisible? And what does
it mean to write the future in this
context? AI also loves to write in
punchy lists of threes, which we see in
that final line that literally counts to
three. Overall, this passage sounds nice
to the ear when you read it,
but the imagery is strained and
collapses under scrutiny. It sounds like
a mimicry of what literary prose should
sound like, rather than prose that is
actually making a point. Here are a few
more contrived, hollow-sounding phrases
that struck me from elsewhere in the
story. "Hard living lays itself on a man
like wet sacking. It never asks
permission. The girl smiled like sunrise
over a sink. She had the kind of walking
that made benches become men." Any one
of these lines on their own maybe
wouldn't raise eyebrows, but one after
the other after the other and the
pattern starts to stand out. At the same
time, there are absolutely human authors
who write in this lyrical, metaphorical
style. So, while I do question if AI was
used to write these passages, it's hard
to make a definitive verdict. Beyond the
pangram score and the prose, there are
two other pieces of evidence that people
have raised in connection with this
story. First is that the author's
headshot published with the story
appears to be AI generated, and second
that he appears to have posted in
support of generative AI on LinkedIn.
Now, you can be an AI enthusiast while
still writing your own creative work.
So, these things don't prove anything,
but they're pieces of the puzzle. I want
to pause here for just a second. I can't
help but notice both this writer, Jamier
Nazir, and Mia Ballard, the author of
Shy Girl, are writers of color. I'm not
suggesting that negates the AI claims,
but any honest conversation about AI in
publishing has to ask who's most likely
to bear the burden of AI accusations,
and who gets the benefit of the doubt
automatically. We need fair systems in
place to handle AI accusations, so
suspicion doesn't fall harder on certain
writers over others, especially those
that already face so many barriers to
getting published. When all of this
evidence came to light, what did the
Commonwealth Foundation and Granta do?
This is honestly the part of this whole
scandal that shocked me the most. Here's
the statement the Director General of
the Commonwealth Foundation made in
response to the allegations. We do not
currently use AI checkers in our judging
process, because this is a prize for
unpublished fiction. To supply
unpublished original work to an AI
checker would raise significant concerns
surrounding consent and artistic
ownership. We also do not use AI to
judge stories at any stage of the
process. As someone who handles writers'
unpublished work for a living, I do
respect this position. You shouldn't
just feed writers' unpublished stories
into AI tools without their knowledge or
consent. And I absolutely would not want
or expect literary judges to use AI in
their selection process. The whole point
of this is that we are humans telling
other humans stories, so outsourcing
those decisions to AI makes no sense and
defeats the purpose. But, the next part
of this statement doesn't at all
mitigate the concerns. All shortlisted
writers have personally stated that no
AI was used, and upon further
consultation, the foundation has
confirmed this. While we acknowledge
there are a growing number of tools that
purport to detect the use of generative
AI in stories, we note that these tools
are not unfailing or infallible. We
therefore believe it is important to
acknowledge and uphold the trust we hold
with our writers. Unlike AI tools, they
can provide backgrounds to the crafting
of their stories and the inspiration and
motivations behind their work. So, the
foundation's final position seems to be
the writers told us they didn't use AI,
we believe them, and that's the end of
that. To me, it leaves a lot to be
desired and feels like a bit of a
cop-out. Then, Granta, the magazine that
published the winning stories, also
essentially just shrugged and wiped
their hands clean of the whole issue. At
the top of each story's page is a
statement saying, "Granta editors were
not involved with these stories or their
selection beyond copy editing them upon
receipt. This year there has been
speculation that some of the stories may
have been at least partially AI
generated. The suggestion that writers
have submitted material not
authentically their own is a charge we
take seriously, but until definite
evidence comes to light, we will keep
these stories on our website." But then,
Granta did something I found completely
bizarre. The publisher of the magazine
released a statement saying that they
took the text of The Serpent and the
Grove and put it into Claude to ask if
it was AI generated. And here's what
happened. The response was long,
concluding that it was almost certainly
not produced unaided by a human. It
ended, however, on a cautious note. "The
strongest evidence against pure AI
authorship is the small number of
passages that don't fit the pattern,
particularly the Zungyi morning greeting
and the agricultural paragraph about the
acre. Those passages carry the kind of
off-shape specificity that models still
struggle to produce unprompted. If the
story has a human core, it is
concentrated there, and the AI has been
used to elaborate around it." So, you're
telling me we have a prestigious
literary magazine using an AI chatbot to
determine if a story they published was
generated with AI, and the Claude
response itself was very odd and
hedging. It said the story was almost
certainly not produced unaided by a
human, which is a clunky way of implying
that AI was used and a human was
involved to some degree. It doesn't say
that a human wrote most of it, and it
even questions if the story has a human
core. If the story is indeed AI
assisted, meaning a blend of human
effort and AI generation, then what
amount of AI use would be considered
acceptable by Granta? None? 30%? 50%?
And if we can't fully trust AI detectors
like Pangram or chatbots like Claude to
give us definitive proof, what would
count as definitive evidence of AI use?
None of this was addressed or answered
in any of the statements. And let me
just say it's really strange to me that
Granta ran the manuscript through AI at
all, especially given the Commonwealth
Foundation's statement that they do not
run manuscripts through AI on principle.
So, apparently once a story is
published, it's fair game to feed it
into AI? What about the Anthropic
lawsuit? What about concerns about it
being used to train LLMs? The internal
logic here is really hard to follow. Are
we okay with any amount of AI assistance
or not? Where do we draw the line? And
what exactly do we use as proof of AI
use? On the burden of proof question,
I'm personally torn because I want to
trust writers to be honest about their
AI use, and I wish we could just ask
them and leave it at that. But,
inevitably, especially after all these
scandals, writers will lie about if
they've used AI because they don't want
to destroy their reputations. Look at
what happened just last week. Nobel
Prize-winning author Olga Tokarczuk
admitted to using AI in her creative
process and faced intense backlash
across social media. No writer wants to
risk sparking that kind of outrage. At
the same time, I'm not sure that AI
detectors are the solution, either. They
are not foolproof, and using them means
that we are essentially admitting we
have no idea how to tell human writing
from AI writing. Which brings me to the
part of this story I find the most
disturbing of all. The more I sit with
this case, the more I think that this
might be the most serious AI reckoning
that publishing has seen yet, even more
than Shy Girl. The Shy Girl outcome was
disappointing, but it ultimately was a
bad business decision. Hachette saw the
book was skyrocketing in sales and
wanted a piece of that pie. They didn't
ask the hard questions about AI use, and
their whole plan collapsed. But this is
something completely different. A panel
of esteemed literary judges, chaired by
an award-winning novelist, read through
nearly 8,000 stories and selected one
that possibly uses AI as the winner of
the prestigious prize. The decision had
nothing to do with business. It was
their view of the quality of the story.
And as far as I can tell, none of the
judges have publicly acknowledged that
they may have praised an AI-generated
story. They claim that what made the
story stand out to them was the author's
writing and voice, which may have all
been generated by AI. Or it may not have
been. We genuinely don't know. But the
fact that we even have to have this
conversation about a story that won a
major prize is what's so unsettling
about all of this. It raises an
extremely uncomfortable question. If
literary judges, whose expert taste
we're supposed to trust are choosing
AI-generated stories over human-written
ones. What does that mean for the future
of literature? Are we reaching the point
where AI-generated prose can pass for
prize-worthy writing? And if it can,
where does that leave the writers who
don't use AI? I've seen tons of posts on
social media this week from writers who
say they feel like giving up. They feel
their creative pursuits are worthless in
an age where they have to compete with
computers. I completely understand how
dystopian and bleak this all feels. But
here's what I want to say to the writers
who are still putting their own blood,
sweat, and tears into their work.
Please, I'm begging you to keep telling
your stories. Because, well, there's no
doubt that AI is going to keep creeping
up into our creative spaces, your
creativity still matters more than it
ever has. I hate seeing writers and
readers and editors and publishers
pitted against one another. The book
community has always been one of the
most genuinely supportive spaces I know,
and it's painful to watch that erode. I
think the only thing that will repair
the broken trust across the industry is
us drawing clear lines and boundaries
around AI use and agreeing on a way to
enforce them. The closest thing we have
so far is the Authors Guild's list of
best practices for AI use, which is a
great start, but it's not enough. Do we
need to be better training ourselves for
how to spot AI tells in writing? Or do
we need to be changing our standards for
high-quality literature in general? That
seems to be what this article in The
Atlantic on the scandal is suggesting.
It will likely get only harder to
definitively prove AI use in writing as
would-be authors get more sophisticated
about it, purging the obvious tells from
their AI-generated drafts, or even
training AI models to imitate literary
authors. Pointing out the ridiculousness
of derivative, soulless writing,
AI-generated or not, might deter writers
from interacting with AI. It also has
the added benefit of maintaining high
collective standards for what real
literature is, at a time when so much of
our language has been colonized by
algorithms and the powerful companies
behind them. What I know is that we need
to protect authors from false
accusations, and we need to protect
readers from being fooled into thinking
AI writing is human writing. And above
all, we need to protect the human art of
storytelling. I know you all must have
strong feelings about this, so tell me
in the comments, how do you think this
short story situation should be handled?
And what do we do about AI in publishing
more generally? If you missed my video
about the writer who used Claude to
generate and publish more than 200
romance novels, watch that one next to
understand the sheer magnitude of this
problem.
Thanks so much for watching and happy
writing.
>> [music]

## I’ve Read 107 Novels That Open Like This. It Never Works.

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bVa4nnf9bwg>
Caption file: bVa4nnf9bwg.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Writing Craft
Secondary Topics: Scene Craft, Character, Story Structure, Editing & Revision
Tertiary Topics: Openings, Character Development, First Pages, Narrative Voice, Protagonist, Literary Agents, Twists & Reveals, Conflict & Stakes

Your opening pages might be the reason
literary agents are rejecting your novel
and readers are abandoning your story
before it even gets going. That's why I
talk about first pages more than any
other topic on my channel, but I keep
seeing writers make this same mistake
over and over. Three of my subscribers
were brave enough to send me the opening
pages of their manuscripts. And what's
wild is that they're writing in totally
different genres for completely
different age categories, and yet all
fall into this same trap. I'll start by
reading all three manuscripts to you and
as I do, I want you to put on your
editor cap and try to spot what the
issue is. Then I'll reveal this mistake
and give examples of how each writer
could revise their manuscript to open
the story much more effectively. You
might catch what all of these
manuscripts have in common pretty
quickly, but understanding why it's a
problem is the thing that most writers
miss. Let's dive into manuscript one,
which is contemporary YA. I think I've
made a mistake. The thought comes out of
nowhere as the plane dips through a wall
of gray clouds. My stomach drops with
it, twisting tighter the lower we go.
For a second, everything feels
suspended. We're hovering somewhere
between leaving and arriving, while my
mind is hovering between it seemed like
a great idea when I booked it and I
should have just stayed home. The cabin
shifts back to life. Seat belts click
into place. Overhead bins creak open and
shut. Passengers rush down the aisle one
last time and babies cry in uneven
bursts as flight attendants move through
the rows collecting empty cups and
crumpled wrappers from lunch. I fasten
my seatbelt and sink deeper into my
seat, trying to steady my breathing. My
chest tightens anyway. In less than an
hour, I'll be in the city I only know
from my grandfather's stories about old
Chevy cars and half-lit cigars, the same
one he left in hope of for a better life
in New York all those years ago. Over a
thousand miles from home, alone, with
nothing but a handful of Spanish words I
picked up in a fluorescent lit classroom
in Brooklyn and my grandfather, before
he died when I was 12. I'll be fine, I
tell myself. It's just a language
course. A month of sun, salsa dancing,
Spanish lessons, and becoming a version
of me who does things like this. But as
the plane dips again deeper into the
clouds, doubt settles in heavier than
before. My hand clenched around my iPod.
A few weeks ago, this seemed like a
desperate escape from the glow of my
laptop screen. I can still see the
Facebook notification that brought my
heart to a halt mid-thump. Leo Ricci is
in a relationship with Sarah Miller. I
spent five years being the girl he
called at 2:00 a.m. The one who held his
place in the cafeteria line. The one who
listened to him play his guitar in his
room while his parents fought in the
other. I thought we were building
something. Apparently, he didn't.
Watching him look at Sarah the way he
used to look at me before he realized I
was just a friend felt like a
slow-motion car crash. I didn't think
too hard when I saw the flyer for a
summer Spanish language course in Havana
pinned to the community center board. I
signed up before the tears in my eyes
could dry, fueled by my grandfather's
stories and a bone-deep exhaustion from
playing the supportive best friend to
the boy I was in love with since middle
school while my own life sat on the
sidelines. I think a part of me knew
that if I didn't put an ocean and a
trade embargo between us, I'd eventually
cave in confess my bottled-up feelings
in a dramatic outburst. The plane jolts
slightly and a soft ding signals that
we're getting closer. Okay, we learn a
lot about the narrator in this opening
scene. She's on her way to Havana to
take a month-long Spanish course, which
she enrolled in spontaneously after
seeing that the best friend she's been
in love with for years is in a new
relationship. We also learn her late
grandfather had ties to Havana and would
tell her stories about it. She has a lot
of internal conflict, which immediately
helps us connect with her. But this
opening isn't quite working and I'll get
to why. Now let's read manuscript two,
which is contemporary middle grade.
Howard and Sasha were going on an
adventure, or so their parents had told
them last Tuesday when they'd announced
the family holiday this year was to
Welkmet on sea. Sasha thought it sounded
suspiciously like being trapped in a car
for four hours with her annoying little
brother. "We're going to the seaside?"
Sasha's mouth turned downwards. The sea
was that salty pool you couldn't swim in
without mom and dad there. "Yep, we've
got a whole week to look forward to."
Howard looked a lot happier. "Awesome,
I'm going to build the biggest sand
castle and it's going to have a moat and
a drawbridge and" his mother and father
gave each other a smile, the same
slightly wobbly smile they'd been giving
each other for a while now. "I have it
on good authority that there's an
excellent fish and chip shop just next
to the inn and there's also spending
money. You two will be completely sick
of ice cream by the end, I guarantee it"
said dad. Sasha rolled her eyes. "But
dad, I wanted to see my friends. How am
I supposed to have any fun at a boring
old inn?" "You'll just have to make your
own fun, miss. There are sand dunes to
explore, there's rock pools at the beach
when the tide's low and there's an
arcade in town if you get really bored,
but you won't." Dad winked at the
rearview mirror. "Humph, fine." She
crossed her arms and huddled up on the
backseat of the car looking like a
miniature storm cloud, a thunderbolt and
all. This writer has a nice handle on
the family dynamics and middle grade
voice. Sasha is doubtful that this trip
will be the adventure her parents are
promising while her brother Howard is
much more excited for it. But again,
this opening isn't doing what it needs
to do. If you haven't spotted the
pattern between manuscripts one and two
yet, this third manuscript will make it
all click. This one is adult
contemporary romance. I wish I'd left
yesterday. But five nights of restless
sleep punctuated by bad dreams about the
town of Augusta fogged my brain,
distracted me from packing. My tour's at
11. As long as nothing bad happens on
the road today, I'll make it on time.
After the second cup of coffee, my heart
pounded in my fingertips with each step
up the three flights to my apartment. I
dragged the last distended trash bag to
the street. The handle of my old cast
iron pan pierces the plastic and clanks
down the last few steps like a bell at a
railroad crossing. At the curb, the
mountain of things I've discarded over
the last few days narrows the downtown
sidewalk. Furniture, old medical
textbooks, my tragically neglected
plants that I hope someone more
nurturing will take. Shadow and I scoot
around it all. Trained for decisive
action, I'm ready to go, but Shadow
needs a little encouragement. After a
few reassuring rakes through the fur at
his neck, he scrambles into the
passenger seat. As we pull away, a peach
dawn glows on the horizon. The saying
goes, "Red sky at dawn, sailor be
warned." Heading to Georgia, a peach sky
seems right. An hour and a half later,
on the two-lane highway, warm air whips
around the interior of the car and over
my skin like a frantic caress. Shadow
sits at attention, panting in the
passenger seat. "You're okay, Shadow." I
pat his leg. He's not a head out the
window, ears flapping sort. The car
stresses him out. His stress mirrors
mine. I've got to call my mother, or
she'll think I'm avoiding her, which I
am. "Evelyn, I haven't seen you in a
while." A pulse blips along my nerves at
the sound of my full name. "You're about
to see a lot more of me. I'm on my way
to Augusta for work." This writer has a
strong sense of voice, and like in the
first manuscript, the narrator
immediately expresses some regret and
internal conflict. We sense something
foreboding awaits her in Augusta, but we
don't know what. Overall, we get much
less detail on the situation at hand
than in the other two manuscripts, but
the writer dangles several interesting
threads. Her old medical textbooks, her
upcoming tour, her actively avoiding her
mother. And yet, this manuscript has the
same problem the other two do. So, what
is this mistake that all three novels
make? And were you able to spot it? They
all open with the protagonist on their
way to where the story actually takes
place, but nothing of substance is
happening to them in the present moment.
Manuscript one opens with the narrator
on a plane descending into Havana.
Manuscript two opens with a family in a
car driving to a seaside town for
vacation. And manuscript three opens
with the narrator cleaning up at her
apartment and then driving on the
highway toward Augusta, Georgia. In all
three cases, we're just watching the
protagonist move from point A to point
B, and the writer is using that
uneventful travel time to provide
backstory and exposition. But that's the
fundamental problem with this approach.
It just gives us setup instead of
actually starting the protagonist's
journey. Rarely are travel periods
exciting in and of themselves. I'm about
to get on a plane tomorrow morning and
plan to sit there for 4 hours and watch
Netflix. So, why would you open your
novel with such a boring scene? When you
open with a character in transit and
they're just reflecting on their life,
you're telling the reader, "I know the
interesting part hasn't started yet, but
just be patient while I catch you up."
And I already know what some of you are
going to say in the comments. "Why are
you so impatient? Why can't you just
enjoy a few pages of setup? This other
novel opens with a character in transit
and it's one of the greatest literary
works of all time. Modern literature is
terrible because of advice like yours."
I get where you're coming from. I really
do, but hear me out. I'm not saying you
can never have a travel scene. I'm just
trying to get you to think seriously
about where your story actually begins.
Because most writers don't take the time
to think about why they're actually
leaning on these types of scenes. When
I'm editing early drafts of manuscripts,
writers almost always start the novel
earlier than they actually should. This
doesn't only happen with travel scenes,
by the way, but those are the most
obvious. Another example is when we open
with the character waking up, going
through their morning routine, then we
see the play-by-play of their entire
work day, all before the important
action begins. Writers start with these
slow scenes because it's typically how
the story comes to them. They're trying
to ground the reader in who the
character is, what their normal life
looks like, and what their primary
concerns are. All of that is valid and
important, but you can still establish
who a character is and what they're
grappling with in the midst of a charged
moment where something consequential is
happening. I promise, if you do this
right, your opening scene is going to be
so much more dynamic, propulsive, and
engaging. And that's how you pull a
reader in from the very first page. So,
rather than starting your novel with
your characters traveling somewhere, try
dropping them at their destination on
page one. Show them in that new location
facing a hostile welcome or an obstacle
they weren't prepared for. You can
almost always start your novel later
than you think you can, and usually your
story will be better for it. There are
always exceptions, by the way, and
opening with a travel scene does not
automatically mean your first page is a
bad. But, if you're going to do that,
something consequential needs to happen
during the journey itself that warrants
showing it on the page. For example, The
Girl on the Train by Paula Hawkins opens
with a transit scene done well. We see
Rachel's daily commute and the
observations she makes during it, but
those observations are important because
they're the engine of the entire plot,
so it makes sense to open with us. But,
for my subscribers' novels, I think the
travel scenes were just being used as
background. So, let's talk about how
these writers could revise to make for a
stronger opening. And it's not as simple
as just cutting the travel scene. By the
way, if you want to submit your
manuscript to me for critique in a
future video, make sure to subscribe to
my newsletter Chapter Break and join the
premium tier. You'll receive weekly
writing insights from me that I don't
post anywhere on this channel, as well
as exclusive interviews with literary
agents and best-selling authors that are
jam-packed with advice for new authors.
Let's go back to manuscript one where we
see the narrator reflecting on the
events that led to her signing up for
the Spanish language course in Havana.
What if this writer instead opened with
the protagonist encountering her very
first problem on the ground in Havana?
Maybe she can't hail a cab because she
can't speak Spanish well enough, which
ties back to her need for taking the
course. Or maybe she's at the doorstep
of her host family and realizes it's the
wrong address. Or maybe she arrives for
her first Spanish lesson and realizes
she doesn't have a textbook that
everyone else does. That way we'll see
that she's overwhelmed and out of her
element without the writer needing to
tell us all of this up front via
exposition. And as we're hooked into the
action of seeing the narrator navigate
this problem, the writer can weave in
the background about her secret love and
her late grandfather's stories. Now,
manuscript two is a middle-grade book,
but the same principle applies. Right
now, the entire opening scene is
essentially logistical exposition
delivered via dialogue. The parents are
explaining what the vacation will be,
Sasha is expressing her doubts that
it'll be any fun, and her brother Howard
is expressing his excitement for it. My
suggestion would be to skip the car ride
entirely and open with the family
arriving at the seaside town. Again,
present that first problem they face on
their vacation. Maybe the inn the
parents booked isn't as it was
advertised and that causes a fight
between them. Or maybe the fish and chip

truly start on page one and that problem

How do each of them react to the
problem? Finally, manuscript three has a

but I still think it would benefit from
a later starting point. As written,
nothing substantial is happening on the
page physically. Evelyn drags trash bags
from her apartment to the curb, then
gets in the car and drives for an hour
and a half. Anytime you have a
substantial time jump like that on the
first page, it may be a sign that you're
taking us through a series of
inconsequential scenes that we don't
really need. These travel preparations
do give us build-up, sure, but they're
ultimately hurting the narrative
momentum and pace. My suggestion is, you
guessed it, to start the novel with her
already in Augusta. We know she's going
there for work, so what happens on her
first day at the job? Or potentially she
runs into a local who creeps her out. It
seems like she's going to see her mother
there, so maybe she could be brought
into the first scene. That way we'll get
to see and experience all of the dread
Evelyn is feeling about Augusta, rather
than just being told about it in
theoretical terms. Figuring out where to
open your novel is one of the hardest,
but most important decisions you'll make
as a writer. If you want a professional
development editor to help you figure
out where your story actually starts,
submit an inquiry through my website.
I've built a team of best-in-class
editors who have worked at the world's
largest publishing houses and top
literary agencies, and we'd love to help
you strengthen your story. Opening with
a character on the way somewhere is
almost always a sign that you're wading
into your story gently instead of
jumping right into it. So, I challenge

your reader will catch up. Here's a
risk-free way to try out a new opening
strategy. Open a brand new blank
document. Don't touch your original
manuscript yet. Then, in the new file,
write the scene where your character
encounters their first real problem.

old manuscript first. I bet you'll find
that you're able to dive right into the
heart of the story with ease. You may
even find it's easier to weave in the
expository and backstory details that
the reader needs. And they likely need
less setup material than you think they

## My Subscribers Sent Me Their Manuscripts…They ALL Make This Mistake

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AHZoqFud44U>
Caption file: AHZoqFud44U.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Editing & Revision
Secondary Topics: Writing Craft, Reader Experience & Engagement, Character, Story Structure
Tertiary Topics: Conflict & Stakes, Character Development, Point of View, Twists & Reveals, Revision, Character Motivation, Dialogue, Narrative Voice

I've been editing books for a decade,
and there's one mistake I see in nearly
half of the manuscripts that cross my
desk, and it's super sneaky because on
the surface, the writing can sound quite
good, but something feels off. You can't
explain why, but you're just not that
invested in the story. It doesn't pull
you in, which means readers might put
your book down, and literary agents
might reject it and move on to the next
in their pile. So, it's critical that
you fix it. Three of my subscribers were
brave enough to send me the opening
pages of their novels, but they all make
this same common mistake. So, first, I'm
going to read through all of them with
you, and as I do, I want you to try to
see if you can spot the issue. Then, I'm
going to reveal what this mistake is and
revise each of the passages, showing you
how to fix this problem. Trust me, once
you can spot this in your own writing,
your story is going to become so much
stronger. All right, so put yourself in
the editor's shoes, and let's read
through manuscript one, which is adult
epic fantasy. Jeran smiled as the
village around him burned. The light
cast by the burning lodges made his
shadow flicker across the twisted body
of the orc chieftain. He sat astride his
massive warhorse at the center of the
village. His eyes moved from the fallen
orc to a human soldier pinned to the
door of the largest structure by a
spear, his feet dangling several inches
above the ground. The door swayed
slightly in the gentle wind. It bumped
against the other body that lay in the
doorway. This one, the chieftain's mate.
The dark tattoos on her face made her
appear even more monstrous in the
firelight. Around him, thick-timbered
buildings sagged and collapsed in on
themselves. Flames raced along rough
oaken beams, consuming the straw from
thatched roofs. Wood creaked as the
structures weakened, and a gout of fire
leapt from a nearby window. Thick smoke
billowed upwards, black against the
fading twilight. Through the gaps in the
smoke, the banners of the empire rose
and fell in the light breeze. A crowned
lion trimmed in gold on a field of
white. He straightened in his saddle at
the sight. The writer really brings us
into the scene here. I can picture the
burning village. The imagery is vivid.
There's a strong sense of atmosphere,
but I'm not feeling that pull to keep
reading. Let's hold that thought and
look at manuscript number two, which is
YA historical fiction. Georgie's bicycle
chain whispered beneath his boots. A
steady whir that almost matched his
breath. The morning was a biter. The raw
North Sea cold gnawed right through his
gloves and made the air taste of iron

familiar rhythm against his hip. A good
weight, important in a way he could feel
with every turn of the pedals. He wasn't
old enough for a proper uniform, the
kind Kitchener's posters shouted about,
but this This was his bit. Danny himself
had written it in his last letter. "Do
something that matters." This counted.
It had to. He pedaled harder, as if
effort alone might make it enough.
Marine Drive curved ahead, slick and
black in the half-light. To his left,
the world was gone, erased by fog. No
gulls cried overhead. Even the surf
below sounded smothered. This is clearly
someone who can write. Again, we have a
strong sense of place with great sensory
details, but it's still missing
something. Now, let's look at the last
manuscript. This one is also adult epic
fantasy. "Damaris." A harsh voice broke
the silence. Young scribe startled.
Damaris hastily brushed aside the river
rocks holding the manuscript on his
desk, allowing it to roll up and fall on
the floor. He left it there as he turned
to see the master scribe striding his
way. The master approached his desk,
glaring. "Damaris, your report was due
hours ago. Where is it?" "It's next on
my list." He picked up another scroll
and waved it at the scribe, whose whole

you'll be removed." Damaris ducked his
head. "Forgive me. I'll work harder, I
promise." The master stalked away with a
look that made all the novices turn back
quickly to their work. I love how we
immediately open with a moment of
conflict between Damaris and the master
scribe. There's tension right off the
bat, which creates narrative momentum,
but I don't think this is the strongest
version of this scene. So, here we have
three completely different stories and
three writers who all clearly have
skill, but where are they all falling
flat? The issue is shallow POV. All
three of these manuscripts are written
in close third person, which means we
are following the perspective of one
character, but none of these passages
are actually bringing us close into the
POV character's mind and body. In

and care about seeing where their

Georgie's interior world remains hidden
from us. Why does this particular
morning matter to him? What is he
working toward? What does he fear? And

action and dialogue. Damaris gets called

we see is what's happening on the
surface of the scene. But what is he
feeling in this moment of conflict? Is
he embarrassed? Enraged? Angry? Scared?
Is he hiding something? We don't know.
Without exploring your POV character's
internal landscape, their thoughts,
feelings, private reactions, and
interpretations, your narrative is going
to feel emotionally distant and flat.
And that's when readers often check out.
They might not even know why. They'll
just think, "The story didn't grab me,"

the scene that you forgot to flesh out
the emotional layer. But once you learn
how to weave in interiority and deepen
the POV, your story is going to become
so much more engaging. We'll naturally
feel more immersed in every scene
because we're experiencing it alongside
the character, and the emotional stakes
will feel so much higher because we'll
understand what they personally stand to

much to them. Shallow POV isn't just an
issue in close third person novels, by

these. You can also have a first-person

not going to get into omniscient POV

before you gripe at me saying, "Well, I

diary," hear me out. Incorporating
interiority doesn't mean dumping every

or adding one revealing gesture. The

But just for the purposes of this video,
I wanted to demonstrate what a deeper

these passages is the best version. It
very likely is not, but it should give

craving more access to the character's

He'd gotten what he deserved. So, here's

This is the biggest scandal to hit the

2025. It's a horror story about a young

pet dog and he'll erase her debt. The

The accountability chain in this whole

would have noticed that major sections

standard for a developmental edit or
even a line edit. As editors, we're

first and foremost, not overwrite it
with our own. We are supposed to guide
authors in the right direction, but we
don't rewrite the book for them. Feeding

At best, it's lazy fake ghostwriting.
And to me, it's just as bad to claim to

author without doing the actual writing.
I'm surprised she didn't have more
questions for this so-called editor when
she received the manuscript back.
Because even if she couldn't immediately

level, the editor is polishing your

overhauling large portions of text. Jane
Friedman says, quote, "Editors are not

I truly believe that AI cannot replace

that editor wasn't the only one who had

about the Hachette editor who acquired

experienced editorial professional
working at one of the biggest publishers
in the world. I've racked my brain

Ultimately, I'm furious that the editor

## How to Tell If Your Writing Is Bad

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M29_fnEQhWI>
Caption file: M29_fnEQhWI.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Writing Craft
Secondary Topics: Reader Experience & Engagement, Character, Scene Craft, Story Structure
Tertiary Topics: Dialogue, Character Development, Narrative Voice, Perfectionism, Pacing, Protagonist, Twists & Reveals, Audience

Over my career, editing hundreds of
novels at a top literary agency, at
Penguin Random House, and through my own
editing business, I'm constantly asked
the same question. Is my writing any
good, or should I just give up now and
find a different hobby? It's a valid
question, but one that's incredibly
difficult to answer, because great
writing is something that you can
immediately see and sense, but it's
difficult to describe. Now, more than a
decade into my career, I've finally
nailed down the single biggest
difference between good writing and
truly great writing. It all comes down
to what the author doesn't say. The best
writers in the world know how to leave
things unsaid, how to let the empty
space between the words do the heavy
lifting. They understand that what's
beneath the surface of a scene is far
more powerful than what's physically on
the page. Ernest Hemingway had a name
for this precise technique, and once I
explain it to you, it will completely
change how you approach your writing.
So, let's break down what this concept
is and why most writers get it wrong,
and then I'll use real examples from
published books so you can see the
difference in action. Let's take your
writing from just good to truly great
together. And who better to learn from
than one of the most acclaimed novelists
from the past century? Hemingway coined
a term called the iceberg theory, also
known as the theory of omission, which
informed his own writing style and
philosophy, and went on to shape modern
fiction at large. He believed that the
text on the page should only contain 1/8
of the actual story, the surface details
like the action and the dialogue, etc.
That's just the tip of the iceberg. And
the remaining 7/8 of the story, the
deeper message, the themes, the
emotional nuances, should be hidden
beneath the surface. So, the majority of
the story is the part of the iceberg
that's sitting beneath the waterline.
All of those elements are, of course,
felt by the reader, but not explicitly
laid out on the page. Now, I'm not sure
I 100% agree with the 1/8 and 7/8
breakdown. Maybe it's closer to
something like 3/8 and 5/8, but I do
think Hemingway's fundamental point
holds. Less really is more when it comes
to fiction. In practice, this means that
instead of explicitly telling the reader
how a character feels, or what theme
your story is exploring, or what they
should take away from a given scene, you
let them pick up on it through the
details you draw their attention to. The
dialogue, the body language, the
imagery, the environment. By far, the
biggest pitfall I see newer writers make
is being too literal, too on the nose.
They spell out every emotion, hit us
over the head with the theme, and don't
trust their reader to pick up on any
nuance. We'll see a heated breakup scene
followed by three paragraphs afterward
where the protagonist reflects on how
furious and heartbroken they are, as if
we couldn't already figure that out from
seeing the scene firsthand. It's
counterintuitive, but the more you
explain something to a reader, an
emotion, a theme, a message, the less
they're actually going to feel it. It's
the same experience as when someone
explains a joke to you. The moment they
start spelling it out word by word, it
stops being funny. Great writing lets
readers feel like they're participating
in the interpretation, but of course,
the author is strategically directing us
to feel and think certain things at
every turn. So, let me show you what the
iceberg theory looks like in real
examples, because seeing the difference
side by side will make it all click for
you. The first example involves one of
the most best-selling, but highly
criticized book series of all time. Love
it or hate it, I want to look at an
excerpt from Twilight. Now, I'm not here
to totally bash Twilight. Those books
were a cultural phenomenon and were read
by millions of people, including me, but
from a craft standpoint, the narration
is incredibly on the nose, especially
when it comes to Bella's emotions.
Throughout the series, Bella tells us
exactly what she's feeling at every
turn. There's absolutely nothing hidden
beneath the surface. Here's a passage
from when Edward, the main love
interest, takes Bella, the narrator, on
a hike. His white shirt was sleeveless,
and he wore it unbuttoned so that the
smooth white skin of his throat flowed
uninterrupted over the marble contours
of his chest. His perfect musculature no
longer merely hinted at behind
concealing clothes. He was too perfect,
I realized with a piercing stab of
despair. There was no way this godlike
creature could be meant for me. She
calls attention to his smooth white skin
and the marble contours of his chest and
his perfect musculature. So, it then
feels repetitive and unnecessary to
declare he was too perfect and call him
a godlike creature, because the reader
already understands that Bella views
Edward in this way from the way that she
observes him. I think this moment would
be far more interesting if Bella
demonstrated how flustered and
overwhelmed she is in his presence, such
as if she trips, or if she notices a
hole in her own old shirt that she's
wearing. Throughout the novel, Bella
expresses her feelings and thoughts very
literally, which I think is what
contributes to her being criticized as a
one-dimensional and superficial-feeling
character. It doesn't feel like there's
that much depth to her or her internal
monologue. So, let's compare that
portrayal of attraction with an excerpt
from Curtis Sittenfeld's romantic
comedy, which is also written in first
person, but leaves so much more white
space. The narrator, Sally, is a sketch
writer for a late-night comedy show, and
she is in a meeting with her colleagues
and the show's next host and musical
guest, who ends up being her love
interest. As Patrick started with an
idea about Trump melting down his gold
toilet to make teeth fillings, I watched
Noah Brewster's cheesily handsome surfer
face watching Patrick, and I continued
to watch Noah's face off and on for
almost 3 hours, because that was how
long pitch meetings lasted. This simple
description of Sally watching Noah's
face is doing so much heavy lifting. We
don't get any internal reflections from
her about how she couldn't take her eyes
off of him, but we understand she's
attracted because she watches him for
the entire duration of the meeting,
which is 3 hours. And that's the iceberg
theory at work. The impact is in what's
not stated explicitly. Both of these
excerpts involved a female narrator
expressing her attraction toward a male
love interest, but the authors handle
them totally differently. In Twilight,
we're told in plain terms about the
attraction, but in romantic comedy, we
are left to infer the attraction. Now,
I'm not saying you should never tell us
how your protagonist is feeling, because
we should feel like we have intimate
access to their minds. But if you want
to elevate your prose, you should try to
illuminate their interiority without
being overly literal or heavy-handed.
Now, this iceberg concept doesn't just
apply to internal reflection. It's
arguably an even bigger issue in
dialogue. So, let's look at another
example from another mega bestseller
that people love to hate, 50 Shades of
Grey. In this scene, the narrator, Anna,
a college student, is interviewing
Christian, a wealthy entrepreneur, for
her school paper. But if you work so
hard, what do you do to chill out? Chill
out? He smiles, revealing perfect white
teeth. I stop breathing. He really is
beautiful. No one should be this
good-looking. Well, to chill out, as you
put it, I sail, I fly, I indulge in
various physical pursuits. He shifts in
his chair. I'm a very wealthy man, Ms.
Steele, and I have expensive and
absorbing hobbies. Now, there are so
many scenes in this book where these
characters' dialogue is cringey, but I
feel like this one is particularly
painful. I'm a very wealthy man, and I
have expensive and absorbing hobbies.
Really? By this point, she's already
painfully aware of his wealth from what
he's wearing, the office environment
that they're in, and their discussion of
his business. And he also literally just
described his hobbies to her as sailing
and flying. Not exactly the blue-collar
man's favorite pastimes. The worst part
is when Christian says this, Anna
doesn't even blink. She just continues
on like that was totally normal. The
reason this dialogue sticks out like a
sore thumb is because in real life,
people rarely talk about themselves so
literally. They deflect. They act fake
humble. Christian could have just subtly
flashed his watch, or he could have said
he's just an average guy when it's
crystal clear he isn't. But no, instead
he just calls it exactly like it is, and
that makes him feel like a caricature.
In great writing, there should be some
kind of gap between what the characters
are saying aloud and what they actually
think and feel. To compare, let's look
at an interview scene from Station
Eleven by Emily St. John Mandel. In this
scene, an entertainment journalist is
interviewing an actor. "You've had
considerable success," Jeevan said, "and
with that comes, of course, a certain
loss of privacy. Is it fair to say that
you find the scrutiny difficult?" Arthur
sighed. He clasped his hands together,
and Jeevan had an impression that he was
gathering his strength. "You know,"
Arthur said clearly and brightly,
playing a new devil-may-care individual
who wouldn't sound in the playback like
he was pale and obviously sleep-deprived
with dark circles under his eyes. "I
just figure that's part of the deal, you
know? We're so lucky to be in this
position, all of us who make our living
as actors, and I find complaints about
invasion of privacy to be disingenuous,
frankly. I mean, let's be real here. We
wanted to be famous, right? It isn't
like we didn't know what we'd be facing
going in. The speech seems to take
something out of him. He wilted visibly
and accepted a new cappuccino from his
publicist with a nod of thanks. An
awkward silence ensued. The conversation
we saw between Anna and Christian was
surface-level and literal. He tells her
outright, "I'm wealthy and have
expensive hobbies." But there are so
many more layers going on in this scene
where what Arthur is saying to Givan

notices that he's sleep deprived and
comments on the dark circles under his

lucky to be in this position of having

complaints about invasion of privacy to
be disingenuous." And claims he knew
what he was getting into with fame. But
as he says this, Givan notices him,
quote, "wilting." Then the awkward
silence that ensues tells us everything
we need to know. That is subtext. That
is the iceberg theory at work in
dialogue. What Arthur is saying aloud is
not at all how he actually feels about
the situation. And the author is
illuminating that to us through the
choreography and Givan's observations.
If Arthur had replied to Givan's
question honestly and straightforwardly,
"Yes, it absolutely sucks to have my
privacy violated and be constantly
scrutinized by the public. I hate it."
The entire scene would fall flat. So
when you write your dialogue, ask
yourself, "What does this character want
to say but can't or won't?" That's going
to make all your conversations feel so
much more raw, authentic, and
emotionally charged. Now let's do an
exercise. Pull up your manuscript and
find a scene in your novel that's
emotionally climactic. Perhaps it's
where the love interests admit their
feelings or the protagonist has to make
a life-changing decision or the family
has a blowout fight. Read through it
line by line and highlight every
sentence where you're over-explaining
the character's thoughts or being too
literal. Now delete those lines. Read
the scene back without them. I bet it
lands even stronger now. Nine times out
of 10, the scene was already doing the
work. You just had to get out of the
way. By the way, if you want an expert

about creating negative space in your

it. Because the most powerful moments in

of their craft. My favorite thing about

## The Plot Trick Every Bestselling Author Knows (That No One Teaches)

why are non-linear timelines so
powerful? The answer requires doing

readers' shoes. When you tell a story
chronologically, "This happened, then
this happened, then this happened,"
you're relying on the events themselves
being exciting enough to keep a reader
interested. You need each event to build

bigger and bigger and bigger. And that

when you throw out the typical
chronological structure, you do
something totally different and unlock
new creative possibilities. To
understand why it works so well, first

psychological principle that keeps
readers hooked in a story. Ultimately,
as humans, we crave closure more than

left unfinished. In fact, I'm thinking
about the dirty dishes sitting in my
sink right now. So, what should you do
as an author to give your reader no
choice but to continue turning the
pages? You withhold closure. You
engineer questions in the reader's mind
that they desperately want to see
answered. I go into more detail about
the psychology behind page-turning
stories in this video, so check it out
if you haven't already. Every effective
story relies on this fundamental
principle, but non-linear timelines take

brain desperately wants to close and
resolve. Let me show you what I mean. I
could write a novel about two friends

in two years? That immediately
establishes a question. What happened
between them? Then when you cut to the
flashback scenes of their trips where
things are going great, we'll naturally
want to keep reading to see where things
go wrong. This example isn't
hypothetical by the way. If you don't
know what novel I'm referencing yet,
just wait. Non-linear storytelling works
because you're not just narrating the
story beat by beat. You're giving the

will not rest until all the pieces fit
together. So now that we understand
reader psychology, let's break down how
Emily Henry uses non-linear storytelling
in her number one New York Times
best-seller, People We Meet on Vacation,
which is now also a Netflix film.
Because what she's doing is not as
simple as just jumping back and forth in
time. Yes, the novel does alternate
between two timelines. The present where
best friends Alex and Poppy haven't
spoken for two years after a disastrous
vacation, and the past where we see
their friendship and their romantic
tension evolve over years of vacations
together. But the real genius behind
Emily Henry's non-linear storytelling
here is that she essentially has two
will-they-won't-they storylines
operating simultaneously. In the
present, we know something terrible
happened between them, but we don't know
what it is. That's the central mystery
driving us through the book, and we
desperately want to resolve it and see

timeline, we're watching two people who
clearly belong together grow closer and
closer, knowing that their future selves
will mess it all up. Every single
chapter, in both the past and the
present, works toward the same question:
Will they find their way back to each
other? Now, if the author had told the
story chronologically, where we see each
of their vacations in order, the story
would likely be fine, but it would lose
its spark. It would be so much harder to
pull the reader all the way to that
climactic moment where their friendship
breaks, because she would have to
engineer other conflicts along the way
to keep us engaged. By alternating
timelines, the author keeps us hooked
from the start. Those happy vacation
chapters are tainted by our knowledge
that everything goes south, and we're
watching for cracks in the relationship
to form. We are unable to stop reading
until the full picture emerges. And
that's the difference between a good

If your story involves a pivotal event

follow the tried and true chronological

I personally love dual timeline novels

prologue philosophy. I know a lot of you
think I'm entirely anti-p prologue, but
I promise you I'm not. If a prologue is
accomplishing the core goal of the
opening pages, pulling us in and making
us desperate to read more, then it's
great. The problem is that most
prologues aren't doing that. Remember
that by design, a prologue is delaying
our arrival at the actual story. So, you
have to ensure that delay is warranted
and is doing important work. Here are
some of the biggest mistakes I see
writers make with prologues. First, the
prologue just becomes an info dump. A
prologue is not the place to dump your
world building, backstory, or historical
context. This happens especially
frequently in sci-fi, fantasy, and
historical novels. If your prologue is
starting to read like a textbook, you
need to rethink it. All of that
exposition needs to be woven organically
into the action of the main narrative,
not front-loaded all at once in a long
passage. That's a surefire way to make
your reader check out. The second
mistake is making the prologue way too
long. When a reader sees the word
prologue, they know that they're in for
an adjacent section, not the main story
yet. So, their attention isn't fully
locked in. They may even be tempted to
skim or skip it entirely. So, then if
your prologue runs 10, 15, 20 pages, we
start to wonder, when are we getting to
the real story? Keep your prologue as
short as possible. I personally think
the sweet spot is between 2 to four
pages max. Most successful prologues
follow just one single impressionistic
scene. If your prologue starts dragging
on, think about what part is really
important to show at the beginning of
the story. Focus on just that one single
moment. Now, the third prologue mistake
is the worst one, making it impossible
to follow. Some writers think that being
mysterious and cryptic in the prologue
will intrigue the reader. But I promise
you, a reader who is confused is not
intrigued. They're frustrated. Your
prologue should be impactful, not
incomprehensible. That doesn't mean you
can't present questions. You certainly
should, but don't leave us so
disoriented that we have no idea what we
just read. Give us enough concrete
details to latch on to. As the story
progresses, we should start to piece
together how the prologue relates to the
main narrative, which we can't do if the
prologue is just a bunch of vague
descriptions. If you're doubting whether
to include a prologue or not, ask
yourself, does the prologue make the
reader desperate to turn to chapter 1?
If your answer is anything less than a
resounding yes, you should probably cut
it. Now, let's put these three
manuscripts to the test and see if the
prologue is drawing us in or pushing us
away. This first manuscript is an adult
thriller. The taste of vomit hung rancid
in her mouth, but it was a distraction
from the mindless blur that suffocated
her every thought. Now, in this first
line, the imagery feels a little bit
clunky and confusing. I might streamline
it to something like the taste of vomit
distracted her from the suffocating
brain fog. But let's keep going. Cars
flashed by the road ahead. A modeled
gray serpent pulling her forward more
than any deliberate intention. The
crack, the shattered glass, the blood.
She was almost unconscious to the world
around her. Just continued south. We get
the first beat of physical action with
just continued south. and I sense that
she's in a car because we mentioned the
road ahead and the crack in the
shattered glass. She glanced at the
phone on the seat beside her. It was
still off. She was isolated. What was
ahead was inevitable as her scars had
been inevitable each one. Now, that line
is very vague. We have no sense of what
is ahead for her or what her scars are
referring to. So, while it sounds nice,
it's really not telling us anything at
all. I really wish we got a few more
grounding concrete details about her
situation. 60 mi from London, but out of
reach anywhere. The car park was
deserted. She stopped, turned off the
engine. A sign in front of her, cliff
edge. The lettering barely visible in
the fading light. She stared at it, her
hands hung on the wheel. In time, she
picked up her phone, looking into the
blank screen, then turned it on. Missed
calls, 8, 9, 10, probably more. All from
the only person who cared. Jess stepped
out into the biting wind above beachy
head. The last of the light was settling
over the sea, casting long, bruised
shadows across the chalk cliffs. 500 ft
below, the channel's waves crashed
rhythmically against the rocks. There's
some nice description there. A monument
to war stood behind her, a stone
sentinel watching over her. She had been
at war for so long. There's another
vague line that hints at her backstory
without giving us any concrete detail.
Of course, we don't want an info dump of
her entire life history. That would
totally bog down the opening. But just a
few well-placed hints will go a long way
toward helping us connect with her. She
walked to the verge of the grass where
the land simply stopped. She sat down,
drawing her knees to her chest, rocking
gently. There was a piece here, a
serenity she hadn't found in the noise
of London, in the heat of the
Philippines, or on the hills of
Tuskanyany. She closed her eyes. The
gargoyle was dead, but the abyss was
ahead. Here's another vague line that I
don't know how to interpret. What is the
gargoyle referring to? And what exactly
is this abyss that she sees ahead? We
understand there's internal conflict for
her, but we have no idea what it's all
about. She took her phone from her
pocket. Her thumb hovered over the
screen, trembling, her only lifeline,
him. She typed, "Can you call?" She
pressed send. That's the end of the
prologue. I do wonder why she doesn't
just call this person rather than text
him asking her to call, but that's kind
of a minor detail. I do like that this
prologue takes place in one contained
singular scene, but I feel like it is
veering into that third mistake of not
giving us enough concrete detail and
really just disorienting us more than
anything. I want to see where this story
goes in chapter 1 and maybe we'll get
some answers. Chapter 1. Dat Pula the
Philippines one year earlier. Jess woke
before the alarm. The sheets were
crumpled at the foot of her bed. She
stared at the ceiling limbs spled. The
fan above hummed. It's dustladen blades
barely disturbing the thick morning air.
So now we're flashing back one year
earlier. So the prologue is really a
flash forward, which is a common
technique, especially in suspense. But I
don't love the scene that the author has
chosen to open this on because it's
falling into one of the common cliches,
which is opening with a character waking
up. Unless there's something really
exciting or special about that moment of
them waking up, usually it's better to
open the novel at a different point in
their day where there's more meaningful
action happening. So, let's see where
this goes. The smells and noises from
the street below drifted through the lou
of windows open in the hope a breeze
might shift the morass that hung like
tepid soup in her room. Tepid soup is an
unexpected image there that I kind of
like. How the hell does anyone sleep
like this? She murmured to herself. At
least Syria was dry. She looked at the
bedside clock. Dust filled the slots
along its top. The time limped to 6:00
a.m. Jess flopped her hand onto the
clock, silencing the alarm before its
shrill. She had to get going. She moaned
as she rolled over. She slowly swung her
legs over the edge of the bed, pushing
herself upright. The wooden floor was
warm. She yawned, then rad her hand from
her head down the back of her neck. Her
hand slipped on the sweat, falling
listlessly to her side. I'm starting to
feel like we're really just going
through the motions of just waking up,
touching the alarm, rolling out of bed,
and it's all just contributing to a
really slow opening. If I skim down a
bit, it seems like quite quickly,
actually, we flash back to Wednesday,
earlier that week, and it looks like
Jess is arriving via a taxi to her
hotel. That leads me to wonder, why do
we need this scene of her waking up
later in the week at all? Why not just
open the novel with this scene here and
have this be chapter one where she's
arriving at the hotel via her taxi? This
feels like a more dynamic and
interesting entry point to the main
narrative than her waking up and all of
that slow action that we got on the
first page. But let's go back to the
prologue for a second. Based on the
genre and what I've seen, I do think a
flashforward style prologue could work
well for this story. However, that
technique works the best if the prologue
teases the climax of the story, the
point where the protagonist is at their
lowest point or facing their biggest
confrontation or in a moment of serious
danger. But what we had in the prologue
was something else. Jess was clearly
distressed and upset, but she wasn't in
any immediate danger. There wasn't any
urgent threat bearing down on her that
we could sense. As a result, we didn't
get that strong sense of urgency or
momentum from the prologue. Part of the
issue is also that the author didn't
give us enough breadcrumbs to really
latch on to her circumstances or her
situation, so we couldn't feel the
weight of it. I'd advise that this
author cuts the first part of chapter 1
and begins the main narrative with Jess
arriving at the hotel and then
reconsider if that prologue is
necessary. if they do want to include a
flash-forward prologue, consider making
it a more action-packed, dynamic,
consequential, high stakes scene than
the one that they chose. Before we get
into the next manuscript, if you want to
submit your pages for critique in a
future video, subscribe to my
newsletter, Chapter Breakak. I extend
these submission opportunities to my
premium subscribers who get a ton of
exclusive writing and publishing
resources from me delivered straight to
their inbox. Okay, now let's dive into
the second manuscript, which is adult
epic fantasy. Music sounds simple when
passing the ear. Only a fool thinks
flesh hears true. The cut of a knife
pierces nothing but the skin. Like a
stone skimming water without troubling
the deep. The ache of despair lives
beneath the waves with its cousins. The
rush of joy and the breath of hope. So
she'd been told. This opening paragraph
sounds very lyrical and is beautifully

how we're meant to interpret it.
Especially the line, "The ache of
despair lives beneath the waves with its

of hope. I'm not entirely sure what
comment the author is trying to make
about music here, so I'm starting off

This point about her being deaf to the
call of their song seems important, but
I'm not entirely sure whose song we're
referring to, and if it's a literal

the forest, the shade of a beach
replacing the roof of her home. Okay, so
now we've arrived at our first beat of

was in the fullness of its bloom. The

too long in the sun. The phrasing here
makes it unclear if we're describing the

simile like stars that sat too long in

the petals as a harpest might, one who
knew the tenderness of things. She tried
to recall her teaching. Resonance of
felos, she whispered to herself. Oh yes,
fourth dietonicamic cadence. Minor
melodic. Come on now. She calibrated her
breathing and stroked the flower to the
rhythm of footsteps. Feet that turned to
a task, not turned away. She sounded her
mind to her secret ear and let her soul

happened. She reached harder for the

appeared to shuffle in its spot like a

steadied on its beat. the cadence
proceeding like a drum. She summoned a
faint rising of a melody in her mind.
The note, a hum she heard inside. She
clutched at it. Okay, so I'm starting to
understand that she's using the daffodil
to recall some kind of song, but I don't
understand her motivations for doing so,
or why she's potentially having trouble
with this task. We are told she's trying
to recall her teaching, but we don't
really know what that teaching entails.
We get a reference to her secret ear
which seems to be a world specific
element that we don't quite have enough
yet to contextualize. The petals began
to dance. The grass swayed in the
windless calm. She looked at a fallen
leaf and lent it her secret ear. With a

arm. She smiled and then began to laugh.
A laugh that ran barefoot through the
air and splashed in a summer stream. I
think in general this prologue and maybe
the manuscript at large could benefit
from some pairing back of the figurative
language and imagery, it is beautifully
written, but we don't always need quite
so much of it. Because when you have so
many images layered on top of each
other, you start to obscure your
meaning, which I feel like could be
happening here, especially because we're
in a fantastical world already, it
starts to become more difficult to make
sense of what's physically happening
when you have so much imagery. I've done
it, she thought. Yet, as she did, the
leaf veered off its course. It plunged

saddened. Then she heard something more.
Remember your tuning, dear? She turned
round, her eyes rolling, to see a tall
woman standing poised, her dark hair
undone. You rushed it again, her mother
continued with that real smile mothers
make. How did you find me? Oh, Stella,
her mother sighed. You are ever
wandering off like an elusive answer.
Stella frowned. But you've caught me,
her mother laughed. No, you are like the
wind. I just know which way you blow.
Stella hung her head in shame at her
mother. Her face was a burning hearth.
Her arms outstretched as an open door.
We don't quite understand what's at
stake for Stella here. Why is it such a
big deal that her mother caught her
practicing her teaching, whatever that
entails? It's great that we see her hang
her head in shame and feel embarrassed,
but we have no context for why this
would be an embarrassing thing. So, it's
difficult for us to really register the
significance of this moment. "That must
be a nice thing to know," she muttered
sadly. Her mother kept the silence for
as long as could be afforded. "Come on,"
she finally said, gesturing to Stella to
go with her. "You'll be late again. The
harmonium won't take more excuses." "But
I'm practicing," Stella protested, and
instantly she hated the sound of her
girlish plea. Her mother nodded,
tutting. "Learn first, practice after."
Stella huffed. She stroked the pedals
once more, hoping they might come with
her. As she skipped off, she turned
around, hoping they might be dancing to
the rhythm of her feet. When she
arrived, she listened again, hoping the
world might hear her trying. There are
certainly a lot of compelling elements
in this prologue scene, but the layers
of imagery and the lack of context
prevent us from really latching on to
what Stella is trying to do and what's
getting in her way. Now, I want to take
a brief look at the start of chapter 1
to see if we can maybe start to make
sense of what was going on in that
prologue. We have part one with two
epigraphs and then chapter one, whispers
at dusk. The sky is getting darker, Luke
coughed, adjusting his mask. He squinted
south where the dust was beginning to
cloak the horizon. We have an hour at
most before that fs us. What would you
know about effing? Croked Mouthus,
continuing to maul the ground with his
shovel? Have your balls even dropped,
lad? Luke knew better by now than to
raise the bait. He was the youngest in
the syndicate, 20, taller than most, and
already hauling more ammonium than
veterans twice his age. But none of that
spared him Mothus daily reminder.
Skiak's no place for a boy. Okay, so we
have quite a dramatic tone and content
shift here from the prologue, which
isn't necessarily a bad thing, but
should be noted. This chapter feels so
much more concrete and grounds us in
place and action right away. We meet
Luke, who is a young man doing manual
labor outside. It seems he is trying to
get more of this resource ammonium and
he's getting teased by his colleagues.
There is immediate conflict established
which is intensified a little bit later
on when his colleague mentions that
they're short on their quota which
immediately establishes some kind of
urgency and stakes. So, while the
prologue came in at just the right
length at under two pages, and it did
just follow one singular scene, I
honestly felt more gripped by this scene
with Luke than that prologue scene.
There are two key issues that prevent
this particular prologue from being
effective. First, the scene feels quite
low stakes. We don't understand exactly
what Stella is practicing, what it means
to her, or what's at risk with her being
late for the harmonium. On first read,
the scene almost feels peaceful, even
dreamy with all of the lyrical imagery.
Remember that in your opening pages,
whether they are a prologue or not a
prologue, you want some source of
conflict to establish momentum and
narrative urgency. But the second
problem with this prologue is the bigger
one. The tone and content are so
disconnected from what we see in the
main story line that it feels quite
jarring. Now, readers will completely
understand that your prologue is
operating independently to your main
story line, taking place in a different
time, place, even following a different
POV. That's all fine, but there should
be some continuity through to the main
narrative that we can begin to perceive.
Whether that's through the characters,
the setting, or the theme. If you're
trying to query literary agents, this
disconnect becomes a problem because
presumably in your query letter, you're
going to describe the main story line,
but then when they get to your sample
pages, they're going to see something
else entirely that doesn't seem like it
relates to that story you described at
all. It'll potentially feel like a bait
and switch, which I worry could be the
case here. So, for this manuscript, I'd
probably suggest cutting the prologue
and letting Stella and whatever she was
doing emerge in the story naturally
whenever it becomes relevant and instead
opening with the scene of Luke at work,
especially if he's the main character
we'll be following for the rest of the
story. That scene feels much more
immersive, grounded, and higher stakes
given the conflict that's established.
Now, let's take a look at the last
manuscript, which is an adult thriller.

## If You Want to Publish a Book in 2026, Watch This

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=52B2LDxxKuY>
