These are the five trends dominating
book publishing in 2026 that every
writer needs to know because if you
don't, you're threatening your book's
success. I analyzed 40 book deals for
debut authors that were announced over
the last month to determine how the book
market is shifting and I was genuinely
surprised by what I found even though
I've been in this business for a decade.
I'll share the five biggest book trends
that we're seeing in 2026 and at the end
I'll answer the burning question, is
traditional publishing even worth
pursuing as a debut author today? This
first trend showed up in nearly all of
the book deals I analyzed and it's
completely reshaping what gets
published. Genre blending. Publishers
are obsessed with genre mashups right
now. The data proves it. 75% of the book
deals that were announced since January
1st for debut authors involve stories
that blend two or more genres and here's
what's especially fascinating. Romance
is almost always in the equation. We're
seeing romance mixed with horror,
romance with historical fiction, romance
with suspense, and even romance with
supernatural thriller elements. This
trend suggests that publishers aren't as
interested in straightforward stories
that check all the typical genre boxes.
They want stories that give readers
multiple experiences in one book and
they want to see unexpected concepts
thrown together. For instance, one book
was pitched as Gilmore Girls meets
Scream. Another was described as a nerdy
friends-to-lovers rom-com that involves
a high-stakes heist. There was also a
book described as My Roommate is a
Vampire meets Netflix's Wednesday set on
a college campus. These books aren't
just being pitched as romance with a
touch of mystery. They're fully
integrated genre blends where both
elements are equally important to the
story. Why do publishers want these
genre hybrids so much? Genre blending
solves a key problem in today's
extremely crowded and saturated market.
Differentiation. When you put two
unexpected genres or comp titles
together, you immediately pique interest
and demonstrate what sets your story
apart. Plus, it means that the book will
automatically appeal to multiple reader
bases. Why do you think romantasy has
blown up so much in the past few years?
It scratches the fantasy itch, the
romance itch, and has become its own
booming genre entirely. So, if your book
doesn't fit neatly into one genre box,
don't try to force it. Instead, lean
into the mashup. Figure out your X meets
Y pitch and use it to your advantage.
This next trend is the secret ingredient
publishers are using to get readers
addicted to their books, and you should
too. Suspense engines. I was stunned to
see that nearly 40% of the book deals
reported for debut authors this year,
across all genres, included some
mystery, thriller, or suspense elements,
even if they weren't primarily pitched
as one of those genres. There was a
speculative historical thriller in the
vein of Sherlock Holmes, a dark academia
thriller, a darkly humorous murder
mystery, even a horror novel where PTA
moms start mysteriously vanishing.
Publishers have figured out that
suspense is one of the most reliable
ways to achieve that page-turning
quality that keeps readers up until 3:00
a.m. to finish the book. That's exactly
why suspense-driven movies like The
Housemaid and TV shows like All Her
Fault are so popular. And yes, both were
based on books. So, how can you add a
suspense engine to your story? The key
is to plant unanswered questions that
readers desperately want answered. This
could be a missing person, a mystery
from the past that's impacting the
present, or even just a looming threat
that's slowly closing in on your
characters. One deal I saw followed a
woman who was searching for the son she
gave up for adoption. And even though
that book wasn't primarily labeled a
mystery or a thriller, that is the
suspense engine that fuels the story.
The suspense in your story doesn't have
to be life-or-death stakes. It just has
to make readers ask, what happens next?
What's the truth? How is this going to
resolve? This next trend might make you
reconsider where your story takes place.
Transportive settings. One in four of
the debut book deals announced this year
so far involved non-US settings with
European settings being especially
popular. And nearly one in five were set
in historical periods. It seems that
publishers are betting that readers want
to be transported to some place
dramatically different from their
present lives. We're seeing books set in
1949 Paris, 16th century England, 1990s
Nigeria, a boarding school in the
Berkshires in 1969. But here's what
makes these settings so powerful.
They're not just window dressings.
They're integral to the plot. Take the
book set in 1949 Paris, which follows a
journalist's wife who finds a body at
her culinary school. The post-war Paris
setting allows her to explore the
complicated truth about Franco-American
relations at the time. In the book set
in 1990s Nigeria, a young girl navigates
the complicated dynamics between her
mother and her father's mistress. The
turbulent political backdrop of that
specific time and place is essential to
the story's themes of independence and
agency. If you're setting your story in
a different time or place, make sure
that it's for a reason beyond it seems
cool. Ask yourself, how does my setting
inform my character's choices and
identities? What conflicts are unique to
this particular time and place? What can
I explore here that I can't in a
contemporary American setting? If you're
not familiar with your setting
personally, make sure to thoroughly
research it so it comes across as fully
developed and authentic. Now, this next
trend signals a shift in whose stories
are being told. Broader representation.
We're seeing an exciting expansion in
the types of characters who are put
front and center in fiction. As I looked
at this year's debut book deals, two
patterns emerged when it came to
representation. The first older female
protagonists. These aren't wise
grandmothers in the background, but main
characters living full and complex
lives. One book follows a fiery
septuagenarian widow who has a dating
app romance. Another features a
71-year-old widow who impulsively buys a
camper van and goes on a road trip to
find her long-lost first love. These
stories aren't about aging entirely.
They're stories where the protagonists
just happen to be older, but are
pursuing adventures that are just as
exciting as those of 20-somethings. This
matters because it expands the pool of
readers who can see themselves in the
books they see on the shelf. And
commercially, publishers are recognizing
that older female readers have
significant buying power and are hungry
for stories that reflect their
experiences. The other major
representation trend is stories that
center queer characters rather than
leave them on the periphery. There was a
contemporary gay rom-com set in Beijing,
a queer Edwardian romance about a
bisexual jewel thief, a historical
mystery with a sapphic subplot set in
16th century England, and a literary
novel exploring queer desire in a black
Pentecostal church. What I love about
these stories is that they don't seem to
be focusing primarily on the queer
character's trauma or struggles with
identity. Many of them are genre novels,
romances, or mysteries where the
characters just happen to be queer. If
you're writing older or queer
characters, don't be afraid to let them
exist in genre fiction. Let them have
adventures beyond their identities. Now,
this next trend was the most interesting
to me because it tells us what themes
are resonating right now. The dark side
of domestic life. Publishers are leaning
hard into stories that explore the
horror and dysfunction in our home and
family lives. Two specific themes rose
to the surface. The first, motherhood as
horror. In my analysis, I noticed two
book deals being pitched as for fans of
Night which is a novel and now a
film starring Amy Adams where a mother
believes that she's turning into a dog.
These stories don't romanticize or
glorify the experience of modern
motherhood, but rather examine mothers'
quiet rage, sacrifice, and psychological
unraveling. They're shining a light on
the ugly, difficult, but undeniable
parts of one of life's most profound
experiences. Now, let's talk about the
second theme. Marriages being pushed to
their breaking point. One of the book
deals from this year a woman trying to
have a smooth divorce, but then facing
brutal legal battles and accusations of
adultery. Another is about a marriage of
convenience between a cafe owner and a
hotel executive. There's even a novel
about a newly engaged couple whose
relationship unravels when they house
sit in a remote location. All of these
books examine the gap between the
idealized version of domestic life we're
sold, a happy marriage, a perfect
family, suburban bliss, and the messy,
sometimes horrifying reality. So, if
you're writing about family, marriage,
or parenthood, don't be afraid to show
the dark sides. The market is clearly
ready for stories that expose the
uncomfortable truths that we all see and
experience, but keep quiet. Now, I know
what you might be thinking. These trends
are great and all, but it's simply
impossible to get a book deal as a debut
author. Publishers only want books from
established bestsellers or celebrities.
So, why does any of this even matter?
Here's what honestly shocked me the most
out of all the analysis I did. The data
proves that publishers are actively
investing, sometimes competitively, in
debut voices. Of all the debut book
deals that were reported so far this
year, 40% were sold in preemps and 25%
went to auction. Let me explain what
these industry terms mean and why they
matter. A preempt is when a publisher
makes an offer so strong that the agent
and author accept it before shopping the
book to other publishers. And an auction
means that multiple publishers were
bidding against one another to try to
acquire the book. So many of these books
being sold in preemps and at auctions
means that there is a ton of demand for
strong debut fiction. Publishers aren't
just casually buying these books.
They're paying more so that no other
publisher has the chance to scoop it up.
And in some cases, publishers are
fighting over these books. Here's
another encouraging stat. 1/3 of these
book deals were for two or three books,
meaning that publishers are investing in
debut authors as franchises. They're
betting on these authors' long-term
potential, not just acquiring a single
book. So, if you're a debut author who
dreams of getting traditionally
published this year, it absolutely still
is a viable path. But know that it does
remain highly, highly competitive. I've
anecdotally seen agents report that
they've received more queries than ever
this year. So do your best to position
your book strategically so it stands
out. And most importantly, make sure
that you're crafting the absolute best
version of your story possible. Your
story concept is super important, but it
ultimately doesn't matter if the writing
falls flat. If your book aligns with any
of these trends I identified, I hope you
use it to your advantage this year. But
if it doesn't, don't panic. Trends
shift, and there will always be room for
exceptionally told stories regardless of
whether they fit the current market. Now
that you know where publishing is
heading this year, you need to craft a
stellar query letter that catches
attention. So, watch this video where I

unlocked new possibilities. By writing a

your writing life. You start thinking,

I've achieved this. Whatever the next

## 7 Dialogue Mistakes That Make Your Story Unreadable

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bWe2Y3KNx9o>
Caption file: bWe2Y3KNx9o.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Writing Craft
Secondary Topics: Reader Experience & Engagement, Story Structure, Character, Scene Craft
Tertiary Topics: Dialogue, Conflict & Stakes, Character Development, Narrative Voice, Audience, Plot, Revision, Sentence Craft

I've edited hundreds of novels and
there's one thing that will ruin an
otherwise incredible story. Bad
dialogue. I see it happen all the time.
A story will have captivating
characters, an action-packed plot, but
the dialogue will be over-the-top,
unrealistic, cringy, or impossible to
follow. So, today I'm breaking down the
seven biggest dialogue mistakes that
sabotage your story and showing you
exactly how to fix them so your
characters sound real. Let's start with
the mistake that I bet you'll find at
least once in your manuscript. Talking
heads. This happens when your dialogue
takes up the entirety of the page.
There's nothing going on in the scene
except the dialogue. No reflection, no
action. You essentially just have
floating voices. When dialogue exists in
a vacuum like this, it's really hard to
keep the reader engaged and immersed in
the story. Here's what talking heads
looks like. Did you hear about the
breakup? Yeah, I feel horrible for Lucy.
We should have seen it coming. Too late
now. Should we reach out to her? I think
she left the city. Who's saying what?
Where are they? And what are they doing
physically while they have this
conversation? How do they feel about the
breakup? We don't know anything other
than what's being said aloud. But what
your characters are saying aloud to one
another is only 50% of everything that's
actually going on in the scene. You need
to include beats of physical action and
narrative reflection from your POV
character to fill in that other 50%.
Because without those emotional and
physical anchors, readers won't know how
to interpret what's being said. "Here's
one way to revise this passage to fix
the talking heads." "Did you hear about
the breakup?" Sam asked, setting his
coffee mug on the counter. "Yeah, I feel
horrible for Lucy." Jared recalled his
conversation with her last month where
she was buzzing about a proposal before
the end of the year. "This one would
take a while to get over. We should have
seen it coming. Too late now." Jared
took Sam's empty mug and began washing
it in the sink. Truth be told, he wasn't
all that surprised. He'd caught Warren
eyeing the waitress on their double
dates more than once. Should we reach
out to her? Sam's voice went up in pitch
at the end, the way it always did when
he was worked up about something, like
when he asked Jared to dispose of the
dead mouse he found last weekend. I
think she left the city. By adding a few
physical beats and narrative reflection
from our POV character, Jared. We learn
so much more about this situation and
about the characters. We know that Lucy
told Jared that she was expecting to get
engaged, which amplifies the impact of
the breakup. We also learned that Jared
had anticipated the breakup based on how
he had observed Warren act in the past.
We even get a detail about Sam in the
line about the pitch of his voice going
up, which helps us understand his
personality. The easiest way to avoid
talking heads is to make sure we stay
closely connected to the POV character's
mind throughout every dialogue exchange.
Make sure to show us how they're
externally and internally reacting to
the major points that are made in the
conversation. This next mistake is my
biggest pet peeve as an editor. Name
dropping. When you're speaking face tof
face to someone, how often do you say

frequently. Certainly not in every
sentence. So, why do characters do this

Hey, Mike, did you send the contract?
Sarah tried to keep her voice calm.
Yeah, Sarah, I emailed it this morning.
Thanks, Mike. You're the best. She

like this, they sound like robots.
Usually, writers do this when they're
trying to clarify who's saying what, but
just use dialogue tags, which will be
invisible to the reader when done right.
This technique, on the other hand, is
very visible and distracting. Your

dialogue tags and action beats will do

just so the reader can overhear it. It's

Let's look at an example and you'll

Here's a revised version. Kira and Lord

gate. She could see the outlines of

next mistake will turn your layered,

Here's what melodrama might look like.
How could you? She shrieked, tears
streaming down her face. You were the
only one I ever trusted. I can't believe
I wasted 10 years on you. Don't make me
say it again, he shouted, throwing his
dinner plate on the floor. It was just a
business meeting. Between
[clears throat] the shrieking, shouting,
tears streaming, plates being thrown,
and three exclamation points, this
exchange is a 10 out of 10 on the drama
scale. And when characters act like
caricatures like this, readers will
check out. It's totally fine to have
dramatic moments and emotional

remember that you can convey tension

Here's how you could revise this

tension. How could you? She said, tears
welling up. You were the only one I ever

years on you. He pushed back from the

And we can change those exclamation

entirely. Too many dialogue tags.
Dialogue tags are how you indicate to
the reader who's saying what. But with
dialogue tags, a little goes a long way.
Most commonly, you will use he said, she
said, wherever you need to clarify who's
speaking. But some writers go overboard

that, Judy exclaimed. Why not? Jake

killed, she retorted. She obviously

Your first page is arguably the most
important in your entire novel. It's
where the reader or a literary agent
makes a crucial decision. Do I keep
reading or do I put this down? When I'm
editing author's manuscripts, we spend
more time workshopping the first page
than any other part of the novel. It has
to pull the reader in and give them no
choice but to turn to the next page and
the next and the next. But that's much
easier said than done. And how do you
know if your first page is working? From
editing hundreds of novels over my
career, including New York Times
bestsellers, I've created a foolproof
formula to nail your first page. I'll
reveal the four critical elements every
first page needs. And then I'll review
real manuscripts submitted by all of you
to see if they pass my first page test.
The first element I look for serves as
the story's emotional anchor, the
person. In almost all cases, we should
meet an important character on the first
page, typically the protagonist. But
your first page has to do more than just
mention this character. You have to make
us feel something about them. Curiosity,
empathy, excitement. The question I'm
really asking on the first page is this.
Am I interested in following this
character for the rest of the book? Do I
want to learn more about them? If the
answer is no, then you'll lose me. You
definitely won't have room to give us
your entire character's life story on
page one, but you should give us a
glimpse of their worldview, personality,
or emotional landscape. That might show
up in a surprising observation they
make, a snarky internal reaction, or a
line of dialogue that displays their
voice. Show us a spark of their humanity
that makes them feel real and unique.
Even one specific, vivid moment on page
one will go a long way to kickstart our
emotional connection to them. The second
element involves how the story is being

Your pros is how you build your trust

## The 7 Most Common Plots Ranked From Worst to Best

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kww_Gj_QleA>
Caption file: Kww_Gj_QleA.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Story Structure
Secondary Topics: Character, Reader Experience & Engagement, Genre, Story Analysis & Examples
Tertiary Topics: Plot, Character Development, Protagonist, Conflict & Stakes, Antagonist & Villains, Genre, Book Covers, Thriller

It turns out we've been telling the same
seven stories for thousands of years,
and we're somehow still not tired of
them. According to Christopher Booker's
narrative theory of the seven basic
plots, nearly every story will fit into
one of just seven categories. I'm an
editor who's worked on hundreds of books
over my career. So, I've seen these
seven plots over and over and over
again. Today, I'm going to define each
one of them, give you some contemporary
examples, and the fun part, rank them
from worst to best in my opinion. Let's
figure out which plot your story fits
into, and if you agree with my rankings,
quick note, many stories will be a blend
of multiple plots, so don't worry if
your story doesn't fit neatly into just
one category. Without further ado,
coming in last place is a pick that
might be controversial, The Voyage and
Return. This is a story where the
protagonist ventures into a strange,
unfamiliar world. In it, they face
hardship and challenges that force them
to grow and change, and then they've
come home transformed. This plot goes
way, way back. Homer's Odyssey is the
quintessential ancient example, and a
perfect contemporary example would be
The Hobbit. Bilbo must leave the comfort
and safety of his hobbit hole in the
Shire to join 13 dwarves on a quest to
reclaim their homeland and its treasure.
After facing trolls, goblins, giant
spiders, the dragon smow, and his own
moral dilemmas, he returns back home,
forever changed by the journey. Just
like the name says, he voyages and he
returns. All the plots we'll go over
today can apply to any genre, but some
are more well suited to certain genres
over others. The voyage and return plot
is especially common in fantasy and
sci-fi stories because you are pushing
your protagonist into a new world that
they must navigate. So, why did I rank
it last? Don't get me wrong, I don't at
all hate The Hobbit or hate this
plotline in general. It can be
incredibly emotionally moving when done
well. But to me personally, it can
sometimes feel a bit overly simplistic,
and the arc is so familiar that it can
be stale and predictable. You don't want
the reader to feel like the voyage is
dragging on and on and on without any
payoff. If you have this type of story,
I'd recommend complicating the return
part of it rather than your protagonist
being welcomed home with open arms. What
if their homeland has changed beyond
recognition? or perhaps they can't
return home, forcing them to reckon with
their sense of belonging even after what
they thought was the hard part of their
journey is over. We see a version of
this in The Hobbit where Bilbo's family
presumed he was dead and is selling off
his belongings, which makes his return
bittersweet. The next plot in my ranking
is one that you'll recognize from many
fairy tales, Rags to Riches. You might
think you know this plot in and out.
After all, it's all in the name. But
riches in this case doesn't actually
have to be financial. In this plot, the
protagonist starts off downtrodden or
struggling in some way. Yes, they could
be financially insecure, but they could
also be a misfit at school, in their
job, or in their social circle. Then
they acquire the thing that they want,
whether that's wealth or power or love.
Typically, they'll come to a point where
they lose or nearly lose everything that
they've gained before earning it back. A
great contemporary example of this plot
is Slum Dog Millionaire where a boy from
the slums of Mumbai wins a game show and
reunites with the girl he loves. The
reason this plot has endured is because
we love rooting for the underdog. We
probably all feel like underdogs in some
capacity. So, we want to see someone
beat the odds, especially when they're
stacked against them unjustly. The rags
to riches structure pops up all the time
in coming of age novels, family dramas,
and romances especially. So, why did I
rank it so low on my list? Because
sometimes the characters acquisition of
their riches can feel a bit unbelievable
and far-fetched. And sometimes putting
so much emphasis on their external
material gains neglects exploring the
deeper internal layers of their story
that also need attention. So, if you're
writing this type of story, make sure
that your character earns their rise.
And once they get there, show us how it
tests them. What new problems arise for
them now that they've gotten what
they've always wanted? Do they even
start to regret it? I'm a huge believer
that strong writers don't just know
sentence level craft, but also
storytelling mechanics at large. But how
do you learn something as complex and
nuanced as storytelling? There's
actually a platform you can join to do
exactly that. Skillshare, who was kind
enough to sponsor today's video.
Skillshare has an entire library of
classes dedicated to creative writing,
including this storytelling 101 class I
took from Daniel Jose Older, who's a New
York Times best-selling author and a
lead story architect for the Star Wars:
The High Republic series. It felt like
having my own personal writing mentor.
And hearing how an expert approaches and
conceptualizes things like character
building and conflict allowed me to
sharpen my own storytelling skills and
vocabulary that I can bring to my work
with authors. Skillshare's creative
classes are taught by amazing
world-class creatives, including the
authors behind some of your favorite
books. If you're ready to level up as a
storyteller, this might be the boost you
need to finally complete your manuscript
with clarity and confidence. Great news.
The first 500 people to use the link in
the description or scan this QR code
will receive a 1 month free trial of
Skillshare plus 20% off their first
payment. This offer is only available
for a limited time, so get started today
and let me know what story you end up
working on. This next plot is a classic,
especially in sci-fi and fantasy epics.
The quest. In this type of story, the
hero receives some call to adventure,
gathers his allies, and then must
navigate treacherous terrain to achieve
some kind of goal, whether it's to
retrieve a specific object or get to a
particular location. Along the way, the
group faces many trials, setbacks, and
temptations. For a textbook example of a
quest plot, let's look at Percy Jackson
and the Olympians: The Lightning Thief.
Percy discovers he's a demigod, then
gets blamed for stealing Zeus's
lightning bolt. He and his friends must
retrieve it and discover who the true
thief is to prevent war from breaking
out. The stakes couldn't be higher, and
the hero has a clear mission with a
ticking clock. This combination means
that quest storylines are often
naturally propulsive, but the reason
they aren't ranked higher on my personal
list is because they can sometimes fall
into the trap of prioritizing plot at
the expense of character. The focus
naturally falls on what's happening
externally. Everything the hero needs to
find, fight, and survive. But the most
successful quest novels also take care
to develop the hero's internal journey.
Sometimes I also find that quest plots
have a large ensemble of characters,
sidekicks, secondary characters, villain
after villain after villain, which can
lead to the story feeling overcrowded
and scattered. So, if you're writing a
quest story, look out for opportunities
to streamline and make sure that each
and every character earns their place.
This next plot plays into our primal
human need to see conflict play out,
overcoming the monster. In this plot,
the protagonist must confront a powerful
threatening force. Sometimes a literal
monster, sometimes a symbolic one. The
monster could be a dangerous creature,
an oppressive system, a villain, or even
nature itself. What I love about
overcoming the monster plots is that
they automatically have two key elements
of effective storytelling. High stakes
and conflict. There is clearly something
on the line for the protagonist, and
there will be severe consequences if
they don't win their battle against the
literal or figurative monster. One
example of this plot that you might not
automatically think of is The Martian.
In this story, an astronaut wakes up on
Mars completely alone and has to find a
way to survive the unthinkable
conditions. You might be thinking, "But
wait, where's the monster?" There isn't
a physical one in this story because
Mars itself serves as the monster. The
astronaut has to use his scientific
skills and ingenuity to survive the
harshest conditions. The brutal climate,
the lack of resources, the complete and
utter loneliness. The best overcoming
the monster plots don't just feature a
black and white good versus evil
dynamic, but force the protagonist to
face their own flaws, fears, and moral
conflicts. The monster holds up a
mirror, revealing to the hero what they
must overcome within themsel to win the
fight. Now, on to my top three favorite
plots. The next one is often
misunderstood. Comedy. Comedies in the
context of these seven basic plots
aren't really about being laugh out loud
funny. They're about chaos, confusion,
misunderstanding. After a lot of drama,
the truth spills out, the protagonist
finds clarity, and we get a happy
ending. Most romances would be
considered comedies, as would some women
fiction. We often see tension between
family members or loved ones spiraling
into mayhem and building up an emotional
crescendo where relationships reach
their breaking point. Then in the end,
we get a satisfying reconciliation. One
of my favorite contemporary romcoms is
Crazy Rich Asians. In it, an economics
professor travels with her boyfriend to
Singapore to attend a wedding, where she
discovers he and his family are
incredibly wealthy. His mother
vehemently disapproves of their
relationship, and she must navigate the
pressures of his community, culture, and
family. Comedies are often funny, yes,
but they're also full of heart and
emotional truth. They reflect real life
chaos and how messy our relationships
can be. And then they deliver the thing
we all crave in our own lives,
resolution and joy. They're your classic
feel-good stories, the ones you know
will warm your heart, and sometimes we
all need a dose of that. My second most
favorite plot might not be one that
immediately comes to mind, but it's
extremely powerful. Rebirth. This plot
is all about internal transformation.
The protagonist experiences a series of
events that force them to undergo
profound change, to let go of who they
were and be reborn as someone new
entirely. The events of the story force
them into an entirely new worldview,
perspective, or sense of self. These
stories speak to our universal desire to
start over, to shed old versions of
ourselves and evolve for the better.
What I love most about The Rebirth plot
is that it doesn't just rely on external
action. It focuses on the protagonist's
inward journey. And as a
character-driven reader, I'm always
looking to emotionally connect with the
protagonist. This plot can be applied to
any genre, but is perhaps most prominent
in coming of age stories and memoirs. A
good example would be the breakout
memoir, Educated. The author, Tara
Westover, grew up in an isolated
survivalist family and was denied a
formal education. The memoir details her
journey to pursue education on her own,
eventually going on to receive a PhD
from Cambridge. As she disentangles
herself from her family and reclaims
agency, she is reborn and paves a new
life for herself. Rebirth stories like
this ask, "What does the protagonist
have to lose to become who they're meant
to be?" And finally, we've reached my
number one pick. It's my favorite type
of story because it sits with you long
after you finish reading. Tragedy. As a
lover of thrillers, it's only natural
that I would pick the darkest type of
plot as my top choice. In a tragedy, the
protagonist is brought down by their own
flaws. There's no triumphant ending. We
see them fall from grace where they're
forced to live with the dark
consequences of their choices. Tragedies
are so powerful because they offer
catharsis. They build up our emotions.
Then the devastating conclusion releases
all our pent up pity and fear that we
feel for the characters. There's
something strangely comforting in
watching characters fall. It reminds us
that we're not alone in our own
failures. At the same time, tragedies
invite us to probe into the parts of
ourselves we don't always want to see.
As such, they tend to match up with
darker genres like thrillers,
psychological suspense, and horror.
Frankenstein is a perfect example of a
tragedy and is one of my absolute
favorite novels. It's also top of mind
as I just watched the Guode del Toro
rendition, which was incredible. Victor
Frankenstein is completely undone by his
own ambition to create life. At first,
he presents as a brilliant scientist,
but quickly his passion project spirals
into obsession and madness. And then,
when he realizes the creature he created
is out of his control, the damage
becomes irreversible. He loses his loved
ones and his sanity. Both the creator
and the creation are left emotionally
devastated. Tragedies often play out our
worst case scenarios. They promise an
unhappy ending and leave us sitting in
the wreckage asking what it all meant.
And those uncomfortable questions are
exactly what make them so unforgettable

## My Top 10 Tips for Aspiring Authors

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tu3J4QkbZ7I>
Caption file: Tu3J4QkbZ7I.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Publishing
Secondary Topics: Writing Craft, Editing & Revision, Story Structure, Reader Experience & Engagement
Tertiary Topics: Literary Agents, Feedback, Sentence Craft, Publishing Industry, Revision, Book Covers, Book Deals, Character Development

When I was fresh out of college, about
to start my first publishing job at
Penguin Random House, I knew my passion
was helping authors share their stories
with the world. But I had no idea just
how hard it was to be a debut author,
how hard it was to write, let alone
revise an entire book, how hard it was
to get traditionally published. Fast
forward to now, I've worked with
hundreds of authors on their books,
including New York Times bestsellers.
So, here are my top 10 tips for aspiring
authors who want to see their book on
the shelf one day, including some hard
truths you might not want to hear, but
need to. This first tip will completely
transform how you think about good
writing. Work on your story as much as
your sentences. Most new authors equate
good writing with beautiful pros, poetic
metaphors, lyrical turns of phrase,
surprising imagery. All of that is
important, of course, but if your goal
is to have people actually read your
book, it doesn't matter how pretty your
sentences are if they don't actually add
up to anything and tell a good story.
Once I started working as a
developmental book editor, I became less
interested in the beauty of individual
sentences and more interested in the
mechanics of effective storytelling. How
to maintain narrative momentum, how to
develop a strong character arc, how to
deliver emotional impact. Think of the
story as the foundation of your book.
The sentences are the rugs, the
wallpaper, the furnishings. But
beautiful decor doesn't matter if the
floor is collapsing beneath it. Now, the
flip side is also true. A solid
structure will feel empty and lifeless
without some style and furnishings. And
even if you have the best plot in the
world, if your writing doesn't hold up,
the story will feel bland. You need both
a strong story foundation and strong
sentence level craft to create a truly
engaging book. So, as you're drafting
your manuscript, ask yourself, am I
spending as much time developing and
refining the story as I am the pros?
This next point might hit too close to
home, but it's probably the one you need
to hear the most. Identify your
procrastination traps. Many aspiring
authors fail not because they don't have
the talent or the ability, but because
they spend their time doing everything
else except for the thing that actually
matters most, writing. I see it all the
time. endlessly tweaking your author
website, designing mock book covers,
getting lost in book talk drama. And
hey, as much as I love that you're here
right now, you might be doing it in this
very moment, watching writing advice
YouTube videos instead of actually
writing. You can do all of these things,
of course, but not at the expense of
actually getting your draft done. There
is, sadly, only one way to finish a
novel. Sit your butt in the chair and
put your fingers on the keys. I have
this friend who's allegedly been working
on a book for literally 10 years. He
keeps promising me that it's coming.
It's coming and I haven't seen any of
it. I'm honestly not convinced he's
written even a full chapter. If that
sounds like you, it's time to look at
where your energy is really going. You
don't need to write every day because
that doesn't work for every writer, but
find a writing schedule that works for
you and stick to it. Procrastination
wears many clever disguises, so identify
yours and snap out of them. Then go
write the dang book. This next tip is so
simple, but you'd be surprised how many
authors skip it. Go to the bookstore. I
talked to so many aspiring authors who
admit they haven't actually read a novel
since they were required to read in high
school or college, and then they say
there's no point in picking up a book
now because they don't want it to
influence their writing, which really
sounds to me like a bit of a lazy
excuse. Sure, avoiding reading of all
kind is a fine approach if you intend to
write only for yourself and never get
published. But if you want to see your
book on the shelf one day, you should
know what's already on that shelf. So
next time you're out and about, stop by
your local bookstore, go to the section
of the store where your book would one
day live. Pick up a book that came out
recently within the past 10 years by a
living author. Bonus points if it's a
debut author. Buy it and then read it.
Not only will this give you a sense of
what your future readers are enjoying
today, but reading is one of the
absolute best ways to improve your own
craft. It'll help you internalize story
structure, pacing, character, and style
in a way that no craft advice can. I'm
not at all saying that you should copy
what's already being published out there
or write to specific trends, but you
should know what the publishing
landscape is like if you intend to bring
your own voice into it. As someone who
reads for a living, I know how hard it
can be to carve out time for pleasure
reading, especially when you have a
million other things on your plate. Two
of my favorite tips for fitting reading
into a busy schedule is to read for 10
minutes just before bed instead of
scrolling on your phone. Or to listen to
audiobooks while you're cleaning,
cooking, or walking the dog. Yes, I do
believe that listening to audiobooks
counts as reading. Reading is going to
make you such a stronger writer, and
it's not even going to feel like work.
This next tip is a brutal one, but it's
the one that separates wannabe authors
from the ones who make it. Pick up the
axe. No book is perfect on the first
draft. No, not even from your favorite
best-selling author. When writers are
just starting out, they often treat
their draft like it's sacred, like no
word can be changed. But if you want to
craft the best possible story, you need
to be willing to break it down and tear
it apart to build it back up stronger.
This is the work that I love doing as a
developmental editor, but I'm not going
to sugarcoat it. It's not easy and
sometimes it hurts. Sometimes you have
to remove scenes or characters or plot
lines that you personally love.
Sometimes, yes, you have to make an edit
that changes every single scene. That's
not because the work you did in the
first draft was bad. It's just that it
was step one in the process of bringing
the strongest version of this story to
life. Great stories aren't written.
They're rewritten. often rewritten many
times. So, the sooner you can stop being
precious with your manuscript, the
sooner you can learn to kill your
darlings, the sooner that you can learn
to embrace the revision process, the
better off you'll be. I promise that
you're going to love your book so much
more once you're willing to take the axe
to it, even if it feels bad in the
moment. This next tip will save you a
lot of disappointment. Don't let the
wrong people read it. Sharing your book
with someone is an incredibly
vulnerable, scary act. So, it makes
sense that new authors often turn to the
people they trust the most first. Your
best friend, your partner, your mom.
But, it's actually very rarely the case
that these are the right people to give
you the feedback that you need at this
point. They can't be objective. They
know how hard you've worked on this
project, so they're likely going to
shield you from their most honest
opinions because they don't want to hurt
your feelings or damage your
relationship. So, they often end up
giving you vague praise that is at best
not helpful and at worst gives you a
false sense of security. What you need
at this point isn't for someone to give
you a pat on the back, but for someone
to give you real actionable feedback
that will make your story better. So, be
incredibly thoughtful and selective in
who you ask for feedback. The quality of
the feedback always matters more than
the quantity. Ask, "Does this person
have a background in writing or editing?
Do they read avidly in my genre and
understand what I'm trying to accomplish
with my book? Do they have the ability
to give me honest, constructive
feedback?" And before you hand your
manuscript over to anyone, ask yourself,
am I really ready to receive critique on
this book? If you'd like transformative
feedback on your story from some of the
best-in-class editors who have worked in
the publishing industry, go to my
website, allymatessic.com, and tell me
about your book. This next tip sounds
counterintuitive, but it's actually your
secret weapon when you get stuck. Walk
away from your story. You've been
grinding away at your draft late at
night for weeks now. You've reread your
draft 10 times now and just feel
overwhelmed by the revision process.
When you are this deep in your story,
you simply can't see the forest from the
trees. You're still likely seeing the
book you intended to write, not what you
actually put down on the page. You're
blind to all of the issues and gaps that
readers will notice quickly. So, when
you're down with a bad case of writer's
block, or you're feeling paralyzed by
the revision process, here's what I want
you to do. Take a break from your
project. There's actually science behind
why a break is so productive and
necessary. It activates a different part
of your brain and allows you to
creatively problem solve when you return
to your project. I promise you're going
to have so much more clarity after you
get some distance from your book. So,
the best thing you can do after you
finish your draft is to let it sit for
at least a week, but several weeks is
even better. Take this time to do
something else entirely and refill your
creative well. Read something new, make

beginning right. When a reader or a
literary agent picks up your book, the
first few pages are everything. It's
where they decide, "Is this worth my
time? Do I want to keep turning the
pages?" I spend more time helping

other part of their manuscripts. The
first pages are so important that I've
been doing a series where I workshop the
openings of novels submitted by all of
you. Those pages need to spark curiosity
in the reader. We need to care about
seeing where the story goes. There needs
to be a sense of momentum propelling us
into the next scene and the next scene
and the next scene. But too often those
first pages are bogged down by backstory

tension or conflict. You can't ask the

The truth is that you're probably not
going to get the opening right on the
first draft. That's totally okay. But
once your draft is complete, go back to
that first chapter. Ask, "Is this really
the right place to begin my story? Do I
plant enough curiosity seeds for the
reader? Do I give them a reason to

into your book. Give the reader no
choice but to accept it. This next tip
is for all of you who are considering
submitting your book to literary agents
or publishers. Don't jump the gun. I get
it. You've finished your draft and
you're excited to take the next steps.
You're starting to envision a book deal,
your book launch party, your book on the
shelf. But querying literary agents too
soon is the biggest mistake I see
authors make when they're trying to get
traditionally published. That's because
your draft probably isn't ready yet. And
once a literary agent passes on your
manuscript, that door is very hard to
reopen. Remember that publishing is not
a race. And there is so much more for

is really ready. You should ideally have
gone through several drafts, including
developmental revisions, before sending
your manuscript out to literary agents.

competitive and agents are looking for
manuscripts that are polished and nearly
ready to send to publishers. It's the
same reason why turnkey houses are
easier to sell than fixer uppers. So,
take the time to go through several
meaningful rounds of thoughtful edits,
get feedback, and make sure to take a
break from your manuscript so you can

publishing process is going to test your
patience. It's slower than any of us
would like, but if it's your dream, take
the time to give your book the best
shot. This last tip is what will enable
you to keep going even when the
publishing process gets you down.
Practice getting rejected. Every writer
you admire has been rejected most, many
times over. So, it's going to happen to
you, too. You'll get bad reviews. You'll
get passed up for awards and bestseller
lists. If you traditionally publish,
you'll get rejected by literary agents
and then by publishers. and it's going
to sting, at least at first. No matter
how many times you hear, "Don't take it

to you. This is your book. But rejection
will become easier to deal with if you
practice not letting it phase you. So,
try facing rejection in small, contained
ways that feel lower stakes. Maybe you

game. You're putting yourself out there

are my final words for you. Writing a
book will be one of the hardest things
you ever do, but also likely one of the
most rewarding. And I hope you'll carry
some of these tips with you as your

and they all fall into one of four

Maybe she's a hardened New Yorker who

Sure, Celia was a native New Yorker and

The ticket agent whistled from behind

In one fluid motion, she grabbed the

## No, You Probably Shouldn’t Write Omniscient Narration. Here’s Why.

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NJGAYA7FgpM>
Caption file: NJGAYA7FgpM.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Writing Craft
Secondary Topics: Reader Experience & Engagement, Genre, Character, Scene Craft
Tertiary Topics: Narrative Voice, Character Development, Point of View, Genre, Audience, Dialogue, Perfectionism, Thriller

The majority of novels published
throughout history were written in third
person. So why are so many aspiring
fiction writers today getting it wrong?
I've edited hundreds of novels,
including New York Times bestsellers. So
today, I'm breaking down the five
biggest mistakes you might be making if
you're writing in third person,
including sneaky ones you think you're
avoiding. The POV shapes your entire
story, so you need to get it right, or
else you'll be facing a huge rewrite.
Most of the issues I see with third
person happen because amateur writers
misunderstand the difference between
omnisient narration and close third
person. Even if you think you understand
the difference, listen up. Because if
you think you're writing one but are
actually writing the other, you'll
confuse your reader, lose their trust,
and end up having to rewrite every
scene. I'm not trying to sound alarmist,
but POV is that important. And a lot of
you think you're writing omnisient POV
when you actually aren't or you
shouldn't be. So, let's set the record
straight. Omnisient narration is when
you have a godlike narrator who hovers
over the story and understands
everything that's going on from a bird's
eyee perspective, including each
character's individual thoughts. This is
what a lot of people miss. The omnisient
narrator actually acts as their own
character and has their own commentary
on things that the characters don't know
about. This is the hallmark of
successful omnisient narration. We
should feel the presence of the narrator
throughout every scene mediating the
events of the story. Close third person,
also called limited third person or deep
third person, is when we only have
access to one character's head at a
time. We are experiencing the story from
inside their mind and therefore only
know what they know at any given moment.
Their observations, their thoughts,
their reactions. Think of the difference
as a drone camera showing you the entire
landscape from overhead and one of those
new smart glasses that records exactly
what you're seeing. Omnisient narration
is still used by authors today, but it
was actually more common decades ago.
So, you'll see many classic and
canonical authors writing in it. In
contemporary fiction published today,
close third person is more common. So,
now let's test your POV knowledge. I've
taken excerpts from two recently
published novels that are written in
third person, and let's see if we can
spot the POV difference. Here's the
first example, which is The Midnight
Library by Matt Heg. 27 hours before she
decided to die, Norah Seed sat on her
dilapidated sofa, scrolling through
other people's happy lives, waiting for
something to happen. And then out of
nowhere, something actually did.
Someone, for whatever peculiar reason,
rang her doorbell. She wondered for a
moment if she shouldn't get the door at
all. She was, after all, already in her
night clothes, even when it was only
9:00 p.m., she felt self-conscious about
her oversized ecoarrior t-shirt and her
tartan pajama bottoms. She put on her
slippers to be slightly more civilized
and discovered that the person at the
door was a man, and one she recognized.
He was tall and gangly and boyish, with
a kind face, but his eyes were sharp and
bright, like they could see through
things. It was good to see him, if a
little surprising, especially as he was
wearing sports gear and he looked hot
and sweaty despite the cold, rainy
weather. The juxtaposition between them
made her feel even more slovenly than
she had done 5 seconds earlier. So, what
do you think? Omnisient or close third
person. This passage is written in close
third person because we're tightly
aligned to what Nora is experiencing in
the moment. In the very first line, we
get the insight that Nora is sitting on
her sofa waiting for something to
happen. Verbs like wondered or thought
immediately tie us to the POV character
and tell us that we are in their mind.
Then we get she felt self-conscious
which is another line that is telling us
what's going on internally. Even when
she is describing the man who shows up
at her door, we understand that it's
filtered through her own perspective.
The description is how she sees him, the
things that she notices about him, like
that he's tall and gangly and boyish
with a kind face and his sharp and
bright eyes. We get her reaction to
seeing him with the line, "It was good
to see him." And again, here what she's
feeling with, "Made her feel even more
slovenly than she had done 5 seconds
earlier." There's really no commentary
from a detached narrator here, so we're
firmly in close third person. Now, let's
look at the second example, which is Lil
Fires Everywhere by Celeste Ing.
Everyone in Shaker Heights was talking
about it that summer. How Isabelle, the
last of the Richardson children, had
finally gone around the bend and burned
the house down. All spring the gossip
had been about little Mirabel Makulla or
depending on which side you were on
Mingling Chow. And now at last there was
something new and sensational to
discuss. A little afternoon on that
Saturday in May the shoppers pushing
their grocery carts in Heinens's heard
the fire engines whale to life and
Karina away toward the duck pond. By a
quarter after 12, there were four of
them parked in a halfaphazard red line
along Parkland Drive, where all six
bedrooms of the Richardson house were
ablaze, and everyone within a half mile
could see the smoke rising over the
trees like a dense black thundercloud.
Later, people would say that the signs
had been there all along, that Izzy was
a little lunatic, that there had always
been something off about the Richardson
family, that as soon as they heard the
sirens that morning, they knew something
terrible had happened. By then, of
course, Izzy would be long gone, leaving
no one to defend her, and people could
and did say whatever they liked. What do
you guess for this one? Omnisient,
right? Because you can't say we're in
any specific character's mind in this
passage. We are really following the
community as a collective and getting
those little bits of insight from the
narrator themsself. It begins everyone
in Shaker Heights, not bringing us into
a specific character, but talking about
the group as a whole. Then we get a
description of what the gossip has been
about, which gives us a sense of the
dynamics among the community, but is
from that bird's eyee perspective.
There's even a moment of second person,
depending which side you were on, where
it feels like the narrator is speaking
directly to us. When the fire is
described, the narrator says, "Everyone
within a half mile could see the smoke
rising over the trees." Again,
describing things in a collective. And
then towards the end of this passage,
the narrator interjects with some future
foresight that the characters don't yet
know when they say later people would
say. And by then, of course, Izzy would
be long gone. This is insight the
characters don't yet have, but the
narrator does. Which is how you know you
have an omnisient narrator. You can feel
the difference in these perspectives,
right? The atmosphere, our connection to
the characters and the narrator's role
are totally distinct across these two
passages. So, how can you tell if you're
writing in close third person or
omnisient narration? First, ask, "Do I
get inside the head of one character or
multiple?" If it's one, you're writing
in close third person. If you get into
multiple characters heads, though, we
need to ask a follow-up question. And
this is where many writers get tripped
up. Does the narrator have their own
distinct presence, commentary, and voice
throughout the story? If no, you're
probably writing rotating close third
person rather than omnisient narration.
I would argue that close third person is
actually closer to first person than it
is to omnisient narration because in
both close third person and in first
person, we are tightly aligned to the
POV character's thoughts and feelings.
And omnisient narration is doing
something else entirely. Now, I'm going
to say something that might rattle some
of you. If you're on the fence about
POV, choose close third person. Too many
new authors start writing in omnisient
POV because they don't take the time to
think about whose perspectives we should
actually be following. But in reality,
they're not ready to tackle the
complexities that omnisient narration
requires just yet. And in many cases,
omnisient narration isn't actually
serving their story's specific needs. I
see this all the time in manuscripts
submitted to me for editing. And
changing the POV from omnisient to
rotating close third person is one of
the toughest but most common critiques
that I give. Now, I'm not saying close
third person is better than omnisient
narration. They can both be great, but
omnisient narration is harder to execute
correctly and is often misunderstood.
And readers today tend to crave the
intimacy of close third person. So
that's why I recommend it to newer
writers. So what do I mean when I say
omnisient narration is often executed
wrong? That brings me to the most common
mistake I see in thirdp person
manuscripts, head hopping. You may have
heard the term before and think you're
avoiding it, but are you really? Most
writers who think they're writing
omnisient narration are really just head
hopping. I know what you're thinking,
but doesn't omnisient narration give me
access to all the characters minds so I
can move between them whenever I want.
And isn't that how insert classic
author's name here wrote? I'm just
emulating their style. Saying you're
writing omnisient narration doesn't give
you a hall pass to do whatever the heck
you want with the POV. With true
omnisient narration, any movements in
the POV are clearly intentional. The
reader trusts the narrator to guide
their experience of the story and hold
their hand throughout the book. But head
hopping is when you switch from one
character's mind to another midcene for
no discernable reason, following no
discernable pattern, all seemingly at
random. you're not actually writing
omnisient POV, but just a messy version
of rotating close third person. It's
jarring, disorienting, and erodess the
reader's trust. Because if we're
constantly shifting perspectives, we
don't have enough time to actually form
a connection to any of them. The reader
doesn't know whose story it actually is
because we're constantly getting jostled
around and it feels like whiplash. So
now I want you to put on your editing
cap and see if you can spot the head
hopping in this passage. Megan watched
the fireworks go off above the ferris
wheel. She remembered the time her first
boyfriend kissed her at the top of the
ride. The electricity between them, the
feeling that the night could stretch on
forever if she'd let it. She had thought
they had so much more time. Jeremy
nudged her, bringing Megan back to the
present. He could tell something was
bothering her. Megan smiled, not wanting
to ruin this perfect night. "I'm craving
some fried Oreos," she said. Did you
notice the head hopping? We begin in
Megan's POV, indicated by the line,
"Megan watched." Then we get a brief
flashback into her memory. And then
here's the slip. He could tell something
was bothering her. That's Jeremy's
internal perception, not Megan's. And
then in the following line, we jump
right back to Megan's POV. Megan smiled,
not wanting to ruin this perfect night.
That quick random jump into Jeremy's POV
is a homework example of head hopping.
Luckily, fixing it is simple. Let's
revise the line. He could tell something
was bothering her. to read. Megan hoped
Jeremy couldn't tell something was
bothering her. The same idea gets
across, but now we stay grounded in
Megan's internal experience. Head
hopping can be tough to fix if you're
doing it constantly across your entire
manuscript. But if you think you might
be running into this issue, take the
time to fix all of the instances of head
hopping. I promise it's going to make
your novel so much stronger. If you've
chosen close third person narration,
remember you have to stick with the
designated POV character's thoughts
throughout the entire scene. You can't
dip to another character, not even for a
single line. All thoughts, emotions, and
judgments must come from the POV
character or at least be observable by
them through the others actions,
dialogue, or gestures. But what do you
do if you need to explore multiple
perspectives throughout your story?
That's when you can use rotating close
third person narration where you switch
between perspectives at designated
chapter breaks. But for each chapter, we
stay within a single POV character's
head. I personally love multi-POV
novels, but they can go wrong, too. So
stay tuned for that mistake in a bit.
Now, let's say you know you're avoiding
head hopping. You know that you're
cleanly switching between your POVs at
chapter breaks, but readers are just not
connecting with your story. That's a
sign you're making the next mistake,
which is not going deep enough with your
third person POV. Like I said at the
beginning, close third person is really
closer to first person than it is to
omnisient. Because readers should get as
much access to the POV character's mind
as they would if you were writing in
first person. The only real difference
between close third person and first
person is that you're not writing in the
character's actual voice. When you don't
go deep enough into the POV character's
mind in third person, you increase
what's called the narrative distance,
which is the space between the reader
and the characters and events of the
story. It's called close third person
because we want to feel close to your
POV character. So, work to remove as
much of the narrative distance as you
can. A problem I see with newer authors
is that they focus only on describing
what's happening externally in a scene.
The physical environment, the characters
dialogue, the action and choreography.
That's all important, but it's missing a
key layer. The POV characters internal
thoughts, reflections, reactions, and
emotions. Those elements are what make
fiction distinct from other storytelling
formats. Bring us into their heads so
that we experience the scene from within
their mind and body, not from afar. Like
we're watching a play at a theater. We
should be on the stage alongside them.
When the narrative distance is too wide,
readers feel like spectators. When it's
close, they feel like participants, so
aim for that. Here's an example passage
where the narrative distance is too
wide. As Cara took off her heels in her
apartment entryway, her phone buzzed.
Her mom was probably wondering how her
date went. "Hey, Mom," she said
excitedly into the phone. "The date went
super well. I might even be able to take
him as my plus one to Jenny's wedding."
"That's great, honey, but I have some
news. What happened?" "Grant had a
stroke, and I'm at the hospital with her
now. We should know more tomorrow. I
feel terrible that I'm not there.
Technically, this passage is fine.
There's no head hopping, but it falls
totally flat emotionally. Cara tells her
mom she feels terrible, but we don't
feel it at all. We don't get inside her
mind. All we see is what she says
externally to her mom. So, we ultimately
don't feel closely connected to her at
all. Narrative distance tends to creep
up in dialogue exchanges. So, make sure
you're weaving in enough of the POV
characters internal responses and
reactions. By the way, I have a whole
other video that breaks down other
sneaky ways that narrative distance
impacts your story, so check that out if
you want a deeper dive. Let's make some
revisions to this passage to close the
narrative distance. As Cara took off her
heels in her apartment entryway, her
phone buzzed. Her mom was probably
wondering how her date went. "Hey, Mom,"
she said excitedly into the phone. "The
date went super well. I might even be
able to take him as my plus one to
Jenny's wedding." "That's great, honey,
but I have some news. Her mother's voice
was uncharacteristically somber.
Something's wrong. What happened? Gran
had a stroke and I'm at the hospital
with her now. We should know more
tomorrow. Cara lowered herself onto the
couch. But she'd seen Gran last Sunday
at brunch. She'd been perfectly herself
teasing her about Jenny's wedding.
You've let your little sister beat you
again, Cara. In the moment, the comment
had annoyed her, but now she wished she
hadn't left early. How often does she
get to see Grant anyway? What if that
was the last time? I feel terrible that
I'm not there. With this version, we're
brought much closer into Carara's
momentby-moment reaction to her mother's
news. First, she notices that her
mother's voice was uncharacteristically
somber and worries that something's
wrong. Then, once she learns the news,
she thinks back to the last time she saw
her gran and her regrets about leaving
early. She questions if that will be the
last time she ever sees her, and we feel
her guilt. This version feels so much
more emotionally rich and layered
because we're clued into everything that
Cara is thinking in the moment. So, if
you get feedback that your reader just
didn't connect with your main character,
you might need to deepen your POV. This
next mistake turns your novel into a
scattered mess where we can't even tell
whose story we're following, including
too many POVs. Like I said, I love
multi-pov books, but there's a right way
and a wrong way to do them. If you get
inside the mind of every single
character who shows up in your novel,
the mailman who shows up in just one
scene, the ex who pops in just to stir
the pot, the villain's sidekick who
doesn't have their own storyline at all,
then it will feel like your novel is
spinning out of control. Each time you
introduce a new POV, the reader must
reorient themselves and reinvest
emotionally in this new story line.
Remember that the POV dictates who the
story is about. If you divide our
attention across too many different
characters, we'll only get to meet each
one superficially, it's often much more
effective to explore fewer POVs in much
more depth. So, ensure that every POV in
your story earns its place. If a
character only appears once or twice or
doesn't have their own full arc, then
they probably don't deserve to have
their own POV. I hear from authors all
the time, well, I have to include this
scene from this other outlier
perspective because otherwise the reader
won't know that XYZ happened. My
response to those authors is always
this. Do we actually need to know that
XYZ happened at this exact moment or
could we learn about it when the other
more important main characters learn
about it? Often keeping certain things
withheld will actually enhance the
suspense and the drama when that event
is eventually revealed. Here's a quick
test. If you're on the fence about a
POV, if you can remove the POV and the
plot still makes sense, it probably
wasn't necessary. There's no official
rule for how many POVs you can include
in a novel. But for authors just
starting out, as a general rule of
thumb, I would say start to audit your
POVs if you have more than four. Ask
yourself, does the story actually demand
all of these POVs, or am I just afraid
to kill my darlings? Now, this last POV
mistake is something that many authors
overlook until they decide they want to
publish their book and realize they've
messed up. Ignoring genre conventions.
Different genres come with different
expectations about POV. I'm not saying
you shouldn't break the rules or
experiment with genre conventions, but I
want to teach you the rules and the
genre conventions first so that you can
do so intentionally and with purpose.
For example, young adult fiction
overwhelmingly favors first-person
narration because it creates intimacy
and immediiacy and allows teen readers
to quickly latch on to the protagonist.
Mysteries and thrillers are often told
in close third person or first person
rather than omnisient narration. This
allows for suspense and misdirection
because we're tightly aligned to the POV
characters experiences at any given
moment and kept on the edge of our seat.
The author intentionally keeps a lot of
things unknown. Romance is also often
written in close third person or first
person, typically following either one
of the love interests or both of the
love interests because that allows us to
witness the development of their
feelings firsthand. These days,
omnisient narration is most often found
in literary fiction, sci-fi, and fantasy
novels, though all of those genres can
also use first person or close third
person. If you're not sure what POV to
go with for your story, do some
research. Pick up five best-selling
novels in your genre and study the POV
choices. How does the chosen POV impact
the reader's experience of the story and
their connection to the characters? And
is that something you want to emulate?
POV is one of the most important
strategic tools in your storytelling
arsenal. And third person is perhaps the
most versatile POV of them all, but only
if you use it with precision and avoid
these pitfalls that many first-time
authors fall into. Now that you've
mastered third person POV, watch this
video where I reveal the other biggest
mistakes that make your writing look
amateur-ish. Thanks so much for watching
and happy writing.

## This Psychological Trick Will Change How You Write Forever

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6p4_JKpshoc>

Why are some books so good that we stay
up all night reading while others are so
boring that they put us to sleep? The
difference comes down to a psychological
principle known as the Zeigarnik effect.
And today, I'm going to reveal how to
leverage the power of this psychological
phenomenon to write page-turning stories
that readers simply can't put down.
First, what is the Zeigarnik effect?
Named after the psychologist Bluma
Zeigarnik who discovered it, the
Zeigarnik effect states that people
remember unfinished or interrupted tasks
better than completed ones. She noticed
that waiters remembered the orders of
customers who had not yet paid, but then
as soon as they did pay, the waiters
completely forgot their orders. This got
me thinking back to my high school days.
Ever stay up all night memorizing
answers for a test only for all of that
information to be totally wiped from
your brain the second the test is over?
That's the Zeigarnik effect in action.
You likely experience the Zeigarnik
effect on a daily basis without
realizing it. Do you find yourself
thinking about the dirty dishes in the
sink and the laundry you have yet to
fold while you're lying in bed? That's
your brain focused on the unfinished
tasks and desperately seeking closure.
But the Zeigarnik effect can also have a
positive angle. Say you go on a first
date and it goes really well. You get
along great, you have a lot in common,
and then after dinner you invite your
dates to come back to your place, but
your date says it's late and they need
to go home. 100% chance that that night
still thinking about them, right? That's
because they've left you wanting more.
To you, the date still feels unfinished,
so it's still on your mind. And therein
lies the key to how we can use the
Zeigarnik effect to craft page-turning
fiction. So let me show you three
practical techniques you can use to
leverage this psychology and make your
story irresistible to readers. First,
build up to an event in your story. When
readers describe a book as a page
turner, what they're really saying is
that they're anticipating something in
the story and they can't stop reading
until they get the answers that they're
seeking. This is why millions of people
watch dating shows like The Bachelor and
Love Is Blind because they want to see
which love interest gets selected or if
the couple ends up together. As stupid
as they are, these shows are engineered
to make people addicted to them because
they're by design building up to a major
event like an engagement or a wedding.
So let's apply that same principle to
your story. What is your plot ultimately
building to? The clock in your story's
world should be ticking down leading up
to some event where something
consequential will happen, typically at
the story's climax. That's how you build
desperate anticipation and curiosity in
your reader. The event doesn't have to
be explosive or far-fetched or out of
left field, but it does have to matter
deeply to your characters because if it
matters to them, it will matter to us. I
was working with a best- selling author
recently who was working on a story
about people in the wine industry. The
story followed restaurant owners,
distributors, sommeliers, and servers
who all had a juicy interpersonal drama
between them. But the story was missing
that ticking clock element. So together
we created a big upcoming event, an
exclusive industry gala where all the
characters would be in the same room and
their secrets would inevitably tumble
out. Suddenly every scene leading up to
that event felt more dynamic, had more
tension, and was charged with an
electric spark. Since the reader knows
this event is on the horizon, we're
invested in seeing what happens when the
characters get there. Another author I
worked with was writing a novel set in
Florida where a tragedy pulled a family
apart. We amplified the suspense of the
family drama by having a hurricane start
brewing off the coast. The storm became
a natural countdown. The closer it got,
the more pressure the characters felt,
and the more the reader was left on the
edge of their seat waiting to see what
would happen when the storm finally
arrived and everything blew apart. The
beauty is that this technique works no
matter what genre you're writing. The
point is to anchor your plot in a
tangible event, then create an
underlying current of momentum leading
up to it. Something that tells the
reader keep reading because something
big is coming. So once you choose your
story's central event, how do you ensure
readers keep turning the pages to
actually get there? That's where this
second technique comes in. Revise your
chapter endings. When I work with
authors on their manuscripts, one of the
most common issues I see is flat chapter
endings. They will have an incredibly
rich scene filled with great scene
setting and conflict, but then end the
chapter with something like and then she
went home exhausted by the day's events.
With that, you've immediately just
sucked the life and energy out of the
story. If you want your book to be truly
unputdownable, you have to treat every
chapter ending as a mini cliffhanger.
That doesn't mean every chapter should
end with someone screaming or gasping,
"Oh my god!" because that will get
cheesy fast. But you do need to leave
something unresolved that leaves the
reader hanging and wanting to read more.
Remember the Zeigarnik effect. As soon
as we get closure, we forget. And you
want readers to keep thinking about your
book nonstop until the end. Think about
the last show you binged. Why do we keep
hitting next episode even though it's
past midnight and we know we'll regret
it in the morning? Because each episode
ends with something unfinished and we
hit the next episode button desperately
seeking resolution. That next episode
button is the same thing as your chapter
breaks. Here's a quick exercise you can
do to audit your chapter endings. Go
through your entire manuscript, then
look at the last paragraph of each of
your chapters. Ask yourself, is there a
question lingering in the air? Is there
a sense of anticipation or unease? Or
does the energy just fizzle out? For
example, instead of closing with a line
like she fell asleep relieved that the
chaos of the day had concluded, you
might try something like she tried to
sleep, but her phone kept vibrating on
the nightstand, the blue light emerging
in her periphery. When would he stop?
It's the exact same moment, the
character is in bed, but they bring
completely different energy. And which
one are you more likely to keep reading?
With the first ending, you could
probably just close the book right there
and forget about it. But with the
second, you're probably going to turn to
the next page to see if the person stops
texting her, right? And here's a bonus
tip if you're writing multiple POVs. You
can use your chapter endings to
strategically create suspense as you
switch between the storylines. If you
end a chapter on a tense moment with
character A, then switch to character B,
you're effectively making the reader
wait to get resolution on character A's
storyline. If you keep that pattern
going for the rest of the novel, you're
going to keep your reader hooked.
Suspenseful chapter endings are the
secret to making your story feel
addictive. I have another video that
does a deeper dive with specific
strategies to write compelling chapter
endings along with more examples, so I
will link that in the description. Now
you know how to structure your plot to
build to something and how to make each
individual chapter leave us wanting
more. But there's one more technique
that ties all of this together that's
critical for every author to master.
Plant Chekhov's gun. If you've ever
heard the phrase Chekhov's gun but
weren't sure what it meant, here's a
quick overview. The Russian playwright
Anton Chekhov famously said, "If in the
first act you have hung a pistol on the
wall, then in the following one it
should be fired. Otherwise don't put it
there." The concept is that everything
you draw the reader's attention to
should have a purpose and ultimately
some kind of payoff in the story. If you
intentionally plant things in your story
that will emerge in significance later
on, you can use the Zeigarnik effect to
your advantage because when readers
notice and pick up on these guns in your
story, they're going to want to keep
reading to see them eventually go off.
These don't have to be literal guns, of
course, and in fact, they don't have to
be physical objects at all. A powerful
Chekhov's gun could be a character's
secret that we sense will inevitably
spill out. If a story begins with a
character's first day at Harvard, then
the character reveals that they only got
into Harvard because they bribed
someone, we're naturally going to
wonder, "When is that going to come
out?" Or a Chekhov's gun could be a
character's fear. If your character has
an intense fear of water like Chief
Brody in Jaws, by drawing our attention
to it, you're signaling to the reader
that that fear is going to be tested in
some way later on. That subconsciously
makes us want to keep reading to see how
the character will confront their fear.
When you plant Chekhov's guns
effectively, when you do eventually set
them off, it's one of the most
satisfying experiences a reader can have
because we've finally gotten closure on
something that's been building for the
entire story. Something that we noticed
and said, "Ah, I knew that was going to
be important." If you use all three of
these techniques together, you'll be
leveraging the power of the Zeigarnik
effect to make your story unputdownable.
By tapping into reader's psychology,
they won't know why they keep turning
the pages, but they'll feel they have
to, and that's the highest compliment
any author could get. But now that you
know how to engineer a page-turning
novel, the next challenge is making sure
every single scene holds up. So watch
this video where I reveal the secret
formula to writing perfect scenes every
time. Thanks so much for watching and
happy writing.

## The 4 Types of Writers (and Which One Actually Makes $$$)

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f6v0ZQyxg5k>
Caption file: f6v0ZQyxg5k.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Story Structure
Secondary Topics: Genre, Character, Reader Experience & Engagement, Writing Craft
Tertiary Topics: Character Development, Audience, Genre, Plot, Story Structure, Romance, Thriller, Fantasy

As a book editor, I've worked with more
than a thousand authors across virtually
every genre, from sweeping fantasy epics
to quiet literary novels. And I've
noticed something fascinating. Every
writer fits into one of four essential
types. No, it's not about whether you
plot or pants your book, or even about
what genre you write. It all hinges on
your answer to a single question. What
drives your writing deep down? Your
answer doesn't just shape how you write.
It can shape your entire author career,
your readership, and yes, even how much
money you make. So, let's discover which
type you are. I'll explain my personal
definition of each writer type and give
some examples of famous authors who fit
into each category so you can figure out
where you fit. Let's start with the type
of writer I certainly wanted to be when
I was an English nerd in school. The
artist. This type of writer is driven by
their deep love for the craft of writing
