## 9 Ways to Make Readers HATE Your Main Character

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iL5JpDVomAs>
Caption file: iL5JpDVomAs.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Character
Secondary Topics: Reader Experience & Engagement, Story Structure, Book Marketing & Platform
Tertiary Topics: Audience, Character Development, Character Motivation, Protagonist, Plot, Perfectionism, Twists & Reveals, Book Covers

If readers hate your main character,
they'll probably hate your entire book.
Your protagonist is the heart and soul
of your story. And while they don't
necessarily need to be likable, they do
need to captivate your reader. I've
edited hundreds of books, including New
York Times best sellers. And today, I'm
revealing the nine biggest mistakes you
might be making with your main
character, and exactly how to fix each
one. Mistake number one is one I see new
authors make all the time because they
don't yet understand what truly makes a
character compelling. Your character has
no flaws. In an attempt to make their
protagonist likable, authors sometimes
make them perfect and flawless, which
actually has the opposite effect. Real
people are flawed, messy, imperfect, and
complicated. So, your protagonist should
be too. If your character is too
perfect, they won't feel relatable,
genuine, or authentic, and it'll be more
difficult for readers to connect to
them. Here's an exercise to do to ensure
your protagonist is layered and complex.
For every positive trait you give them,
give them a negative trait that
counterbalances it. For example, on the
positive side, perhaps your protagonist
is courageous, enabling them to take
bold, brave acts. But on the negative
side, they're also impulsive, and their
rashness sometimes gets them into
trouble. One of my favorite character
development tricks is to find their
internal misbelief. This is something
that they believe is true about themsel
or about the world that shapes their
motivations and actions throughout the
story. For example, you could have a
character who believes that trusting
others always leads to hurt because
their best friend who they trusted
betrayed them years ago. Flaws,
contradictions, and misbeliefs not only
humanize your protagonist, but sew the
seeds for their internal growth and
transformation over the course of the
story. Remember that readers aren't just
coming to your story for an entertaining
plot. They also want to connect with
your protagonist's personal journey. And
a character that's perfect from the
start will have nowhere to go. The
second mistake is one of the most
frustrating for readers because it
causes your plot to feel boring. Your
character is too passive. If your entire
story is just your character reacting to
things outside of their control and not
taking any action for themsel, then it's
going to become a snoozefest. Your
protagonist must drive the story forward
and have agency. They must take critical
decisions in pursuit of some kind of
goal. The reason that this mistake is so
deadly is that you might not even
realize that your protagonist is too
passive. For example, I edited a mystery
recently where the protagonist was an
amateur sleuth who was exceptional at
solving puzzles. Yet, all of the clues
in the story were found by their
sidekick, and their sidekick was the one
that eventually solved the mystery. This
didn't make for an effective plot
because we wanted to see the main
character step up, take charge, and
solve problems independently of their
sidekick. I began to wonder why the
sidekick character wasn't the
protagonist because she was far more
dynamic and interesting and did way more
in the story. Passive protagonists will
make your story feel static. So, take a
close look at your plot and make sure
your protagonist is making decisions and
taking actions that directly influence
the chain of events. Watch for areas
where secondary characters make a
discovery or take an action that your
protagonist could do instead. For
instance, do you have someone else
discovering a dead body or making an
important phone call? What would happen
if your protagonist did that instead?
Mistake number three is a guaranteed way
to make readers dislike your
protagonist. Your character feels like a
stock character. Stock characters might
be the first that come to mind when
you're crafting your story's cast. After
all, they're instantly recognizable and
have been used in stories for centuries.
This could be a fem fatal, a wise old
mentor, or a damsel in distress. There
are definitely cases where these
archetypes can work, but you want to
make sure you bring a fresh spin to
them, so they don't feel overly familiar
and cliche. If your protagonist is just
one of these stock characters and
nothing else, then they're going to lack
depth. Take Bella Swan from Twilight for
example. She's often criticized as being
a damsel in distress because she relies
on Edward and Jacob rescuing her for
much of the series. You don't have to
avoid archetypes entirely, but if your
protagonist falls into one, make sure to
give them a fresh, exciting trait that
differentiates them from the norm. For
example, if you have a wise old man
character, why not make them a wise
young girl instead? Simply changing
their gender and age makes them feel
much more intriguing while retaining
their core function. Mistake number four
is something I'm constantly discussing
with my editing clients because it's so
critical to an effective story, but is
often misunderstood. Your character has
no objective. What is your main
character's goal? If you can't define
it, you have a fundamental issue not
only with your protagonist, but with
your entire story. Your protagonist must
be working toward something, or else
readers will quickly lose interest
because we won't have a sense of where
the plot is going or what we're reading
for. Your character's objective gives
the story purpose, momentum, and
direction. But authors often don't
define the objective effectively. The
objective should be clear, concrete, and
specific. Vague goals like my character
wants to find happiness or my character
wants to be successful won't resonate
with readers or serve a function in the
plot because they're difficult to
measure and track. Instead, define a
tangible goal that will achieve the
protagonist's desire to find happiness
or success. For instance, that could be
moving to Hawaii and starting a bed and
breakfast or finding a cure for a rare
form of cancer. Here's an easy way to
tell if your protagonist's objective is
specific enough. By the end of the
novel, can we definitively say whether
they achieved it or not? It's hard to
definitively determine if they found
happiness or became successful, but we
can definitely say if they moved to
Hawaii and started a bed and breakfast
or if they cured a rare form of cancer.
Without a clear objective, your reader
won't become invested in your
protagonist's journey or in the story as
a whole. So, drill down your character's
objective until it becomes that
specific. Mistake number five causes
your protagonist to feel one-dimensional
and superficial. Your character has no
past. Your character had a life before
the events of the story, so make sure we
know about it. That history that they
bring to the story should inform their
present-day actions, motivations, and
decisions. If we don't know what led
them to where they are today, we won't
feel as emotionally connected to them.
Imagine if you didn't know anything
about your significant other's past
before you started dating them. How
superficial would that relationship be?
For example, look at the Hunger Games.
Katniss Everdine's father's death years
before the events of the first book led
her to have to provide for her family
and especially be protective of her
younger sister. This backstory shapes
her desires, fears, and motivations
throughout the entire series. That said,
you don't want to overwhelm your story
with too much backstory because you
won't ultimately have room in a single
novel to go through your protagonist's
entire life, but use strategic
flashbacks or brief passages of
exposition to orient the reader to those
key events from the past that have led
them to where they are today emotionally
and physically. That could be their
greatest heartbreak, a family tragedy,
or a personal regret. I have another
video with my top tips for writing
effective flashbacks, so I will link
that in the description. Now, if you
make mistake number six, the entire
ending of your story will fall flat.
Your character doesn't evolve. We don't
want to see your protagonist stay
exactly the same from the beginning to
the middle to the end of the story. We
want to see them grow, evolve, and
change in meaningful ways. If they're
the exact same person that they were on
page one, it'll feel like the entire
journey was meaningless. The events of
the plot should push them past their
comfort zone and force them to transform
in some kind of way. To ensure you craft
a meaningful transformative arc for your
protagonist, I recommend building a
character profile for who they are at
the beginning of the story and who they
are at the end of the story. Some
elements might overlap, but there should
be a few notable differences. As part of
this exercise, return to that idea of
the internal misbelief we talked about
earlier. How is that misbelief
challenged? And what does the character
learn from it in the end? Use this
internal misbelief to fuel their
transformative arc. For example, perhaps
they realize that there is value in
trusting others or that they do have the
capacity to be brave. Ultimately, your
character's evolution is what will make
your story emotionally impactful and
fulfilling because it mirrors how we
ourselves change due to our experiences.
We should see the protagonist learn from
their failures, overcome their fears, or
change their worldview. Mistake number
seven is admittedly one of the hardest
things to see in your own work, but can
immediately turn readers off. Your
character is out of touch. If your
character is super naive, if they're
concerned about trivial or superficial
things, or if they have controversial or
problematic views, you run the risk of
alienating your reader. Now, I'm not
saying your character can't feel this
way or can't have these views, as that
might be a defining part of their
persona or a flaw that you've
intentionally created for them, but the
issue arises when the protagonist is
never challenged on these fronts. For
example, perhaps you have a main
character who's exceedingly privileged
and their primary concern in the story
is that they don't have enough money to
move from their multi-million dollar
penthouse in Manhattan to a mansion in
the Hamptons. that isn't going to be
relatable for most of your readers and
it will be difficult for them to become
emotionally invested in the character's
journey since it feels out of touch. So
to give this character more dimension,
have them have conversations with other
characters that come from different
backgrounds. How do those differing
perspectives force them to observe and
confront their own personal views and
biases? put them in situations where
they begin to question their limited
understanding of the world and begin to
expand and stretch their perceptions.
That growth is going to make them so
much more empathetic. Mistake number
eight is something I see to some degree
in nearly every manuscript I edit. Your
character doesn't reveal their emotions.
The beauty of fiction over other
storytelling mediums is that it allows
you to directly immerse the reader in
your character's emotional experience.
That closeness is what readers will
crave. Whether you're writing in first
person or third person, you should grant
the reader access to the POV character's
mind. A common mistake newer authors
make is withholding the character's
thoughts, feelings, and emotions from
the reader, which makes them
inaccessible and feel distant. Authors
will often stop at just describing
what's happening externally in a scene,
which makes it feel more like a play or
a film than a work of immersive fiction.
There's almost always room to bring us
deeper into the POV character's mind. If
we don't understand how your character
is responding and reacting to the events
of the story, you're going to sever our
connection to them. Don't make us guess.
Show what's going on through their mind
and body. We should feel what they feel,
especially at pivotal turning points in
the story. And if we don't, the story is
going to lack emotional impact. I have
another video with my top tips for
writing character interiority
effectively, so check that out if it's
something you struggle with. Finally,
mistake number nine will almost always
lead to readers disliking a character.
Your character is melodramatic. This is
the opposite of the last problem. In
this case, your protagonist's emotions
are exaggerated to an unrealistic
effect. Rather than us empathizing with
the character, we get irritated.
Melodramatic characters might use
exaggerated dialogue like scream in all
caps or use a bunch of exclamation
points. Or they might react dramatically
like sobbing constantly. Melodrama can
also come up in characters internal
monologues if you have them lamenting
about their life for a prolonged period
of time. These moments feel fake and
readers typically prefer more nuanced
subtle portrayals of emotions that more
closely mirror our complicated human
experiences. Subtle moments are often
much more impactful than loud emotional
expressions. So go back through your
manuscript, especially dramatic
confrontation scenes, and watch out for
any moments of melodrama. then try
scaling them back. I bet you'll find the
scene is actually much more effective
that way. By correcting these nine
character mistakes, you'll ensure your
protagonist is someone readers genuinely
root for, care about, and remember long
after finishing your book. But there's
one thing that every strong protagonist
needs, and I only hinted about it in
this video. So, click this link where I

## 8 WORST Ways to Start a Novel

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=phE5jfTynQc>

Primary Topic: Writing Craft

A generic, cliché, or overdone opening
scene can sabotage your story before it
even begins. As a book editor who
previously worked in the publishing
industry, I've read hundreds of
manuscripts, and today I'm sharing eight
lazy openings I see time and time again.
If you have one of these scenes, don't
worry because I'll also share exactly
how to fix them to create a much
stronger start to your story. Also, keep
in mind that I'm not saying you can
never open with these scenes. You'll see
some of them in published books, and
they can definitely work in certain
cases. But, if you have one of them,
it's worth considering if that is
actually the best entry to your story.
The first opening is my biggest personal
pet peeve. If I'm editing a manuscript
that starts with this scene, I'll almost
always recommend the author changes it.
It's beginning on a plane. If you have
your main character arriving at a new
destination at the start of your story,
this might feel like the perfect place
to begin. But, in reality, putting your
character on a plane means locking them
in a metal tube where they can't go
anywhere or do anything. They can't make
meaningful choices. They can't interact
with their environment unless they start
up a superficial conversation with the
stranger next to them. So, they end up
just sitting there, reflecting on their
life and why they're traveling. This
often leads to a lengthy internal
monologue or a backstory dump, which
we'll talk more about later. It's a
boring start, and the reader is often
itchy to see them get to their
destination and really start their
journey. So, begin your story after the
travel ends and the trip really begins.
The next lazy opening is admittedly
really tempting for new writers, but
it's also one of the most annoying ways
to start a novel. It's beginning with a
dream sequence. You think you're
starting with intrigue and mystery, but
what you're really doing is tricking the
reader. Here's what typically happens.
You hook us into a scene where something
thrilling or threatening is happening.
Maybe something strange or supernatural
occurs. Things start to heat up. Your
character is about to commit a crime or
about to kiss someone or they're about
to die. The stakes feel so high. Then,
surprise! They wake up. It was all a
dream. And just like that, you've pulled
out the rug from under us. All that
tension you built immediately fizzles
because we know that this isn't the
character's actual situation and
therefore didn't really matter. The
biggest issue with opening with a dream
sequence is that it breaks your trust
with your reader. Now you have us
wondering what else might be a fake out
deeper in the story. It puts us on edge
and not in a good way. Typically, what
an author is trying to do with a dream
sequence is establish the character's
inner conflict. But rather than putting
this behind the curtain of a dream,
instead show that inner conflict play
out in a scene where something real is
at stake. You can perhaps move that
dream sequence to occur later on in the
story and it may actually be more
effective there once we've already
gotten an understanding of the
character's inner conflict. Dream
sequences can be effective, but only
when used sparingly and strategically
and almost never on page one. The next
lazy opening is especially prominent in
mysteries and thrillers. It's opening
with a phone call. A character will be
interrupted, often in the middle of the
night, with a phone call that brings bad
news. A body has just been found or
their mother is in the hospital. The
instinct behind this tactic is good. You
want to immediately establish stakes and
kickstart action. While it is important
to establish strong momentum in your
opening scene, it's only going to have
the intended impact if we understand
what the character's life was like
before they got that phone call that
changed everything. If we don't know
what their normal life looks like or
what's at stake for them, then the phone
call is not going to mean anything to
us. So instead, show us the character in
their element first. Establish their
circumstances, even just for a page or
two, before that call comes in. That way
we'll understand who they are and what
they stand to lose when their life
changes forever. You can still use the
phone call as a plot development, just
don't open with it totally cold. Give us
a reason to care about the character
before they get the call. The next lazy
opening is one of the most disorienting
ways to start your novel, in the middle
of a conversation. It might seem like a
clever way to drop us right into the
conflict. A character says something
emotionally charged, like, "I didn't
kill her." or, "Have you seen Anna
today?" We can sense the drama, sure,
but without more context on who the
characters are and what their
relationship is, that drama won't
actually land. Again, there are no
stakes yet, so the reader isn't
emotionally invested. When you open your
novel mid-dialogue, it feels like we're
eavesdropping, and we'll only be half
interested in what we're overhearing.
You can certainly keep that tense
dialogue exchange in your opening scene,
but don't have it as the very first
sentence. Start with a line or two of
narration to anchor us in the scene and
what's happening, and sprinkle in enough
exposition for us to make sense of the
conversation as it progresses. Newer
authors often think that they must avoid
exposition at all costs, but I promise
you exposition is not the enemy. I have
a whole other video that talks about how
to write exposition effectively, so I
will link that in the description for
you to check out if you struggle with
knowing how much exposition to include.
The next lazy opening will lead your
reader to immediately put down your
book. It is dumping your character's
entire life story. It sounds something
like this. Alyssa Matessic always loved
reading and writing growing up. English
was her favorite subject in school. Then
she went on to study English and
creative writing in New York City. There
she decided she wanted to become a book
editor. Boring, right? We get line after
line of background information about the
character, but no actual story or scene.
We presume this story will be about
Alyssa, but we have no sense of what's
going on in the present timeline of the
novel. And it sounds more like a
Wikipedia entry than a compelling scene.
Remember, readers don't want to be told
the story by the the narrator dumping a
lot of information on us. We want to be
immersed in the story via scenes. The
reader does want to learn about your
character's past, but not all at once
right at the start of the story.
Instead, begin with action. Put your
character in an interesting situation,
then weave in those backstory details as
they become relevant. The next boring
opening scene feels like a good starting
point, but is really just a way of you
procrastinating kickstarting the plot.
It's showing a character moving in or
moving out of a house. We see the
character carrying boxes into their new
home, reflecting on how they're about to
have a fresh start, or they're packing
up box and saying goodbye. Like with the
plane scene, this transition point might
be the first thing that comes to mind
when you think about where to begin your
story. But the problem is nothing is
actually happening yet. Plus, let's be
real, moving is a long, tedious, often
stressful process. Who wants to relive
that at the start of your story? Don't
open with the boring logistics of
moving. Instead, open with the first
obstacle, big or small, that your
character confronts in their new home.
Perhaps it is on moving day, but it's
likely a little bit deeper in the story.
Brainstorm. What happens to them once
the dust has settled? Okay, this next
lazy novel opening is probably the most
overused of all the examples I'm going
through today. If I had a dollar for
every time a manuscript opens with this,
I could fund an entire writing retreat.
It's opening with the character waking
up. For many writers, when they start
their novel, this is immediately where
their brain goes. And it makes sense.
You want a fresh start, a blank slate.
But waking up is not really an
interesting event. It's just a
biological function. It's mundane, and
not in a way that makes your character
feel relatable, but in a way that makes
us wonder what we're reading for. Unless
something truly extraordinary happens
the moment your character's alarm goes
off, starting this way is a missed
opportunity. Instead, focus on the
moment that your character encounters
some kind of tension in their day. Start
with the moment the character realizes
they're late for an interview that could
change their life, or when they go to
start their car and realize it's not in
the driveway. In almost every single
case, opening the novel deeper is much
more effective than opening right when
they wake up. Now, the final lazy
opening scene is one of the most debated
topics among the writing community. It's
an unnecessary prologue. Let me be
clear, I'm not anti-prologue. I've seen
plenty of brilliant ones, but many of
them are not actually necessary and can
sabotage the opening of your novel. The
typical bad prologue falls into one of
two traps. It's overly vague and
cryptic, and therefore disorienting, or
it's just a massive world-building dump.
If you're using the prologue just to try
to create mystery or atmosphere, or
you're trying to unload a lot of
exposition on the reader, ask yourself,
is it really necessary? Or am I delaying
the reader's arrival at the true start
of the story? Try cutting it entirely
and drop the reader in chapter one and
see how it feels. You'll often find that
you didn't need the prologue after all.
Effective prologues are short, specific,
and essential to our understanding of
the rest of the story. They either show
a key moment that is relevant to the
rest of the novel, or flash forward to a
pivotal scene that we will get to later.
If you have a prologue, make sure it
belongs. Otherwise, you're wasting your
critical opening pages. Now that you
know the eight laziest ways to start a
novel, you also know how to avoid them.
If you're not sure whether your current
opening scene is working the way you
intend, here's a challenge. Try cutting
that first scene and beginning with the
second one. Maybe try cutting the
entirety of chapter one and starting
with chapter two. Start deeper in the
story and see how it feels. You'll often
find the pacing is so much stronger that
way. But once you find the right opening
scene, the next challenge is to make
sure you write it effectively. So watch

Some genres also have a whole list of

many different varieties of fantasy. If
your subgenre is widely known in the
industry like epic, high, or urban
fantasy, then that term is also
perfectly fine to use in your query
letter. Agents will also need to know
whether your book is intended for an
adult, young adult, middle grade, or
children's audience. Some agents only
work within some age categories, while
others will work across multiple age
categories. Some genre terms like
literary or upmarket fiction are only
used to describe adult novels, while
others could refer to novels across
different age categories like mysteries
or romances. So, in the latter case,
make sure that you specify which age
category your book is for. Now, let's
talk about word count. You can round
your word count to the nearest thousand
word. For instance, if it is 84,434
words, you could just round to 84,000
words for the purposes of the query
letter. Always include an accurate word
count in your query letter, even if it
is above or below industry standards for
your genre and age category. Because
remember that agents are going to see
your word count whenever they request
the full manuscript, which is the next
step in potentially offering you
representation. Plus, word count is
something that most agents want to know
right off the bat because it gives them
a sense of if the manuscript is
currently falling within industry
expectations, and therefore is something
feasible that they could sell to a
publishing house. If you are querying a
book that falls widely outside of the
industry norms for your genre and age
category, it is not impossible to find a
literary agent and a publisher, though
you might have a more difficult time. In
that case, your agent might work with
you to get your manuscript to the more
accepted range in terms of word count,
but it is typically best to do that work
up front on your own prior to querying
to give yourself the best shot. Now,
once you've collected all your necessary
details, your word count, genre, and
title, all you need to do is string them
together in a single sentence for that
snapshot line in your query letter. The
standard language would be, "I'm seeking
representation for title, {comma} an age
category genre novel complete at number
words." That said, many authors forego
the first part of that sentence about
seeking representation since it's
implied that you're seeking
representation if you are querying an
agent after all, and simply say, "Title
is an age category genre novel complete
at number words." If you choose to
include a personalization line, the
snapshot line can come in the same
paragraph as that one, directly after it
typically. If you don't have a
personalization line, the snapshot
should either be the first line of your
query letter or come directly after your
description section. Next up is the
description. This is the most important
section of your query letter because
it's where you're going to give the
agent a taste of your story and make
them want to read your sample pages. It
should be written in third person and
include all of the foundational aspects
of the story, including the setting, the
protagonist's name and age, the setup.
What is the protagonist dealing with at
the start of the novel? The inciting
incident. What happens to the
protagonist to kickstart the events of
the plot? The objective. What is your
protagonist seeking to achieve over the
course of the story? And the main
conflict. What obstacles does your main
character face in their attempt to
achieve their objective? What crossroads
or difficult decision do they face?
Think of the description as the movie
trailer for your book. You don't want to
give everything away, of course, but you
should describe it in enough detail to
pique the agent's interest. You should
end the description with a cliffhanger
of sorts that leaves the agent wondering
how the story pans out. The description
should fall somewhere between 150 to 300
words and span about two to four
paragraphs. You don't want it to be too
short and overly general or vague, but
at the same time, you don't want it to
be too long and include too many plot
details that become cumbersome to read.
Do not give away the ending or any major
spoilers, especially if you are writing
a suspense novel. As a general rule of
thumb, the description really only needs
to cover about the first quarter of your
story. A template I like to use is the
following. Paragraph one. Introduce the
protagonist, the setting, and the setup.
Where does the story start? What is the
protagonist's situation? Paragraph two.
Describe the inciting incident. What
happens to jumpstart the protagonist's
journey? How does their life change? And
what objective do they set as a result?
Paragraph three. Describe the ensuing
conflict they face. Make sure we
understand what is at stake for your
protagonist in achieving their goal.
What do they stand to gain from
achieving that goal, and what do they
stand to lose if they fail to achieve
it? End the description with an
intriguing line that teases the main
source of intrigue or mystery that the
story explores. More or less, the
description should sound like the copy
that goes on the back jacket of a
hardcover novel or on the online
description page. So, look at other
books in your genre, maybe by authors
that you admire, and model your
description after the descriptions of
their novels. You will want to avoid any
prefatory language like, "My book
follows a character named" and instead
dive straight into describing the
character and plot action. Ideally, your
description would also be written in the
same tone as your novel. So, if it's a
lighthearted rom-com, feel free to
include puns or humorous language. If
it's a thriller, the language can sound
more ominous and intense. Five.
Comparable titles. Many querying authors
dread coming up with comparable titles,
also known as comps for short. These are
books that are similar to yours,
typically within your genre, and the
purpose of comps is to give agents a
sense of what types of audiences will
gravitate toward your book. In other
words, what reader is going to pick this
up and buy it? If you are able to
demonstrate to them that other similar
novels have been sold successfully and
garnered strong sales, then the agent
will feel more confident in their
ability to sell your book to a
publisher. Including comps also helps
show the agent that you have a sense of
the current publishing landscape.
Comparable titles don't only come into
play at the querying phase. If an editor
at a publishing house is interested in
buying the rights to your book, they
will put together a profit and loss
statement, which will include sales
figures for other comparable titles in
your genre. This profit and loss
statement helps the publisher determine
how much they expect to make on your
book, and therefore what they feel they
can offer you as an author as the
advance. If you don't already read
widely within your genre, then you will
want to do some research to come up with
suitable comparable titles. Even better,
check out a few books that were recently
published in your genre from your local
library and read them. This will not
only help you come up with other
possible comparable titles, but reading
is one of the strongest ways to enhance
your own storytelling. For the query
letter, I recommend including two or
three comp titles. Having one comparable
title might not be enough for the agent
to visualize the type of audience that
you are intending to write for, and
having more than three can confuse the
agent as to which audience you are
targeting exactly and where your book
fits in the market. There are several
guidelines for choosing strong
comparable titles to keep in mind.
First, the general rule of thumb is to
include comparable titles that were
published no more than five years ago
because you want them to reflect the
current publishing landscape. Books that
are older than that won't necessarily
reflect current reader appetites. You
should also typically stick to comps
that were traditionally published since
that is the publishing path that you are
seeking by reaching out to literary
agents. And those are the types of
publishers that your agent would look at
placing your book with. That said, if
there is a great comp that was
self-published and sold extremely well,
you can use it, but I recommend pairing
it with at least one traditionally
published comp as well. Comps should
also be within your same genre and age
category. The one exception is that you
can use recent TV shows or films as
comps, especially if they share a
similar story premise or tone or theme.
But in those cases, I recommend pairing
the TV show or movie with at least one
novel comp within your genre as well.
Avoid any comparable titles that have
low sales figures, which you can
typically glean from seeing the number
of Amazon or Goodreads reviews, or those
that are outlier best-seller hits like
The Hunger Games or Gone Girl. When
presenting comps in your query letter, I
recommend specifying what about each
comp aligns with your novel rather than
just listing them generally. This should
only take up one to two sentences max.
Some authors like to put the comps right
at the top of the query letter after the
snapshot line, but I only recommend
doing this if you feel really strongly
about your comps or they are
particularly eye-catching. Otherwise,
comps can go after the description.
Number six. Author bio. Fiction authors
should include any relevant writing
credentials, previous publications, or
education in their author bio section.
This could include any writing awards,
any creative writing programs you were a
part of, any short fiction or poetry
that you've published, or any well-known
writing workshops or retreats that
you've attended. None of these
qualifications are a requirement to
getting a literary agent, but they're
definitely worth mentioning if you have
any of them. Also, if you have
previously published a book with a
traditional publisher, no matter how far
in the past, you should mention that in
your author bio section. If you have
been previously represented by a
literary agent, you might also choose to
mention that in your author bio section
whether or not that went on to lead to a
book deal. Regardless, you will discuss
any of your prior publications or your
prior representation with an interested
literary agent so they have the full
picture of your writing career up to
this point. If you've previously
self-published a book, it's up to you
whether you want to include that in your
query letter or not. Some agents will
ask for this information, in which case
you would definitely want to include it.
If you can cite any positive reviews or
industry awards or sales figures, that's
a plus. Again, you would discuss your
publication history with any interested
agent before going on to sign an offer
of representation. In your author bio, I
also recommend including where you
currently live, as well as what you do
for work outside of writing, if
anything, just to give the agent a
better sense of how writing fits into
your life. And for professional
purposes, they will eventually need to
know where you are based. Your bio might
come out to be anywhere between one to
five sentences. And remember that agents
will not automatically reject your query
if you don't have a laundry list of
writing credentials or education. And
they do not expect a debut fiction
author to have a ton of writing
credentials. Number seven, the sign-off.
Your sign-off should be short and
straightforward. You don't need to
include any niceties other than thank
you for your consideration. Sign-off
with standard language like sincerely or
best and include your full name. You
don't typically need to include your
email address or website or social media
handles underneath your signature
because the agent is going to contact
you directly via the email that you used
to query them. If you're submitting your
query via an agent's form, they may have
specific fields for you to include these
links. Query letter variations.
Generally, there are very few
modifications to these seven essential
components of a strong query letter. And
following this format is going to cover
the vast majority of cases. That said,
if an agent's query instructions specify
that you include some information that
doesn't fall into one of these sections,
definitely go ahead and include it for
that agent. You always want to default
to their query instructions. Remember
that it's best to stick to this
tried-and-true formula rather than
trying to be creative and eye-catching
in your query letter. This can have the
opposite effect and actually turn the
agent off and make it more difficult for
them to find the information they need
to consider your query letter
thoughtfully.
that you would potentially move around
from the format that I just went through
would be the snapshot and the comparable
titles. Some authors prefer to put the
snapshot line after the description,
particularly if they don't have a
personalization section, in which case
the first line of the body of the query
letter, right after the greeting, dives
straight into the description.
Alternatively, some authors like to put
the comparable titles up at the top
along with their snapshot line if they
feel especially strongly about their
comps or it is part of the general
premise of the book. Tone. Remember when
I said at the beginning of this lesson
that writing a query letter is somewhat
akin to writing a cover letter for a job
application. One similarity is that you
should include a professional tone in
both. Query letters that sound overly
casual, that disclose unnecessary
personal information, that badmouth the
publishing industry, or that are
self-deprecating
could rub agents the wrong way. At the
same time, the query letter is not the
place for a high-flying sales pitch.
Don't oversell yourself by saying that
you promise you will sell a million
copies of your book. Or kiss up to the
agent by talking at length about how
honored you would be to work with them.
Be authentic, realistic, and humble.
Just be yourself. Length. In total, your
query letter should come out between 200
to 400 words max. That length might flex
a little bit depending on whether you
personalize or not and how lengthy your
author bio is. In general, it's always
best to err on the shorter side.
Remember that most literary agents have
hundreds of unread queries in their
inboxes at any given moment. And they
try to get through as many as they can
as quickly as they can. So, the more
easily skimmable it is, the better.
Agents are likely only going to spend a
few minutes reviewing your query letter
anyway. So, if yours is overly long,
they probably aren't going to read the
entire thing. Now that you know the
seven essential components of a strong
query letter, let's go through three
examples of hypothetical ineffective
query letters that reflect some of the
most common mistakes authors make. At
the end, I'll show you a revised version
for the same hypothetical book that is a
much stronger query letter. Bad query
letter example one. Dear Agent's First
Name, I am seeking representation for my
novel All Downhill, which has elements
of suspense, mystery, horror, romance,
and even a little humor. The book
follows Abby, who is 27 years old and on
her honeymoon with her new husband Matt
at a luxurious ski resort in the Swiss
Alps. They're having the trip of a
lifetime until they discover that
something sinister is happening on the
slopes. Three skiers have been found
dead. As the body count rises, Abby will
have to find a way to escape before her
dream trip becomes her worst nightmare.
This book is a must-read for anyone who
loves pulse-pounding thrillers with
shocking twists and wants to be kept on
the edge of their seats. This is my
debut novel. Thank you for your
consideration, sincerely Name. Let's
break down all of the problems with this
query letter. First, it doesn't have a
personalization line, which is okay, but
the snapshot line doesn't specify a
specific genre and instead mentions five
distinct genres. That doesn't give the
agent a good sense of where this book
could be placed on the shelf. Even if
the book encompasses elements of
multiple different genres, you should
still choose the most prominent genre to
classify your book under. This author
should also mention the age category
that they intend to be writing for. In
this case, the ideal genre
classification would be adult thriller.
The word count is also missing from the
query letter as well. Then, the
description does tell us the
protagonist's age and name, but it is
only three sentences long and otherwise
extremely vague. It doesn't give the
agent enough insight into what actually
happens in the plot. It begins with the
preparatory language The book follows
Abby rather than describing the starting
point of Abby's journey. We get no
insight into the circumstances of the
death or the specific obstacles that
Abby faces in trying to escape the
resort. There are no comparable titles
and instead the author makes some
general editorial commentary after the
description section, which isn't likely
going to be particularly persuasive to
the agent. While it's totally fine to
mention in your author bio that this is
your debut novel, this author doesn't
include any other details about them.
Ideally, this author bio would include a
bit more about the author's work and any
other writing experience and their
location. This query letter comes out to
just 137 words, which demonstrates that
there is a lot more the author could do
to bolster the query letter and provide
more essential information to the
literary agent. Let's look at another
example. Bad query letter example two.

Abby wants to leave the resort

My inspiration for writing All Downhill

While this is my first novel, I have

Given your extensive expertise in the
thriller genre, as evidenced by the

All Downhill with a top publishing house
a reality. Thank you for considering my
query, sincerely Name. Whereas the last

short, this query letter is too long and
too overly detailed. Let's start with

The genre, adult thriller, looks good as

letters, let's look at a good query
letter example. Dear Agent's First Name,
I enjoyed your client's book title and
I'm excited to share All Downhill, my
80,000-word adult psychological
thriller.
At the luxurious Grand Alpenglow Resort
nestled in the Swiss Alps, the party
begins once the ski lifts close. The
fireplace is roaring, snow is falling,
and drinks are flowing.
It should be heaven on earth for
27-year-old newlywed Abby Coulter,
except something has felt off between
her and Matt ever since their wedding 5

billionaire Rich Sterling and his French
wife Lisette. As they dance and swap

jealous of the couple's playful
chemistry, something she's always longed
for with the serious Matt. Their plans
to hit the slopes together the next

Abby and Matt see paramedics crowding
around the main lift with a stretcher. A

the circumstances look suspicious. Abby
is ready to pack their bags, but Matt
and Rich reassure her that ski accidents

One death could be an accident, sure,

across the resort, Abby wants nothing

ever came to the Grand Alpenglow. Then a

to find them before she becomes the next
target. But when Abby discovers a
shocking connection between the three
victims, the couple they've come to
know, and her new husband, she'll be
forced to decide if saving her marriage
is worth risking her life. All Downhill
shares the tense interpersonal dynamics
and atmospheric setting of The Guest

mystery style of Glass Onion.
I've taken two fiction intensives
through Gotham Writers Workshop where I
refined this novel. An avid skier, I
live near Denver and work as a pediatric
nurse. Thank you for your time and
consideration. Sincerely, Name. This
query letter checks all the boxes and
includes all seven essential components
of a strong query letter. It begins with
a strong personalization mentioning a
specific client the agent has
represented and includes all the
necessary details in the snapshot. The
description follows the three paragraph
structure, first introducing the
protagonist and their circumstances,
followed by an explanation of the
inciting incident in the second

comparable titles section includes a

and includes a reference to where they

In total, this query letter comes out to

below, so make sure to download it and
use it as a template for yours. But a
common mistake I see authors make when
querying is writing the query letter
once, then sending it off to every agent
they possibly can and never revisiting
or revising it. Instead, it's a better
strategy to send out your queries in
batches of 10 to 15 at a time so you
have the opportunity to iterate on your
query letter. This way, you can swap in
a better comp title that you find or
play with your description language if
you want to and see which version query
letter gets you more positive responses.
The last querying tip I'll leave you
with is also my biggest one. I cannot
overestimate the value of getting a
fresh set of eyes on your query letter
and on your manuscript for that matter
to spot things that you may have
overlooked and ensure that your book
sounds irresistible to read. I offer
query reviews and editorial services, so
check out my website in the description
below if you're interested in getting
feedback. I talk a lot about querying
and traditional publishing on this
channel, so make sure to subscribe if
you are hoping to get published. And
also let me know in the comments if you
changed anything in your current query
letter based on this course. Thanks so
much for watching and happy querying.

book deal. While some imprints of Big

have a literary agent and they get you a

commission on both your advance and any
royalty payments. To get a literary
agent, you have to write a query letter.

step-by-step. So, what do you do if you
feel confident in the commercial

publishing. It's mid-size publishers. As

plotting involves creating a detailed

middle and end of the story in some
capacity plotters may include a very

continually reference their outline so

plumbing will run and where the
electrical outlets will be in its room

narrator's voice for whatever reason or

for you to consistently write in their

character in close third person and they
added this second character and close

again because for a strong compelling

affects what information the POV
character or characters and therefore
the reader has access to at any given

within close third person or first
person you can play with having multiple

one character is aware of something that
another character isn't yet and that

omniscient narration you have full Reign

the characters themselves don't even

to talk about the reasons that it ruins
your novel but before I do so I want to

why does it ruin your novel the first
reason is that it prevents deep
character connections when considering
what povs you are going to include in
your story or not the question really
boils down to whose story is this who
does the story belong to the POV
ultimately is what determines which
characters the reader is going to be
invested in because we're naturally
going to feel most closely connected to
your POV characters the issue with head
hopping is that you are often scattering
the story across many perspectives I've
edited novels where we have 11 12
different povs in one single story and
typically in those cases is we're never
spending enough time with certain povs
to fully get invested in them and
thereby you are preventing us from
having deep character connections with
each of them a novel that on the flip

on a consistent basis is likely going to
feel much more engaging than one that
hops between a dozen perspectives
because we're going to feel so much more
immersed and invested in those
characters that the story truly belongs
to so when I'm working with clients who
are head hopping in their current draft

close third-person perspective rather

remember that your goal as the author is

exciting reading experience where the

Because receiving feedback and then

what's going to make it as strong as

the truth is that the feedback stage of
the process often takes much longer than
most writers anticipate. Having someone
read an entire book and take the time to
provide thoughtful, constructive
feedback just takes quite a while. It is
a very time-intensive and
energy-intensive process. So, if you
have sent your manuscript for feedback
either to beta readers, critique

even your editor at your publishing
house, it is likely going to take them
quite a while to get back to you. In the
case that you are working with a

weeks. If you're working with a beta

don't set a clear expectation for when
you are going to hear back, then you
might find yourself waiting months and
only hearing crickets. The best way to
reset your expectations when it comes to
feedback is to be upfront with whoever
you are sending your manuscript to in
asking for an estimated turnaround time.
But, even when you do that, I would
still recommend being quite flexible on
your end. Because, for instance, in the
case of a beta reader or a critique
partner, it's likely that that person
has a lot of other responsibilities and
likely a job that they need to
prioritize, and they are doing this
favor for you in their free time. So,
you do want to be understanding of that.
When it comes to working with your
literary agent and the editor at your
publishing house, the publishing
industry is just notoriously slow
moving, and the professionals who are
working in the industry are notoriously
very backlogged. So, I promise that it
is not due to a lack of interest in
wanting to work with you. Obviously,
your literary agent and your editor
signed with you because they want to
work with you on this story. It is just
a case that they need to find the time
to sit down and do it. And ultimately,
fit it into their other priorities that
they have at the moment. The next big
disappointment I see authors facing is
underwhelming feedback from friends and
family. The story you've written is
likely incredibly personally important
to you. Whether it is a personal story
in some aspect or it's a fictional world
that you have created, it's likely that
you want to share that with your loved
ones because it is such an important
part of your life and you've put so much
time and energy into it. But, in the
event that you do decide to share your

or family, I really recommend trying to
resist the temptation to put a lot of
weight into how they are going to
respond. Especially if they are not a

don't read widely in the genre you are
writing in. That's because I've seen

Remember that simply being in the

Awards can certainly feel good, and to

## Are Your Characters Cliché?

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0FvNw_bcp1U>
Caption file: 0FvNw_bcp1U.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Character
Secondary Topics: Story Structure

whether in books movies or TV shows we
all can come to recognize some cliche
stock characters these are certain
character patterns or formulas for
creating character types that have
become recognizable and familiar because
they've been used so many times in
different storytelling mediums often
they are used so much that now they come
across as a bit cliche or even
caricature-ish as a developmental book
editor I very frequently will work with
authors on their character development
to ensure that their characters are
coming across as realistic authentic and
that their objectives motivations and
desires are resonating with the reader
you want to ensure that your characters
are multi-dimensional so that their
character Arc is engaging the reader as
they move through the narrative and
experience the events of the story so
today I want to talk about five of the
most common cliche stock character types
that I come across in novel manuscripts
especially and talk about how you can
make these types of characters more
intriguing and unique if you have any
that fall into these categories in your
own book note that I am not saying that
you need to avoid these stock character
types entirely in fact you may already
have one or several of them in your
current draft and that is totally fine
it's all about recognizing these stock
character types and then ensuring that
you are doing everything you can as the
author to make that character unique and
authentic to your own story if you are
currently working on a novel and you
haven't already I recommend subscribing
to my channel every week I either post a
video with writing tips like this one
geared toward helping you strengthen
your manuscript and your storytelling or
I talk about the publishing industry
because my background is in the
traditional publishing world and I'd
love to have you around for all of my
latest videos I also have a freebie in
the description below for all of my
YouTube viewers it is my free story
self-assessment designed to help you
identify the strengths and weaknesses in
your current work in progress and
identify what you potentially need to
revise to take it to the next level that
is also going to sign you up for my
newsletter where I have exclusive tips
and insights that are not available on
my channel so now let's dive into the
first cliche stock character which is
what I'm calling the damaged one this is
a character typically the protagonist or
a main character who has some kind of
trauma in their past that they are now
grappling with in the present narrative
they have experienced something very
terrible whether the reader is made
aware of that terrible event from the
beginning or not and it is affecting
their current situation and their
headspace in many cases it is
potentially even overwhelming them and
it might be the main thing that the
character is dwelling on oftentimes this
ends up being a female character and it
can even in some cases be a Damsel in
Distress type character but it does not
necessarily have to be a woman now
giving a character a traumatic or
problematic backstory is absolutely not
a problem and in fact many characters in
many well-known and best-selling books
do have this type of struggle in their
background the key is that you want to
ensure that that trauma is Justified and
that it is coming through authentically
in the narrative it should be reflected
in the way that the character thinks and
acts and even potentially speaks in the
story so that it really feels believable
and like a part of their character
sometimes authors in an attempt to give
their character more layers or more
backstory they slap on this kind of
traumatic event from the past and kind
of stop there and say see I gave my
character depth because look at this
traumatic incident that happened but you
really have to see this element of their
backstory all the way through the story
and illustrate how it impacts the
character's world view and their desires
and their objectives otherwise the
character's trauma is probably not going
to feel authentic and they're going to
fall into this superficial Trope so the
way that you ensure that this character
is coming across well in your story is
to make sure that you have developed a
transformative Arc for that character
how do the events of the novel change
them for Better or For Worse they don't
necessarily have to overcome or fully
resolve their Trauma from the past but
we should see them undergo some kind of
development and some kind of Reckoning
regarding that past ultimately you don't
want this character to feel static and
stuck in this space where their trauma
and the problems of their past are
really overwhelming them the reader is
going to crave a dynamic character whose
backstory absolutely informs them and
reflects who they are today but isn't
necessarily the only identifiable part
of their Persona the next cliche stock
character is what I'm calling be perfect
savior this character often comes in
tandem with the damaged one that I just
described and they save them from the
characters trauma in some way kind of
like a knight in shining armor this
character is often a male character
especially if you have a damaged
character who is a damsel in distress
but it really doesn't have to be for
instance you could have a character that
falls into the damaged cliche who is a
veteran struggling with PTSD and then in
that case the perfect savior might be a
female love interest that enters their
life the issue with the perfect savior
is that they can come across as
unbelievable and inauthentic because
they are just too perfect they're always
doing the right thing they are so
benevolent and nice and they seem to
have no flaws they really swoop in and
save the day and seemingly can do no
wrong so how do you ensure that this
savior type character feels authentic
and is more interesting make sure that
that you give them their own personal
objectives and that those come through
to the reader what do they want at the
end of the day surely not the only thing
this character wants is to heal the
damaged character they need to have
their own personal drives and desires as
well let them be a little bit selfish
even in that vein try to illuminate even
some of the darker sides of this
character what mistakes have they made
what regrets do they have do they have
any unflattering qualities even
typically no character should be all
good or all evil because people aren't
that way so your character shouldn't be
either their flaws are at the end of the
day actually going to make them feel
more human and make your reader connect
with them even more the next cliche
stock character is the Wayward hero this
is a main character who is a lost soul
perhaps they are at a juncture in their
life where they have lost Direction and
really have no sense of what the future
holds or what they should do or where
they should go next they're ultimately
just lacking personal drive and lacking
Direction the issue with the Wayward
hero is that it can be difficult to
invest emotionally in this character's
Journey because their objectives are
nebulous and difficult to pinpoint in
fact they might even not know what they
want as a result we may not have a good
sense of where the plot is heading which
makes it difficult to get the reader
invested in the story so my tip for
making the Wayward hero more effective
is to give them some source of
motivation that propels them forward
even in a small way even if they're
overarching goals and objectives remain
unclear and they aren't quite sure where
their journey is going to take them have
them take some kind of small step for
instance if you have a wayward character
who just lost their job for instance and
they don't really know what job they're
going to hold next you could have that
event of them losing their job propel
them to move to a new city that is going
to give us some kind of plot event to
look forward to and will be intrigued to
see what happens when when they do take
that step of moving to the new city also
as the plot develops make sure you are
revisiting the characters objectives
desires and motivations in showing the
reader how they are transforming as they
are experiencing these new events are
they starting to find a sense of purpose
are they starting to be able to
articulate their overarching goals and
desires that's going to help us connect
with what they want to achieve and
invest in seeing if they do actually
achieve their goals the next cliche
stock character is what I'm calling the
domineering figure this is a figure
whose purpose in the narrative is to
holy Lord over another character's
decisions this could be a parental
figure like an overbearing mother or it
could be a spouse who is a controlling
husband or something like that the issue
with the domineering figure is when they
start to overtake the plot and the
reader can become frustrated if they
have so much influence over the main
character's decision visions and actions
they also tend to be quite one-sided and
overwhelmingly negative and are
typically presented with very little
backstory or redeeming qualities that
all feeds into them feeling more like a
superficial cliche than a layered and
complex character how to make sure that
the domineering figure works well in
your story is to flesh them out and make
them more multi-dimensional perhaps they
can be domineering sometimes but then
other times they can actually be quite
genuine and reasonable also try to
explore why they feel compelled to have
so much control over this other
character where does that desire come
from and why deep down are they lashing
out in this way I also recommend
experimenting with trying to show scenes
where you reverse some of the power
dynamics between the domineering figure
and the character they are domineering
over if the other character starts to
gain ground how does that impact the
domineering figure how do they respond
how do they feel that's going to unlock
other layers to the care character and
make them feel more multi-dimensional
the last cliche stock character that I
want to go over is the Epic villain
think of the Epic Villain Like a comic
book or a superhero villain they have a
singular very Broad and holy evil goal
like to take over the whole world in a
novel The Epic villain could take the
form of a political figure or a serial
killer for instance they have a very
lofty and delusional goal and they have
a complete tunnel vision and are only
focused on it no matter the costs the
issue with the Epic villain is similar
to the other stock characters in that
they can start to feel one-dimensional
especially if we don't understand what
ultimately is their underlying drive and
motivation that is laddering up to this
desire to achieve this lofty goal so the
key to making them effective in your
story is to help the reader understand
what deep down they are actually seeking
to accomplish with this lofty goal on a
basic human level what are they seeking
more of is it attention is it affection
or is it even validation another
consideration with the Epic villain is
to actually make their objective a bit
more specific and defined rather than
something so broad like taking over the
whole World perhaps they just want to
take over a specific City for instance
because they are harboring some sort of
resentment for those specific residents
often the more specific you are the more
the reader is actually going to be able
to connect with that character's drives
I hope this helped you think about how
to craft more Dynamic interesting and
engaging characters that come across
authentic to the reader let me know in
the comments if you recognize any of
these character types in your story I
promise it's not a bad thing in fact I'm
sure you can find these across so many
novels and other storytelling formats if
you're interested in more tips on
character development check out my video
on writing authentic characters I go
through some top mistakes I see in

literary agent with this book and they
reject your query, even if you do more
revisions to strengthen it and make it
better, you typically cannot query them
again with that same book. For that
reason, it is very, very important that
you put your best foot forward and make
the draft as strong as it possibly can
be before you reach out to literary
agents. So, you're referencing an
unedited manuscript, which does give me
pause. The manuscript at a minimum
should at least have gone through some
drafts on your own. Ideally, you would
have worked with someone who has given
you external editorial feedback, whether
that be beta readers and critique
partners or a professional editor if you
have the ability to invest in that
because there's going to be room for
improvement that you cannot see in your
own work, especially if it is a first or
second draft. What I highly recommend
against is sending out your queries and
sending out your pages without anyone
else having ever read them because at
that point, you really have no idea how
your story is coming across and if the
story is actually resonating with
readers as you intend. So, I definitely
recommend getting external constructive
feedback from a trusted source and then
incorporating that feedback and doing
some substantial edits on your end to
ensure that the story is as strong as
you can possibly make it. That's going
to increase your chances of engaging a
literary agent. That's all we have time
for today. Keep the questions coming. If
you want to be added to my queue, leave
your question in the comments here. This
is what I use when I'm going through and
filming these videos. And as I
mentioned, make sure you hit that like
button, subscribe, and download my free
story self-assessment waiting for you in
the description

determine if your ending is effective or
not after all you hooked the reader into
the story with this intriguing point of
conflict or tension that they were eager
to see how it played out and after all
they stuck with you throughout the
entire middle portion of the story
because they were invested in that
conflict or point of tension so now that
they have reached the ending they're
going to be craving some kind of
resolution now remember that resolution
does not mean that your story has to
have what we call a happy ending that is
not the case at all there are plenty of
instances where a sad or even tragic
ending also provides a sense of closure
and resolution the example i'm going to
use throughout the video today is the
movie titanic one of my favorites i know
it's a little sappy but i do love it i'm
a little bit obsessed with titanic
history overall that's a little fun fact
about me but the ending of that movie is
a good example of a resolved ending that
is not necessarily a happy one we see
the image of the elderly rose and
realize that she has lived a very full
life even though
jack her lover on the titanic has died
so it is bittersweet in that way the
ending is still however resolved because
we saw the full experience of their
relationship and their experience on the
boat which was the main plot conflict
that we were following from the
beginning of the story this ending would
not work well if for instance we never
see how their relationship plays out or
we never understand what happens
whenever the ship starts to sink now in
some cases it is possible to have an
ambiguous ending that still feels
resolved in this case it's important
that the reader at least understands
what the different possible outcomes are
for the characters in order to provide
that type of resolution that they are
seeking so they might not know for sure
whether the characters went down x path
or y path but at least they know it's
one of those two situations for instance
let's spend some time talking about the
next question to ask yourself to
determine if your ending sucks and that
is did i tie up all of the loose ends
remember that character that you
introduced way back in chapter four but
then they never reappeared in the story
or what about that subplot that you
followed for a few chapters in the
middle of the story and then kind of
dropped off by the end of the book all
of those loose ends should have some
sense of closure make sure that your
reader doesn't have any lingering
questions about what happened with that
character what happened with that
subplot because that's going to be
distracting at the end of your book keep
in mind that these loose ends do not
necessarily need to be tied up right in
the final scene or in the final pages of
your manuscript they can be tied up at
any point throughout the story you just
want to make sure that by the ending you
have addressed all of those plot threads
that were introduced earlier on in the
process of revisiting these loose ends
you might realize that maybe that
subplot or that secondary character
actually isn't necessary at all and the
earlier scene that introduced this point
might actually be better served if it
was cut from the manuscript i have a
whole other video on scenes to cut from
your book so i recommend checking that
out if you are interested in potentially
trimming the manuscript down the next
way to determine if your novel ending
sucks is to ask yourself has the
protagonist undergone some kind of
transformation think about where your
protagonist or protagonists were at the
start of the story
what was their age where were they
physically emotionally mentally
spiritually what was their state of life
what were their dreams and aspirations
and now as you're thinking about the
books ending
where are they what has changed in their
life for better or potentially for worse
in some cases it is possible that your
character actually has ended up right
where they began and that is completely
okay for an ending however you still
want to ensure that they have taken some
kind of journey that brought them back
to that place what i'm speaking about
here is ensuring that your ending
completes your character's arc from
point a to point b and in your ending i
recommend illustrating that
transformation by giving us an image of
what that point b looks like for your
main character or characters think about
the final shots of the titanic movie we
see the image of the elderly rose
passing away in her sleep and then
entering the afterlife where she is
reunited with all of the passengers and
jack who died on the titanic this is a
great way of completing her character
journey and showing where she is at that
final end of her character arc the next
question to ask yourself to determine
your ending effectiveness is is the
final sentiment appropriate take a look
at your final paragraph and your final
sentence specifically what is the tone
what feeling or emotion is that final
sentence meant to evoke in the reader it
could be for example melancholy or
optimism or distress even now that
you've determined what that feeling is
try to decipher if that feeling is
appropriate for the genre and for your
specific story is this sentiment in line
with the overarching message and the
takeaway that you are going for with
your story for instance ending with a
distressed sentiment might actually work
perfectly well for the thriller genre
where you're kind of keeping the reader
on edge and they have this feeling that
maybe the threat that you saw in the
story is going to return however a
distressed sentiment is likely not going
to be appropriate for a rom-com it's not
going to be what the reader expects it's
not going to provide them that sense of
resolution that they are seeking so
keeping with the titanic example the
ending scene of rose reuniting with jack
in the afterlife is appropriate for the
romance slash drama genre and it evokes
that feeling of tenderness and even joy
ultimately after the reader finishes
that final sentence and puts the book
down you want to make sure they feel
something and that it is the right
sentiment otherwise it's possible that
they could feel like the book was
unsatisfying or that the ending really
let them down and kind of ruined the
rest of the story for them which is
absolutely what you want to avoid the
last question to ask yourself to
determine if your book ending sucks is
did i avoid cliches now i'm guessing you
probably
didn't end your book with and they lived
happily ever after because that's a very
well-known cliche but there are a few
other cliche type endings that you might
want to reconsider such as having a
proposal or a marriage in the final
scene this happens especially in romance
and sometimes it can work perfectly well
but keep in mind that it is not always
necessary for the lovers in the story to
get engaged or have a marriage in order
to provide that sense of resolution for
the reader so sometimes it can just feel
a bit over dramatic in the thriller
genre maybe resurrecting the villain
could end up being a bit of a cliche
where we see that they have now
re-emerged from the dead or something
like that and are on the prowl to
potentially terrorize the characters
again again it can work in some
situations but just something to be
aware of a pregnancy announcement or a
birth is another common ending trope so
just make sure that the plot actually
warrants and asks for that development
at the ending and try to avoid falling
into these tropes or cliches just
because you feel like you need something
like that to happen at the ending
oftentimes a more subtle
ending is just as if not more effective
than one of these big plot developments
right at the end keep in mind that if
the ending feels overdone or too
predictable then you might end up with
the reader rolling their eyes at the
ending which is definitely not the
reaction you're going for as i said
cliches are not totally off limits by
any means we see movies all the time
with tons of cliches in them you just
want to make sure that you don't lean on
them too much
and that you are offering your own spin
on them that way they will feel fresh
and creative rather than tired and
overused i have a whole other video on
common plot cliches in fiction so go
ahead and check that out if you're
worried about falling into any of these
cliches i hope this video helps you
determine if your ending is effective or
if it could use some work to ensure that
it provides that sense of resolution for
the reader remember that it can be
