don't understand why they care about
making this decision or taking this
action it's going to be very difficult
for you to get the reader invested in
the story and therefore engaged with it
all the way through to the end we need
to understand the characters underlying
objectives in order to connect with them
and then want to see the story through
and see if they achieve those objectives
the next mistake that i see first-time
novelists make is what i'm calling a
bait and switch this happens when you
set up those critical first 50 or so
pages of the novel to follow a specific
character and you establish a point of
conflict with this character and the
reader gets really hooked in on that and
interested to see how that is going to
unfold and then at some point the novel
abruptly switches and actually we no
longer follow that character or that
narrative or that point of conflict and
it transforms into something else so
you've hooked the reader in on this
primary point of conflict that we
thought was the primary point of
conflict all the way through and then
that actually ends up not being an
integral part of the story and most of
the story follows something else or
someone else entirely this can happen if
say you introduce a new pov character a
third or half of the way through the
novel and then we follow them for the
rest of the story and never really
revisit that first point of conflict or
that first character keep in mind that
the reader is going to get invested in
whatever you present them at the very
beginning of the novel and that is what
they are initially going to consider the
main narrative and then because that's
what they got interested in in the first
place they are going to feel a little
bit cheated if that's not what the story
is actually about for the rest of the
novel so you want to make sure that the
first 50 pages are actually
representative of the story to come make
sure that you introduce those primary
characters that are going to make up the
bulk of the story in those first 50
pages now some writers might say you
know i need to establish a historical
background scene at the beginning of my
novel because that then informs you know
when i flash forward 100 years and the
characters are now living in this
totally different situation in cases
like that i really would challenge you
to try and bring in the main narrative
into the first 50 pages and maybe
integrate that background context or
whatever you're trying to convey
in that first section later in the
narrative to avoid this bait and switch
tactic because it really is risky and it
is possible that once the reader feels
like the narrative is veering off course
or veering in a direction that they
didn't expect they could put the book
down which is the last thing that you
want i would say in almost all cases the
primary true narrative does need to be
in the lead of the novel the next
mistake that i see first time novelists
make is underdeveloped character
relationships just like we need to
understand the primary characters
motivations and underlying objectives we
need to understand why their
relationships look the way that they do
in most cases your characters or at
least some of your characters will have
some kind of personal history that
occurred between them prior to the start
of the novel so it is important to bring
the reader up to speed
on what has happened in their past
whether they are really really close or
whether they have a fracture in their
relationship we should know what has led
up to the present state of their
relationship and therefore we will be
able to properly interpret the dynamics
that we see in the scenes for instance
if the protagonist in the present day
narrative clearly has a tense
relationship with their mother we should
at some point understand what has led to
that troubled relationship for instance
maybe you will reveal eventually that
the mother cheated on the father and
therefore the child now has a bad
relationship with their mother because
of that incident most novels include
some kind of troubled relationship
whether it be a parental one like i just
outlined or trouble between friends or
fights between lovers so anytime you are
conveying characters who are not getting
along make sure that we understand why
they have that tension and conflict
between them and where each of them are
coming from we should have a good sense
of what exactly they don't see eye to
eye on because then we're going to
understand both of those individual
characters in much more depth and
ideally you would show some kind of
growth across the course of the novel
especially if you do have some kind of
troubled relationship which most novels
have that doesn't mean that the
characters have to end up reconciling by
the end though of course they can but it
can be just as satisfying for the reader
to see the protagonist for instance
realizing that they're simply never
going to have a relationship with their
mother you know and coming to an
internal acceptance
of that what you don't want to do is
just
leave these tense unresolved
relationships just
out without any kind of acknowledgement
or resolution by the end because the
reader will be craving that kind of
growth trajectory in your character
relationships the last mistake that i
see first-time novelists make is having
a lackluster ending your ending should
have a strong enough sense of resolution
such that the reader doesn't have any
lingering questions and does feel like
they can see a difference from point a
when the novel began to point b now that
the novel has ended how have the
characters progressed have they changed
have they transformed or haven't they
and if they haven't what have they
learned or what have they realized there
should be some kind of arc such that we
are in a different place at the end of
the story than we were at the beginning
remember that establishing resolution at
the end of the narrative does not mean
that you have to have a happy ending by
any means the reader can get just as
much resolution if the character doesn't
set out what they had accomplished to or
what they had set as their objectives in
the beginning however we do want to have
a sense of how the main character feels
about where they are at the end of the
novel after the journey that they have
undertaken through the course of the
narrative so make sure to clue us in
as to how the events of the novel have
affected them one way or another
positive or negative something else to

not so you want to make sure you thread

to the end and
resolve each of them in some way again
it doesn't have to be a happy ending but

then when we get back to it we're just

so make sure that there is no extraneous

don't spend any time describing what the

flashbacks should be hyperfocused even

because you have to pretty much justify

show the reader a longer stream of
events in the past you don't want to

for far too long my next d for writing

an effective flashback requires a

into the main narrative so when you
first dive into the flashback to make
the transition super clear to the reader
you want to use a different tense than

you will be writing the flashback in the

dove into the flashback so make sure to

could be having another character in the

could see or hear or notice something in

action just make sure that this isn't
too abrupt and that you have tied up
your flashback neatly before jolting the
reader back into the present scene also
make sure that you reestablish where the
character is and what they are doing now
that they are out of the flashback my
next don't for writing a flashback is
don't disorient the reader what I mean
by this is that flashbacks have to be
very clearly rooted in a specific time
and place if we don't know where or when
it happened it is going to be very
difficult to register its significance
to the present narrative so you need to
clarify exactly where and when this
happened in relation
to the main narrative that we are
following throughout the rest of the
story you should also give the reader
any important context for when the
flashback took place along the
Milestones of that character's life so
we can see where it fits in on the
events of their life that we know
already happened based on what you have
told us in the present narrative thus
far so for instance in this example of
the character having a flashback of
their relationship with their late
mother you could say something like 2
months before she died she gave me her
wedding band I was 14 at the time and
still living in the Atlanta suburbs
we're getting a lot of great information
in those sentences first we know that
the mother gave the narrator The Wedding
Band 2 months before she died so this
significant event in the character's
life of the mother dying this happened 2
months prior so we can immediately
register the timeline of events and the
significance of this moment we also know
that the narrator was 14 at the time and
they were living in the Atlanta suburbs
so again we can compare that to what we
know about the characters present day
presumably they are some years older
than 14 now and maybe they were living
in a different place but now we can
register how old they were what they
were doing and when this particular
event happened in their life that's all
going to help the reader contextualize
the flashback and ultimately register
its significance and implications on the
narrator my next due is you do want to
describe a specific memory in your
flashback you want to avoid using a
flashback passage to describe repeated
events of the past or just generally
explain what was going on in the past
instead you want to focus on one
specific memory that then exemplifies
what the character was experiencing
throughout that time in their life it is
going to be so much more engaging for
the reader to experience this specific
memory this specific scene that you are
showing us versus you just telling us
this General description or expository
information about their past for
instance instead of saying something
more General like when I was in high
school every week my father would come
home drunk and scream at my mom you
should describe a specific instance
where the narrator's father came home
drunk and screamed at their mom and then
you can explain that instances like this
continue to happen once a week that way
the reader is going to register the
emotional impact of that type of
incident because you are going to be
able to describe it in more specificity
and detail by getting in depth with that
one scene versus just giving us a
general overview of how this event would
continue to happen over time my final
don't for writing flashback is don't
misplace the flashback passage one of
the biggest keys for writing effective
flashbacks is to place it right if the
flashback is misplaced then the reader
is likely either going to skip over it
or they're going to forget what is going
on in the present narrative typically
you don't want to include a substantial
flashback passage when there is a lot of
dramatic action happening in the present
scene such as during the middle of a
fight scene if you do that the reader is
likely so invested in the fight scene
that they're just going to skim over the
flashback to see how the fight pans out
because that feels more urgent to them
at that moment instead I would recommend
placing the flashback right after the
main drama of the fight scene or
whatever action subsides in the present
narrative because at that point the
reader will actually crave a little bit
of a break and a pause from the action
and they are going to be much more
open-minded to diving into those types
of Reflections because now the action
has kind of resolved and subsided so be
really strategic with your placement of
your flashbacks they can be a really
effective tool for giving your narrative
a nice Cadence and a nice flow to
explore the more emotional landscape of
your characters at those opportune
moments typically after a major dramatic
plot development is a pretty good time
for you to step back and dive into a
little bit more of that reflection I
hope these tips help you write stronger

ton of writing advice on the internet
that is frankly bad not helpful and in

my goal with this channel is to bring
you truly helpful and practical advice
that you can immediately start applying
to your manuscript and seeing results
i'm really passionate about helping
aspiring authors with actionable advice
and insights that strengthens your story
and helps you navigate the very
confusing publishing process so with
that i want to highlight five pieces of
writing advice that i disagree with and
frankly think is bad these are pieces of
advice that i think you should honestly
ignore and i'm going to explain what i
would recommend doing instead if you're
anywhere along the book writing or
publishing journey i recommend
subscribing to my channel every week i
either talk through writing advice like
this one or offer insights on the
publishing industry and i would love to
have you around so let's talk about the
first piece of bad writing advice which
is that exposition is the enemy a common
piece of writing advice is to not spend
time
giving the reader information about the
character's backstories or explaining
any background context about their
situation which is what we call
exposition because the argument is that
the reader is smart enough to figure it
out on their own and you should just
keep going with the story while it's
true that you don't want to spoon feed
everything to your reader and they
should be able to figure out certain
things as the story progresses some
amount of backstory is actually
necessary for the reader to get oriented
in the story and for them to get a clear
picture of the novel's world the
characters and what is at stake in the
story this is especially true for the
critical first pages of your book if
there is no exposition whatsoever it is
going to be very difficult for the
reader to get grounded in the story for
them to even get hooked and intrigued to
continue reading you might lose them
before you even begin if you don't give
them some sense of who the characters
are where they are what the context of
their situation is and what the conflict
of the plot is building to effective
exposition comes down to a delicate
balance of giving the reader enough
information to feel situated in the
story and follow the action of the plot
but not so much that you end up taking
them out of the story for prolonged
periods of time you do not want to
provide pages and pages of exposition or
even in most cases paragraphs and
paragraphs of exposition it really
should be woven throughout the main
narrative and integrated organically so
that it becomes a natural part of your
story i have a video on how to nail the
opening pages of your story so i
recommend checking that out if you are
worried about making sure you're hitting
the right balance of exposition in
action in those pages the next piece of
writing advice that i think you should
avoid is to aim for literary style
writing have you ever read a passage
that is just so dense with imagery and
s.a.t vocab words that it's difficult to
interpret what the actual meaning is you
can tell when a writer is trying to
elevate their writing and make it sound
more literary but remember that quote
unquote literary writing is not by any
means necessarily better if you have any
question on what i mean when i'm using
terms like literary or commercial or
upmarket i recommend checking out my
video where i go through all of the
different fiction genres and what those
terms mean trying it too hard to make
your writing sound literary can actually
turn into what we call purple prose and
that is when there is just too much
overly verbose or ornate language that
actually obscures the meaning of what's
trying to be conveyed this type of
language will also immediately become
distracting to the reader so i really
recommend letting your writing take
whatever style feels natural and organic
to you you can and should always work to
improve your writing craft but do not
feel the need to fit a specific mold or
to even classify your writing as
literary the third piece of bad writing
advice is to never write a prologue
there is a lot of debate in the author
communities about whether or not to
include a prologue and it honestly kind
of surprised me because when i worked in
the publishing industry the editors and
agents that i worked with never really
had an issue with well done prologues
they never expressed that there was some
kind of blanket ban on prologues or deem
them unacceptable in any scenarios my
view is that for some novels a
well-crafted prologue can actually be
quite effective especially if you're
writing historical fiction or thrillers
and teasing some of the plot action that
is to come later on but of course as
with honestly any scene in your novel if
it is poorly executed it is going to be
distracting to the reader and you should
not include a prologue just for the sake
of it so if you find yourself leaning
towards a prologue or feeling like a
specific scene could hook the reader's
interest right at the beginning of the
story don't feel like it's off limits at
all a good prologue in my opinion
actually really helps a lot with framing
the story effectively and hooking the
reader's interest to see what's to come
the next piece of bad writing advice is
that every story needs an antagonist or
a villain character now it may be
immediately clear to you maybe it was
even clear before you even started
writing the novel who your antagonist or
villain is and that is perfectly fine
and that is great however if you are
struggling to figure out who the
antagonist or villain is and it's
keeping you up at night don't worry
because your story doesn't necessarily
need a character that is an antagonist
or a villain it's simply not true that
every protagonist has to have an
antagonist character and actually some
of the most captivating and compelling
stories are the ones where there isn't a
character who is acting out as an
antagonist or a villain there doesn't
always need to be the single
identifiable person that represents all
of the evil and negative energy in your
story because remember that sometimes in
life not one thing or person can be put
to blame for everything that happens to
us sometimes there are stories where
characters are just grappling with
whatever life throws their way and that
is perfectly valid and that can be just
as captivating as a story that has a
clear enemy or villain you'll see
examples of both approaches in
best-selling books for example harry
potter has a very clear villain in
voldemort but a novel like the fault in

character in that case the characters

throughout the story again both
approaches are totally valid so if your

do not worry it might not need one the
last tip of bad writing advice is write

this piece of writing advice for a
couple of reasons i really don't think
your personal writing style or even the

outside of writing so i would personally

say
write the book that you want to write

to read i hope these tips help you
ignore all these pieces of bad writing

to open a novel in the hopes that you
will avoid them and find a more engaging
and effective opening to your story i'm
also going to read through some examples
of what these cliche or overused

be nice but i know they're not going to

alarm clock who could possibly be
calling at 3 44 am
he snuck out of bed quietly to avoid
rousing amy as he stood he saw the

in 1988.
he was pre-med and she was studying art

that this isn't really an effective

i could feel myself getting bored just

information to the reader all at once
particularly at the very very beginning
of the novel it's really hard for the

where you need to do world building to

a sentence or two of exposition or

it's really almost always a better

so this could look something like this

john woke up next to amy so this

kind of reveal that oh it never really

you can kind of lose your reader's trust

feel that there's a risk that you're

every story when it's broken down into
its parts is ultimately just a
collection of scenes so strengthening
your scene writing skills can really
help you ensure that you are telling the
most effective overall story possible so
today's topic is going to go through
some of my top tips for crafting better
stronger more effective scenes with
specific elements that you should look
out for in your own writing as well as
some helpful approaches to take and keep
in mind as you are crafting your story
if you are working on a novel if you're
interested in fiction writing if you're
interested in potentially publishing
your work down the line i recommend
subscribing to my channel all of those
topics are things that i cover in my
weekly videos and i would love to have
you around my first tip for crafting
stronger scenes is to ensure you track
the character's choreography now your
character should not begin the scene in
their bed and then all of a sudden
partway through the scene appear in
their driveway we should be able to
track their movements as they are going
about those movements throughout the
scene this is what is going to enable
the reader to visualize what's actually
happening as they are reading on the
page they will then be able to translate
that into a visual in their mind and if
you skip over choreography such as just
having the character kind of suddenly
transport themselves into a different
location then it's going to be jarring
to the reader and you want to ensure
that you avoid anything that's going to
confuse them and make them think that
they missed something now at the same
time and this is important to note you
do not want to overly describe the
character's movements in every single
little step that they take or micro
movement or gesture that they make
because then that is going to become
very daunting to read so you just want
to make sure you're tracking their broad
strokes movements so we can see how
they're interacting in their environment
how they are moving about the scene and
keep in mind your reader will be able to
fill in these smaller details my second
tip for crafting better scenes is to
ensure that every revelation has an
adequate reaction what i mean by that is
whenever there is something dramatic or
consequential happening in your scene
which in many cases there likely is
because you wrote that scene in order to
develop the plot in some way so whenever
that type of momentum occurs in the
scene you want to ensure that your
characters react to it now this is the
same no matter if you are writing in
third person omniscient close third
person or first person in all of these
different perspectives you should still
in some way register the character's
reactions before moving on with the
scene or moving on to the next scene
that's because if you have one of the
characters drop a bomb or something
really crazy happens in the scene and
the characters just kind of move on and
act like nothing happens or if the
narrative just moves on and cuts to the
next scene the reader is going to feel
like something is missing because the
reader is going to crave seeing the
characters reactions to this big event
so these reactions could take a few
different forms in the story itself it
could be describing the character's
facial expressions or their tones of
voice shifting whenever they hear or see
something it could be having them
verbally express disbelief or shock or
concern whatever that emotion may be or
if you are writing in first person or
close third person you have the ability
to go into the character's mind so i
really recommend leveraging that in
these moments and actually showing the
reader verbatim what crosses through the
character's mind whenever they encounter
this plot development or this dramatic
reveal all of these are going to help
enrich the story enrich our
understanding of the characters and help
us as the reader connect with the plot
as it progresses my next tip for writing
better scenes is to avoid melodrama so
we just talked through how to treat any
dramatic or consequential moments in
your scenes and in this tip i want to
expand on that by talking about what you
don't want to do in those moments you
ultimately don't want to overdo your
descriptions of the scene or of the
character's reactions because then that
can feel like it is a bit overly
exaggerated and it becomes melodramatic
and whenever you veer into melodrama
territory it actually then diminishes
the overall dramatic effect that you are
going for so to be more specific you
would want to avoid having the
characters use a ton of exclamations all
in a row even if something really
warrants that intense emotional reaction
in the vast majority of cases you can
really convey that through statements
and maybe one exclamation or two having
so many in a row is going to just turn
the reader off and it's going to feel a
little bit overdone another example of
melodrama is if you have the character's
facial expressions or their gestures be
overly dramatized you can think of this
like a soap opera whenever there are a
lot of people yelling and screaming and
kind of throwing a fit you want to avoid
that in your novel because you want the
reactions to always feel genuine maybe
you do have a character who is a bit
over dramatic in which case have the
other characters call them out on that
so the reader understands oh okay you
know this is not meant to be a normal
reaction the other characters are seeing
what i'm seeing and seeing that this is
kind of melodramatic something to keep
in mind is that the reader really is
going to be able to register the drama
of the moment if you convey it properly
you shouldn't have to utilize these
melodrama tactics such as exclamations
and extreme reactions by the characters
if you feel like you are leaning on
those a bit too heavily revisit the
scene and really try to convey that
drama more subtly because i promise that
it will come through to the reader and
it will be much more effective that way
my next tip for writing better scenes is
to clarify the character's emotional
states within each and every scene we
should have a sense of the emotional
states of all of the characters who are
present in that scene because then as
the scene progresses as those plot
developments occur we are going to be
able to track how those plot
developments affect each character's
emotional state and how they evolve from
the beginning to the end of the scene
for example at the start of the scene
are they feeling optimistic or are they
feeling upset or concerned or down on
their luck that is really going to set
the tone of the scene from the very
beginning and help set the reader's
expectations for what's to come there
are several different ways that you can
illustrate a character's state of mind
or emotional state throughout the scene
the first is to specifically call out
how they're feeling in the narration
particularly if you are utilizing a
third person perspective so an example
would be john woke up feeling sad you
can also convey their emotional states
through physical descriptions such as
john could barely find the energy to get
out of bed and lastly you can again
utilize the character's inner thoughts
if you are using close third person or
person narration and really just grant
us that inside access to what's going on
in their minds in order to convey their
emotional state so an example would be
upon waking up john thought i've never
felt worse than today through a
combination of those different
approaches and tactics the reader's
going to get a very strong sense of how
the character is feeling what they're
thinking in that moment and we will feel
that much more engaged with and
connected to the scene my final tip for
crafting strong scenes is to contain the
scene to the action so what i'm talking
about here is trying to cut down as much
of the fluff or extra material at the
beginning or the end of the scene so
that each one is really tight and
purposeful for example if the most
consequential plot development of a
specific day in your story happens once
the character gets home from work then
there really isn't any necessity or
reason to
explain what happened throughout their
day leading up to it you don't need to
show them getting ready for work you
don't need to show them going to the
office all of the earlier part of their
day can really just be confined to one
or two sentences a quick paraphrase of
what happened and then you can jump
right in and have the scene really kick
off when they get home from work
similarly you don't want too much extra
material at the end of a scene for
example if you are ending the day and
the next consequential thing is going to
happen in the following day you don't
really need to show the characters
getting ready for bed or going to bed
unless something significant happens in
those moments you can end the scene
shortly after the main action has
concluded and then pick up the start of
the next scene when the next major piece
of action is going to happen using a
little bit of paraphrasing to fill in
the gaps in between containing every
scene to just the main points of action
is really going to improve your pacing
because you're going to omit any of
those sections that really aren't doing
anything for the plot they're not
progressing the story further and
they're ultimately just acting as lulls
in the story so this is a way to ensure
that the action of the story moves
quickly and swiftly and you keep the
reader engaged the whole way through i
hope these tips help you write stronger
and more impactful scenes to convey your
story in the most effective way possible

## Common Mistakes When Writing Multiple Storylines

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kahUXqY2cDk>
Caption file: kahUXqY2cDk.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Reader Experience & Engagement
Secondary Topics: Story Structure, Writing Craft, Scene Craft, Character
Tertiary Topics: Conflict & Stakes, Story Structure, Character Development, First Pages, Plot, Book Covers, First Drafts, Pacing

one of my very favorite and one of the
most common novel structures is the
multiple storyline structure which is
where we switch between different plot
lines with each chapter or section and
follow the stories as they progress
simultaneously this could mean that we
follow different character points of
view across the same time period or it
could mean we're following the same
character across two different time
periods sometimes these storylines
intersect in some way and sometimes they
operate wholly independently
specifically if they're taking place in
different time periods it is perhaps the
most complex novel structure to write so
today i want to talk through the five
most common mistakes that i see in
novels written with multiple storylines
so if you're writing one of these or
thinking about writing one of these you
can check your manuscript against these
and ensure that you are fixing these
mistakes if you are writing a novel and
maybe in the process of self-editing or
interested in thinking about publishing
down the line i recommend subscribing to
my channel i am a professional book
editor and i upload a new video every
week with either writing tips like this
one or advice about how to go about
getting your novel published and i would
love to have you around so let's dive
into the first mistake i see with
multiple storyline novels and that is
switching storylines too frequently if
you end up switching between your
storylines after just a page or so of
text then ultimately the reader is going
to feel like we're getting jostled
around too much it's almost like you're
on a bumpy rollercoaster ride and we
never really feel situated in the
narrative we never feel fully invested
in the storylines because we're just
switching between them so so frequently
it's almost like we're getting some kind
of novel whiplash you want to avoid this
by ensuring that you really spend ample
time within each storyline so the reader
can really get situated understand the
characters and get invested in each
storyline before you move on to the next
one you need to make sure we get the
chance to spend a good amount of time in
each storyline otherwise the novel is
just going to pass us by in a blur the
next mistake is the opposite it is
switching story lines too infrequently
you also want to ensure that you don't
sit with a particular storyline for too
too long because this will ultimately
result in a narrative imbalance if we're
sticking with one storyline for a long
time then the reader is ultimately going
to sit there and kind of start ticking
the clock and wonder when we are going
to switch back to that other storyline
that we were also invested in we're
going to crave switching to the next one
and seeing what actually is going on in
that other storyline sticking with one
storyline for too long is also going to
have an effect on the pacing and make
the novel drag so a general rule of
thumb is if you have stuck with a
particular storyline for two pretty big
consequential scenes then it's probably
time to switch to the other one in many
cases you can probably switch to the
other storyline after just one
consequential scene so long as that
scene isn't just a single page as i
mentioned in the last tip now when
you're thinking about establishing the
cadence of switching between your
storylines you ultimately want to make
sure you are spending as close to equal
as possible
of the page time on each storyline so if
you typically switch every 10 pages try
to keep that consistent throughout the
novel as much as you can it's okay if
there are a few exceptions but try to
keep it as consistent as possible
because as the reader is reading they're
going to register that pattern and come
to expect it so any anomaly is going to
throw them off and it's going to feel
jarring at the end of the novel ideally
in each storyline you will have roughly
the same total number of pages dedicated
to each one the third mistake when
writing multiple storyline novels is
introducing a new storyline too late
when you have multiple storylines that
you are balancing you want to set up the
reader's expectations for all of the
storylines as early in the novel as
possible ideally within the first 20 to
40 pages you have introduced all of the
storylines that you're going to be
covering in the entire novel that's
because those first pages of the novel
are critical for setting the reader's
expectations for what the story is going
to include which characters are
important what plot lines we are
following and where the story is
ultimately headed so you need to signal
to the reader as early as possible which
storylines you are going to be switching
between if you wait longer than around
40 pages into your manuscript to
introduce a new storyline then you run
the risk of it feeling really abrupt and
jarring to the reader because you've
already spent all of those critical
first pages establishing the other
storylines and getting the reader really
really invested in those so to suddenly
have this other storyline thrown in is
going to feel really jarring the fourth
mistake i see with multiple storyline
novels is dropping off a storyline every
single storyline that you choose to
include in your novel must have a
well-developed beginning middle and end
just as you don't want to randomly
introduce a storyline part way through
the novel you don't want to randomly
just omit a storyline and have it
disappear with no resolution because
remember you've made the reader invested
in that storyline so they're going to
want to see it the entire way through
for the best balance when it comes to
multiple storyline novels each storyline
should begin at the beginning of the
novel and end at the ending of the novel
each storyline should extend the full
length of the novel and have its own
sense of resolution when you are coming
to the closing portion of the novel so
it's almost like making sure you are
sending off each individual storyline in
a very deliberate and clear way right at
the end of the story i'm not going to
say you have to tie everything up
because i don't think all endings do
need to have things tied up in a bow
however you do want the reader to get
some sense of finality and resolution
with each storyline toward the end of
the novel now the fifth mistake that i
see in multiple storyline novels is just
having too many storylines all together
sometimes when you've written a novel
with multiple storylines the truth is
that you've actually written multiple
novels in one especially if your novel
is over say a hundred thousand words it
is possible that you're trying to do too
much and bake too many stories into a
single novel and in some cases it might
actually better serve the story you are
trying to tell if you omit one or more
of the storylines it's something that i
see
a lot and if you fall into this boat do
not feel bad because it's almost like a
bonus you just have an extra novel on
top of the novel you thought you already
wrote so it's a two-for-one deal it is
an edit that i have made several times
when i am working on a structural edit
with an author and it's an early draft
of the manuscript we come to the
revelation that there really are two or
even in some cases three novels all in
one and in order to give each one its
due attention and the time it really
deserves you actually need to break them
up a general rule of thumb is that two
to three storylines tends to be the most
manageable for a standard length novel
however of course there are exceptions
there are exceptions in even
best-selling books out there so if you
have more than three storylines it's not
off the table i would just advise that
you proceed with caution and you really
ask yourself the hard question of if you
have multiple novels in one you want to
make sure that we are able to deeply
connect with each storyline and each
protagonist without the story becoming
overly complex and convoluted so just
think really carefully about why you
have the storylines that you do in this
novel and really ensure that they do
belong together and shouldn't be broken
up i hope these tips help you write a
stronger novel that engages the reader
from beginning to end through all of its
storylines let me know in the comments

as a developmental book editor one of the most
common elements that i am discussing with writers
i work with is the length of their novel and
if they should expand it or condense it and
i've even talked about novel length quite a few
times on this channel in different contexts so i
know it's something that's often top of mind if
you are working on a manuscript draft you might
be asking yourself how do i know what the right
length for my novel is how do i know if it's too
long or too short so i'm going to give you some
advice and some pieces of framework here in order
to help you identify the perfect novel length
now admittedly there is no one specific answer
but i'm going to give you some strategies and
factors to consider whenever you are thinking
about your novel length and if it perhaps should
change if you're working on a book i do recommend
subscribing to my channel every week i talk about
an aspect of books or novel writing like this or i
talk about the publishing industry so if any of
that interests you i'd love to have you around
so let's dive into the first factor that you
should consider when thinking about the optimal
length for your novel and that is genre genre is
probably the most important factor to consider
when you are thinking about your novel's
length because there are benchmarks out there
for every specific genre as to what the ideal
length is especially when it comes to books that
have been traditionally published so first you'll
want to think about the age range for your target
audience if you are writing a middle grade novel
they should typically be between twenty thousand
and fifty thousand words if you are writing y
a it should typically be between forty thousand
and eighty thousand words and for adult novels i
find the ideal range to be between 60 000 and 90
000 words when it comes to adult let's dive a
little bit deeper into the most common genres that
fall under adult fiction if we're talking about
thrillers or women's fiction what we also call
beach reads or book club reads those tend to
fall on the shorter end of the spectrum if we're
talking about literary fiction sci-fi or fantasy
then it typically falls on the longer end of the
spectrum and potentially goes over that 90 000
word count now anything shorter than 60 000 words
would be considered a novella rather than a
full-length novel so now you might be wondering
what if you have written in one of the genres
that i just specified but your novel falls out
of the range that i gave what should you do
then do you need to overhaul the whole thing
or give up your dreams for publishing no what i
want you to do is consider the other two factors i
am going to go over next now if you're struggling
to determine what your genre even is then i
recommend checking out my video where i talk about
all the fiction genres so you can start there and
then come back to this video and figure out which
range is really optimal for your book so now that
we understand the basic framework regarding how
word count aligns with your genre let's talk about
the next factor that will go into the length of
your novel and that is your publishing goals if
you hope to get your book traditionally published
by a major publishing house then the word count
is going to be significantly more important in
that scenario than if you are self-publishing
that's because literary agents and publishers are
going to expect that your book falls within the
standard range for that genre and if it doesn't
then you're going to have to have a conversation
as to why your novel justifies that shorter
or longer length so keep in mind that when
you query literary agents you are typically going
to put the word count in your query letter itself
and so if it falls outside of the typical range
for the genre you describe the literary agent is
immediately going to register that and it might
be a little bit of a red flag to them and that
is just because if the novel does fall outside of
the typical range it is considered an outlier and
it is ultimately harder for the literary agent
to sell a book that is significantly shorter or
significantly longer than the standard range to a
publishing house now why does the publishing house
care about the length that's because the length of
your manuscript actually has a direct correlation
to the production cost of making the book
physically a significantly longer book is
going to require more formatting work as well as
just physically more pages that will ultimately
affect the price that the publisher can set for
that book they might have to price it higher
than another similar book which then affects
their willingness to ultimately pay you as the
author through the agent if it goes on the other
end of the spectrum too maybe it is significantly
shorter then the publisher feels they have to
set a lower price point and they worry that they
can't make a profit on that book so all of that is
why it really is best if at all possible to stay
within the designated word count range for your
genre if you want to be traditionally published
that will ultimately increase your chances
of getting a literary agent's representation
and then in turn increase the chances that the
literary agent is able to successfully sell your
book to a publishing house so let's talk about
the flip side and if you are self-publishing
you truly have the freedom to publish whatever
length you want however that doesn't necessarily
mean that you should remember that you're most
likely going to have the most success if your book
follows the typical standards for whatever
genre it is for example if you're writing
a thriller and self-publishing i would not
recommend exceeding 200 000 words because
readers of thrillers just likely aren't going
to be expecting that long of a work and they're
likely not going to engage well with it also keep
in mind that you when you're self-publishing just
like i described that publishing houses do should
match the length to the price point that you are
setting books that are significantly longer should
be priced higher and books that are novella length
should be priced shorter but keep in mind that
that also will affect the readership and the
audience that you are able to attract because some
people maybe won't want to put in the investment
for a longer book the final consideration when you
are thinking about what the ideal length for your
novel is comes back to the narrative structure
of your story beyond the genre and publishing
goals that you have for the book there are two
key elements of your story itself that will
naturally help determine the length the first
is the time span that your novel covers is the
novel taking place just over a single day or is
it taking place over the course of years a longer
time span might but not necessarily not in every
case but it might correlate to a longer word count
the second narrative element that you want to
consider when it comes to length is the povs that
you are following in the novel are you following
just one single protagonist's journey from
beginning to end or do you have three interlocking
storylines the latter might justify a longer
word count now depending on how you treat those
narrative elements they will ultimately require a
different amount of space on the page that really
is unique to your own storytelling approach
you'll ultimately want to find that goldilocks
balance in your novel's length that is neither
too long nor too short but is just right and if
you are really struggling to figure out if your
novel is too long or too short or you know it's
too long but don't know what to cut then i really
recommend working with a professional editor
because they will definitely be able to identify
if the novel's length feels right and provide you
guidance on what you might do to correct it if
not i hope this helped you determine the optimal

setting but don't spend too too much
time describing the setting you don't
want to have pages and pages of
background information on the setting
before we really get going with the
story that said as with the other
techniques this one will work for any
novel especially one that has a strong
sense of place which i think all good
novels do have so let's go into an
example see if you're able to guess this
one
the nightclub is a temple devoted to the
sacred worship of indulgence
inside these walls there is no judgment
you'll find no populists no protesters
no spoilsports who might ruin the fun
the velvet ropes out front stand sentry
against all that
instead there are girls in fur and
designer silk swanning and preening like
exotic birds and men with diamonds in
their teeth
this is from pretty things by janelle
brown admittedly this one is not taking
place in a fantasy or sci-fi realm
however i really love how the author has
set the stage in this opening paragraph
and i think it is such a great example
of how you can use scene setting even
for a novel that takes place in our
regular world she takes the setting of
the nightclub which is something that
the reader will already be familiar with
to some degree but twists it and makes
it really intriguing with the way that
she describes it calling it a temple and
discussing the girls who are preeming
like birds and the men with diamonds in
their teeth you can immediately see the
setting see the people that are
occupying the space and feel immersed in
it and want to learn more about what's
going to happen there so if you open
your novel with scene setting like this
one see if you can describe the place in
a really unexpected way because that's
going to be what intrigues the reader to
keep going now is the moment that we

frequently
this can be a problem if you have a lot
of point of view characters
or if you have multiple storylines

and you're switching between them

is that instead of becoming interested

lines
the reader actually becomes interested

each of those narrative threads needs to

fully fleshed out authentic feeling

the second reason why your novel might

if you rely too much on action so

there should be an equal and appropriate

what i mean by this is that we need to

choreographically in a scene or you just

all the different actions the characters

to really help us understand how the

then that's going to make the story fall

novel but we cannot get inside their

unless you take us there so don't just

dive in deep and really help us

showing your characters inner thoughts
and feelings and reflections and

can take the form of something as simple

about what just happened so they're

which in novels are often italicized to

novel is one that has an equal balance

make sure you're not just giving us

to help writers strengthen their stories
and create the most effective and
engaging narrative possible. And a
question I often get asked is what makes
a novel successful and stand apart from
all the rest out there. As I reflected
on this question, which was really,
really tough to answer, I realized that
the novels that I respond most

at the top of besteller lists all seem
to have one thing in common. So, today
I'm going to reveal what that key secret
is behind every great and successful
novel so that you can make sure you
integrate it in your story. And one
caveat, I am going to say this is all my
personal opinion. This is what I feel is
the key ingredient to the perfect novel,
but it's not going to be the same
opinion that every editor has or every
reader has. So, feel free to let me know
if you disagree below and we can have a
bit of a conversation about what you
think that key secret is to the perfect
novel. So, after I reveal that secret, I
am going to walk through some examples
of how it plays out in some well-known
published books so that you can see a
real life example. Now, if you find this
type of content helpful or you're
working on a novel currently, it would
really help me out if you hit that like
button below so that YouTube knows that
this is the type of content that you're
interested in. And head on over to my
channel and check out my other videos. I
have a lot of writing tips as well as
advice for how to get published if
that's something that you're interested
in down the line. While you're there,
hit that subscribe button so that you
will get notified every time I post. All
right, with that, let me reveal what the
secret behind every great novel is. Drum
roll, please.
It is suspense. Now, it is a really
common misconception that suspense is
reserved for thrillers or mystery or
crime novels, which admittedly are some
of my favorite novels. But really, every
single novel should integrate an element
of suspense in it. The reason being is
that suspense does three really critical
things. First, it immediately provides a
sense of momentum and urgency so that
your reader feels compelled to keep
turning the pages. Secondly, it
immediately establishes the stakes of
the story. If there's really no
consequences to the character's actions,
there's really no reason for the reader
to get invested and care. So, you really
need to make sure your story has high
stakes. And then lastly, it's ultimately
what keeps the readers reading. readers
aren't going to necessarily want to
engage with a 300page novel unless there
is something that they're reading to
uncover, something that they're looking
to figure out as the story develops and
as they go through chapter by chapter.
So, now that we know that every great
novel needs an element of suspense, how
do you go about actually establishing
suspense in your novel? I'm going to
start with some common myths and explain
what suspense does not necessarily look
like in a novel. Suspense isn't these
cheesy cliffhanger chapter endings like
little did she know what would happen
next or a year later everything would
change. You don't need to resort to
those types of potentially cheesy
tactics in order to feel that you are
actually successfully establishing
suspense in your story. Suspense is
something that can be nuanced. It can be
integrated really seamlessly in your
narrative. It doesn't have to be called
out with those somewhat overt lines.
Suspense also isn't necessarily someone
committing a crime or someone
disappearing into thin air or someone
being murdered. Again, those are often
the subject matter of thrillers or crime
novels, but that doesn't mean that
suspense is solely reserved for murder
mysteries. Suspense could be something
as small as wondering if a character is
going to go to this college or that
college. It's just something that your
reader is looking for you to uncover.
and reveal as they go through the novel.
So, I want to cut any ties that you may
have in your head with suspense and
crime because honestly, when I was
starting in the industry and I was
starting to read novels every day as
part of my job, it's something I
immediately associated. That's really
not the case. Lastly, suspense is not
necessarily a huge dramatic twist that
we never saw coming. Novels like Gone
Girl that have really elevated the genre
of thriller may make it seem to a newbie
writer that you really have to have this
dramatic twist, you know, midway or 2/3
through the novel in order for your
reader to stay engaged and in order to
establish that element of suspense. That
is not true at all. Again, suspense is
not equal to a twist of any kind.
Suspense is something that can build
slowly and slowly crescendo over time.
It doesn't have to be something that
just is so dramatically slammed on the
reader. Now, that said, a dramatic twist
or some type of crime could potentially
be elements of suspense in your novel if
that is the type of story that you're
writing, particularly if you're a
thriller or mystery writer. However,
what I'm trying to express here is that
every single novel, even without those
types of story elements, still has
suspense, and suspense is still key to
what makes it successful. So, that's
really what I'm going to go through with
the examples I'm sharing in just a bit.
